KOBES, Circuit Judge.

 The City of Omaha closed the Yale Park Apartment Complex for building-
code violations. Yale Park’s owner AB Realty, LLC and tenants Kay and Janea
Anderson sued the City, Omaha’s Assistant Director of Human Rights Gerald Kuhn,
Housing Inspectors Scott Lane and Kevin Mulcahy, and citizens Hannah Wyble and
 Lori Vlach under 42 U.S.C. § 1983. AB Realty, LLC and the Andersons1 appeal the
dismissal of their Fourth, Fifth, and Fourteenth Amendment claims. Reviewing de
novo, we affirm. Meinen v. Bi-State Dev. Agency, 101 F.4th 947, 950 (8th Cir. 2024)
(standard of review).

 I.

 We describe the facts alleged by AB Realty and established by the exhibits
attached to or referenced in the complaint. See Miller v. Redwood Toxicology Lab’y,
Inc., 688 F.3d 928, 931 (8th Cir. 2012) (“[We] may consider some materials that are
part of the public record or do not contradict the complaint, as well as materials that
are necessarily embraced by the pleadings.” (citation omitted)).

 During the summer of 2018, housing advocates Wyble and Vlack started
talking to Yale Park tenants about their living conditions and took pictures of the
building. They offered to document building code violations, helped tenants fill out
complaint forms, and sent information about violations and complaints to the City—
which began planning Yale Park’s closure. Omaha’s Chief Housing Inspector Lane
applied for and received a warrant to inspect and search Yale Park, relying mostly
on Wyble and Vlack’s information. Lane’s application cited suspected health and
safety violations in 84 units. It contained factual errors, including a false statement
that Kay denied Lane’s request to enter and inspect the building. Nonprofits and
local media knew that the City planned to close Yale Park, but AB Realty and Kay
did not.

 1
 Janea Anderson is a member and manager of AB Realty, LLC. Kay
Anderson disputes his role in the company, but a state-court jury found he was either
Yale Park’s owner or building manager. State v. Anderson, 10 N.W.3d 334, 360,
362 (Neb. 2024). As the district court noted, the “plaintiffs routinely fail to
adequately distinguish between themselves as individual plaintiffs and the rights
they each assert . . . repeatedly refer[ing] to themselves as a group and blend[ing]
their rights and interests together.” Where their allegations and arguments overlap
we refer to them collectively as “AB Realty.”
 -2-
  The City executed the warrant on September 20, 2018. Police and housing
inspectors searched the property and tenants were forced to relocate. A few days
later, the City mailed AB Realty a list of alleged code violations, citing carbon
dioxide leaks, holes in the roof, non-functioning heat, exposed electrical wiring,
broken windows, faulty plumbing, and moldy circuit breakers. The City ordered
that Yale Park could not reopen until the violations were cured. AB Realty started
work on repairs but wanted to challenge the code violations and the closure of the
building. The City referred them to the Property Management Appeals Board, which
handles building code disputes, and AB Realty appealed to the Board in January
2019.

 Meanwhile the City mailed AB Realty notices of around 2,000 total violations
and prosecuted Kay for misdemeanor violations of the City’s property maintenance
code. After finishing repairs, AB Realty reopened Yale Park in the spring of 2021
and filed this lawsuit. The district court2 granted the defendant’s motion to dismiss
in part and stayed the case pending the resolution of Kay’s criminal case. After a
jury found Kay guilty on a few counts but acquitted him of most, see State v.
Anderson, 10 N.W.3d 334, 346 (Neb. 2024), cert. denied sub nom. Anderson v.
Nebraska, 145 S. Ct. 1331 (2025); see also Carter v. Ludwick, 139 F.4th 982, 987
(8th Cir. 2025) (taking judicial notice of related state supreme court opinion), the
district court dismissed the remaining claims.

 II.

 AB Realty first argues the search warrant was invalid because Inspector Lane
lied about asking for permission to enter Yale Park and falsely alleged that police
were called to the complex, that the City had conducted inspections, that Kay used
“threat tactics” against tenants, and that a gas leak caused an explosion. According

 2
 The Honorable Laurie Smith Camp, United States District Judge for the
District of Nebraska, now deceased, granted in part the motion to dismiss. The
Honorable Robert F. Rossiter, Jr., Chief Judge, United States District Court for the
District of Nebraska, dismissed the remaining claims.
 -3-
 to AB Realty this rendered the warrant invalid under Franks v. Delaware, 438 U.S.
154, 155–56 (1978), which made the search unconstitutional, see, e.g., Cronin v.
Peterson, 982 F.3d 1187, 1195 (8th Cir. 2020).

 To establish a Franks violation, AB Realty must show that (1) Lane
deliberately, knowingly, or recklessly made false statements in the supporting
affidavit and (2) “the affidavit’s remaining content is insufficient to provide probable
cause.” Williams v. City of Alexander, 772 F.3d 1307, 1311 (8th Cir. 2014) (citation
omitted). Probable cause for administrative inspection warrants “may be based on
specific evidence of an existing violation or a showing that reasonable legislative or
administrative standards for conducting an inspection are satisfied with respect to a
particular establishment.” United States v. Jamieson-McKames Pharms., Inc., 651
F.2d 532, 541 (8th Cir. 1981) (cleaned up); see also Camara v. Mun. Ct. of S.F., 387
U.S. 523, 538 (1967).

 Even excluding the information disputed by AB Realty, the warrant
application established probable cause for the inspection warrant. Lane wrote that
he received code violation complaints for 84 of the 100 units and referenced holes
in the building’s roof, untreated natural gas leaks, and Kay’s admission that he has
been “lackadaisical” in completing maintenance requests. See Anderson, 10
N.W.3d. at 356–57 (finding the revised warrant still supported a probable cause
finding in Kay’s criminal case). That was enough for probable cause.

 Pointing to state law that allows inspection warrants to issue “only upon
showing that consent to entry for inspection purposes has been refused,” Neb. Rev.
Stat. § 29-832, AB Realty argues that the warrant was deficient because Lane never
asked for consent. The Nebraska statute is beside the point; a violation of state law
alone does not state a § 1983 claim. Stevenson v. Blytheville Sch. Dist. #5, 800 F.3d
955, 965 (8th Cir. 2015) (“Section 1983 guards and vindicates federal rights alone.”
(citation omitted)); Holloway v. Reeves, 277 F.3d 1035, 1038 (8th Cir. 2002) (“[A]
suit under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 can remedy only a violation of federal rights, and so any
violations of rights guaranteed by local or state laws are irrelevant for present
 -4-
 purposes.” (citation omitted)). “[W]hether state law authorized the search [is]
irrelevant” because “state law [does] not alter the content of the Fourth
Amendment.” Virginia v. Moore, 553 U.S. 164, 171–72 (2008).

 III.

 According to AB Realty, “[t]he Defendants effectively deprived the Plaintiffs
of virtually all significant due process.” To state a procedural due process claim,
AB Realty “must demonstrate that the state deprived [them] of some ‘life, liberty, or
property’ interest” and “then establish that the state deprived [them] of that interest
without sufficient ‘process.’” reVamped LLC v. City of Pipestone, 163 F.4th 462,
466 (8th Cir. 2025) (citation omitted), cert. denied, 146 S. Ct. 2676 (2026). And AB
Realty must plead “factual content that allows the court to draw the reasonable
inference that the defendant is liable for the misconduct alleged.” Ashcroft v. Iqbal,
556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009). “[L]egal conclusions” or “[t]hreadbare recitals of the
elements of a cause of action, supported by mere conclusory statements,” is not
enough. Id.

 Reading AB Realty’s second amended complaint, we cannot decipher who is
allegedly responsible for what due process violation. Among other things, it alleges
that Wyble and Vlanch collected “invalid complaints” used to get the warrant; that
the City closed the entire building rather than individual units; that all the tenants
were evicted; that “Danger Closed” signs were wrongly posted on the buildings; that
Yale Park was not allowed to reopen before every purported violation was corrected;
that repairs were “delayed or impeded,” and that AB Realty was denigrated to
potential contractors. These scattershot allegations involve different defendants and
distinct interests, which change depending on which plaintiff is asserting them. See
Devines v. Maier, 665 F.2d 138, 142 (7th Cir. 1981) (discussing the difference
between landlord and tenant rights); see also State ex rel. Wagner v. Evnen, 948
N.W.2d 244, 257 (Neb. 2020) (per curiam) (noting the difference “between the
nature of rights held by an individual and by a business or other legal entity”).

 -5-
  Since AB Realty has failed to identify what constitutionally protected interests
are at stake, see reVamped, 163 F.4th at 466, and who violated their due process
rights and how, we cannot assess what process was constitutionally due, see Dover
Elevator Co. v. Ark. State Univ., 64 F.3d 442, 445–46 (8th Cir. 1995) (“Analysis of
either a procedural or substantive due process claim must begin with an examination
of the interest allegedly violated.”); Temple v. Mercier, 127 F.4th 709, 714 (8th Cir.
2025) (“[T]he extent of procedural safeguards required depends on the nature of the
interest at stake.”); see, e.g., Rochling v. Dep’t of Veterans Affs., 725 F.3d 927, 932
(8th Cir. 2013) (dismissing a due process claim because plaintiffs “speculative and
conclusory” allegations did not sufficiently state a deprivation of a constitutionally
protected interest), and we affirm the dismissal of these claims.3

 IV.

 AB Realty finally alleges that “[t]he City’s actions constitute an effective and
inverse taking, causing damage to AB Realty’s real property rights.” It is not clear
what that means. 4 Under the Fifth Amendment, there are two kinds of takings: per
se takings and regulatory takings. Hawkeye Commodity Promotions, Inc. v. Vilsack,
486 F.3d 430, 440 (8th Cir. 2007). AB Realty has not clarified which kind they are
alleging and, like the district court, we are not convinced they properly pleaded
either.

 3
 Since AB Realty’s claim fails the first step of our due process inquiry, we do
not address their additional arguments that the City’s failure to follow its procedure
for issuing code citations violates due process and that the City is liable for Wyble
and Vlanch’s alleged due process violations even though they are private citizens.
See Rochling, 725 F.3d at 931 (“A procedural due process analysis has two steps,”
and “[t]he plaintiff must first show deprivation of a ‘constitutionally protected life,
liberty or property interest.’” (citation omitted)).
 4
 If AB Realty means inverse condemnation, that is a state-law cause of action
to remedy an alleged taking, not a type of taking. See, e.g., Am. Family Ins. v. City
of Minneapolis, 836 F.3d 918, 923 (8th Cir. 2016) (discussing Minnesota’s inverse
condemnation procedure).
 -6-
  At times, AB Realty seems to raise a per se takings claim. The operative
complaint says

leads.caseName: Bethlehem Landfill Co. v. Lower Saucon Twp.
leads.text:
IN THE COMMONWEALTH COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA

Bethlehem Landfill Company, :
 Appellant :
 :
 v. :
 :
Lower Saucon Township, Lower :
Saucon Township Council, Priscilla :
Deleon, Laura Ray, and Victoria :
Opthof-Cordaro in their official :
capacities as elected councilpersons :
for Lower Saucon Township, and :
Steven Goudsouzian in his official :
capacity as Lower Saucon Township : No. 737 C.D. 2025
Solicitor : Argued: October 13, 2026

BEFORE: HONORABLE ANNE E. COVEY, Judge
 HONORABLE STACY WALLACE, Judge
 HONORABLE MARY HANNAH LEAVITT, Senior Judge

OPINION BY
JUDGE COVEY FILED: November 6, 2026

 Bethlehem Landfill Company (BLC) appeals from the Northampton
County Common Pleas Court’s (trial court) May 14, 2025 order (as amended May
15, 2025) overruling in part, and sustaining in part with leave to file an amended
complaint, Lower Saucon Township’s (Township),1 the Township’s Council’s
(Council), the Township’s councilpersons Priscilla deLeon’s (deLeon), Laura Ray’s
(Ray), and Victoria Opthof-Cordaro’s (Opthof-Cordaro) (collectively, Township
Defendants), and the Township’s solicitor Steven Goudsouzian’s (Solicitor)
(collectively, Appellees) Preliminary Objections to BLC’s Complaint for Sunshine
Act Violation and Declaratory Judgment and Injunctive Relief against the Township,

 1
 The Township is a second class township. On November 6, 1973, the citizens of the
Township voted to adopt an optional plan of government pursuant to the Home Rule Charter and
Optional Plans Law, 53 Pa.C.S. §§ 2901-3171, and to be governed under the Council-Manager
plan beginning January 5, 1976.
 the Council, and the Township Defendants and Solicitor in their official capacities
(Complaint). BLC presents five issues for this Court’s review: (1) whether this
Court has jurisdiction over this appeal; (2) whether the trial court erred by dismissing
Counts IV and V of BLC’s Complaint; (3) whether the trial court erred by dismissing
Counts I, II, and III of the Complaint when it was not clear and free from doubt that
BLC failed to state a claim therein; (4) whether the trial court erred by dismissing
Counts I, II, and III of the Complaint with prejudice based on an improper
determination that the Township Defendants’ alleged secret vote was properly
ratified on May 1, 2024; and (5) whether the trial court erred by dismissing Counts
I, II, and III of the Complaint with prejudice as moot based on its finding that the
BLC failed to appeal from the Council’s May 1, 2024 ratification motion. After
review, this Court quashes the appeal.

 Background
 BLC owns and operates a municipal solid waste landfill located in the
Township at 2335 Applebutter Road, Bethlehem, Pennsylvania (Landfill).2 deLeon
was a Township resident and Council president. Ray was a Township resident and
Council Vice President. Opthof-Cordaro was a Township resident and Council
member. Solicitor was the Township’s appointed municipal solicitor.
 In the process of obtaining federal, state, and local approvals necessary
to effectuate a planned expansion of the Landfill (Landfill Expansion), BLC
requested that the Township rezone 275.7 acres of Township land (the Property),
including the proposed Landfill Expansion area from the Township’s Rural
Agricultural (RA) zoning designation to the Light Industrial (LI) zoning designation.
In addition, because the Property encompassed in the Landfill Expansion was

 2
 BLC is a Texas business corporation organized and existing under Delaware law.
 2
 encumbered by two separate instruments in favor of the Township filed with the
Northampton County Recorder of Deeds at Volume 1994-6, Page 10281 and
Volume 1994-6, Page 102074 (collectively, 1994 Recorded Documents), that would
preclude development of the Landfill Expansion on certain portions of the Property,
BLC also requested that the Township release or terminate the 1994 Recorded
Documents to allow for the Landfill Expansion.
 On August 14, 2023, Bruce and Ginger Petrie, Andrew and Tina-Louise
Krasnansky, Robert and Elizabeth Blasko, and Robert and Cynthia McKellin
(collectively, the Petrie Plaintiffs) filed a complaint in the trial court seeking the
following declaratory judgment and injunctive relief against the Township and BLC:
(1) a declaration that because the Property is subject to what is commonly referred
to as the Donated or Dedicated Property Act (DDPA),3 BLC may not utilize it for
purposes inconsistent with the 1994 Recorded Documents without approval of the
trial court’s Orphans’ Court division (Orphans’ Court);4 (2) a declaration that the
Township is subject to the DDPA and may not rezone the Property in a manner
inconsistent with the 1994 Recorded Documents without Orphans’ Court approval;
(3) an injunction enjoining the Township from adopting proposed Ordinance No.
2023-05, that would change the Property’s zoning designation from RA to LI and
change a landfill and waste disposal facility use from one permitted by special
exception to one permitted by right in the LI Zoning District, without Orphans’ Court
approval; and (4) an injunction enjoining the Township from terminating the 1994
Recorded Documents (Petrie Litigation).5 The Township and BLC jointly defended
the Petrie Litigation.

 3
 Act of December 15, 1959, P.L. 1772, 53 P.S. §§ 3381-3386.
 4
 Under the DDPA, the Orphans’ Court has jurisdiction over donated property held by a
municipality in public trust for use as a public facility. See Section 4 of the DDPA, 53 P.S. § 3384.
 5
 The Petrie Plaintiffs initiated the Petrie Litigation at trial court Docket No. C-48-CV-
2023-6089.
 3
  On August 30, 2023, Council - then consisting of Jason Banonis
(Banonis), Mark Inglis (Inglis), Sandra Yerger (Yerger), Thomas Carocci (Carocci)
and deLeon - took three actions related to the Landfill Expansion. First, Council, by
a 4-1 vote - with all members, except for deLeon, voting in favor - authorized the
release of the 1994 Recorded Documents in exchange for grants of new and entirely
separate conservation easements from BLC on two properties formerly subject to
the 1994 Recorded Documents, as well as on other surrounding properties, totaling
approximately 193 acres of land. Second, Council, by a 3-2 vote - with Banonis,
Inglis, and Carocci in favor, and deLeon and Yerger opposed - adopted Ordinance
No. 2023-05, thereby changing the Property’s zoning designation from RA to LI and
allowing a landfill and waste disposal facility use as one permitted by right in the LI
Zoning District. Third, Council, by a 4-1 vote - with all members, except deLeon,
voting in favor - adopted and approved an Amended and Restated Host Community
Agreement6 with BLC. Thereafter, BLC filed with the Township its Phase V
Preliminary Land Development & Lot Consolidation Plan seeking approval for
Landfill Expansion onto portions of the Property (Preliminary Land Development
Plan). On December 6, 2023, Council, by 3-2 vote - with Banonis, Inglis, and
Carocci in favor, and deLeon and Yerger opposed - granted conditional approval of
the Preliminary Land Development Plan.
 In the November 7, 2023 municipal election, Township residents re-
elected deLeon, and elected Ray and Opthof-Cordaro to replace Inglis and Yerger
on Council. Before Ray and Opthof-Cordaro took office on January 2, 2024,
Opthof-Cordaro made clear her intention to reverse Council’s position on the
Landfill Expansion and to have the Township join with the Petrie Plaintiffs in the
Petrie Litigation in opposing the Landfill Expansion. Although the Township and

 6
 The record does not further describe the Amended and Restated Host Community
Agreement.
 4
 BLC filed joint preliminary objections to the complaint in the Petrie Litigation, after
the Petrie Plaintiffs filed an amended complaint in January 2024, the Township
neither joined BLC’s preliminary objections to the amended complaint, nor filed an
answer to the amended complaint. Instead, on April 15, 2024, Solicitor filed a brief
joining the Petrie Plaintiffs and intervenors’ preliminary objections to BLC’s
preliminary objections (Joinder Brief). See Reproduced Record (R.R.) at 155a-156a.
 At Council’s April 17, 2024 meeting, Banonis and Carocci confirmed
that Council had not, either in public or in executive session, voted on the
Township’s position change in the Petrie Litigation, nor did Council vote to
authorize or direct Solicitor to file the Joinder Brief. Thus, BLC objected to the
Township’s reversal in policy and filing of the Joinder Brief, arguing that either the
Township Defendants took official action not voted upon at a public meeting in
violation of the Sunshine Act, or Solicitor acted without Council’s permission,
which was beyond his power under Section 5-12 of the Code of the Township of
Lower Saucon (Township Code).7
 At Council’s May 1, 2024 meeting, Banonis and Carocci again
confirmed that Council had not voted on the Township’s realignment in the Petrie
Litigation, either in public or in executive session, before Solicitor filed the Joinder
Brief. Nevertheless, Council considered a motion to authorize Solicitor to ratify the
Township’s Joinder Brief in the Petrie Litigation (Ratification Motion). Before
Council voted on the Ratification Motion, BLC declared that because the
Ratification Motion was not on Council’s May 1, 2024 meeting agenda, and no
motion had been made to include it before the meeting commenced, Council’s vote
thereon would further violate the Sunshine Act. Therefore, BLC objected to
Council’s adoption of the Ratification Motion and demanded that Opthof-Cordaro

 7
 https://ecode360.com/6772414 (last visited Nov. 5, 2026).
 5
 recuse herself from voting on Landfill Expansion issues generally, and the
Ratification Motion in particular, due to her obvious bias and pecuniary conflicts of
interest.8 Opthof-Cordaro refused to recuse herself, and Council passed the
Ratification Motion by a vote of 3-2, with Opthof-Cordaro, Ray, and deLeon in
favor, and Banonis and Carocci opposed.
 On May 15, 2024, BLC filed the Complaint in the trial court: (1)
alleging that Appellees violated the Sunshine Act by taking official action to reverse
the Township’s position in the Petrie Litigation at a meeting that was not open to the
public (Count I); (2) claiming that Appellees violated the Sunshine Act by depriving
the public of the statutory prior notice of its vote on the Ratification Motion (Count
II); (3) seeking a declaration that the Joinder Brief in the Petrie Litigation was null
and void because Solicitor filed it without the express permission of a Council
majority (Count III); (4) seeking a declaration that Opthof-Cordaro has conflicts of
interest that preclude her from voting on matters related to the Landfill Expansion
(Count IV); (5) seeking an injunction preventing Opthof-Cordaro from participating
in any future Council vote relating to the Landfill Expansion (Count V); and (6)
alleging a promissory estoppel claim against Appellees regarding the Township’s
previous promise to release the 1994 Recorded Documents (Count VI). See R.R. at
4a-159a. Regarding Counts I and II, BLC asked the trial court to declare Council’s
Joinder Brief null and void, require the Township to rescind the Joinder Brief, and
enjoin the Township from re-filing it or otherwise taking action to reverse the

 8
 In the Complaint, BLC declared: Opthof-Cordaro campaigned on her position against the
Landfill Expansion; she is the founder and spokesperson for Citizens for Responsible
Development, a grassroots Landfill opposition group; she raised funds to fight the Landfill
Expansion; her parents own property they claimed in separate litigation challenging the validity of
Ordinance No. 2023-05 would be negatively affected by the Landfill Expansion; and she
conducted legal work on her parents’ behalf alongside their counsel, Gary Asteak, Esquire, in that
litigation. BLC claimed that Opthof-Cordaro’s parents have since withdrawn from that litigation
so that she would not have a conflict of interest in voting

leads.caseName: Devosky Hood v. Barbara L. Smith
leads.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
leads.text:
Rel: November 6, 2026

Notice: This opinion is subject to formal revision before publication in the advance sheets of Southern Reporter.
Readers are requested to notify the Reporter of Decisions, Alabama Appellate Courts, 300 Dexter Avenue,
Montgomery, Alabama 36104-3741 ((334) 229-0650), of any typographical or other errors, in order that corrections
may be made before the opinion is published in Southern Reporter.

 ALABAMA COURT OF CIVIL APPEALS
 OCTOBER TERM, 2026-2027
 _________________________

 CL-2026-0393
 _________________________

 Devosky Hood

 v.

 Barbara L. Smith

 Appeal from Montgomery Circuit Court
 (CV-26-120)

EDWARDS, Judge.

 On December 12, 2025, Barbara L. Smith commenced in the

Montgomery District Court ("the district court") an action asserting a

claim of unlawful detainer against Devosky Hood. Smith asserted that,

in July 2022, she and Hood had entered into a "commercial lease" ("the
 CL-2026-0393

lease agreement"), pursuant to which Hood agreed to lease from Smith

certain real property ("the commercial lot"). According to documents

accompanying Smith's complaint, on August 25, 2025, Smith notified

Hood that he owed her approximately $53,500 in outstanding rent under

the terms of the lease agreement and that he had seven days from the

date of the notice either to satisfy his financial obligation or to vacate the

commercial lot.1

 In his answer, Hood asserted that he had not been properly served

with Smith's complaint. He also asserted that he was not Smith's tenant

but, rather, that he and Smith had executed a purchase agreement ("the

alleged purchase agreement") in July 2022 for Hood to purchase the

commercial lot from Smith, and he attached documentation in support of

his assertions. Hood also presented a 2024 addendum to the alleged

purchase agreement that provided that Hood would receive a deed to the

commercial lot after paying Smith $53,000.2

 1Smithalso filed an application and affidavit for the entry of a
default judgment against Hood, requesting $53,000 in monetary
damages.

 2That amount was to be paid in monthly installments of $500.

 2
 CL-2026-0393

 On February 26, 2026, the district court entered an order noting

that it had conducted a trial on Smith's complaint but that, "[d]uring the

course of the trial[,] it became apparent to the [district court] that the

case involved potential equitable issues, in particular, a dispute over the

sale of real property, in addition to a one[-]page commercial lease." The

district-court judge observed that "the issues of real property" were

beyond the scope of the district court's jurisdiction, and he transferred

the unlawful-detainer action to the Montgomery Circuit Court ("the

circuit court").

 On April 2, 2026, after the unlawful-detainer action was docketed

in the circuit court, Hood filed in the circuit court a counterclaim against

Smith, alleging that the parties had previously entered into the alleged

purchase agreement, pursuant to which, he said, he had purchased from

Smith an interest in the commercial lot and had taken possession of the

commercial lot "consistent with a purchaser's interest." Hood requested

that the circuit court find that the "matter [was] a contract dispute, not

a landlord-tenant relationship," and that Smith had breached the alleged

purchase agreement by engaging in conduct that had "interfered with

and prevented [Hood] from performing under the [alleged purchase]

 3
 CL-2026-0393

agreement" by refusing to accept payment from Hood and failing to

provide Hood with receipts for the payments that she had accepted. Hood

requested that the circuit court order Smith to complete the sale of the

commercial lot or, in the alternative, award him appropriate monetary

damages.

 The circuit court conducted a trial on April 29, 2026. On May 6,

2026, the circuit court entered a judgment holding that Smith was the

legal title holder of the commercial lot and that Hood had defaulted on

the terms of the lease agreement. The circuit court specifically noted

that, in ruling on Smith's unlawful-detainer action, it was "declin[ing] to

address the validity of the Land/Sales Contract entered into between the

parties, whether [Hood] maintain[ed] a right to purchase the [commercial

lot, and] whether [Hood was] entitled to a refund of his earnest money."

Hood appeals.

 Although neither party has questioned this court's jurisdiction,

" 'jurisdictional matters are of such magnitude that we take notice of

them at any time and do so even ex mero motu.' " Hubbard v. Hubbard,

935 So. 2d 1191, 1192 (Ala. Civ. App. 2006) (quoting Nunn v. Baker, 518

So. 2d 711, 712 (Ala. 1987)). We conclude that the district court lacked

 4
 CL-2026-0393

the authority to transfer Smith's unlawful-detainer action to the circuit

court and that the circuit court's judgment is, therefore, void. We find

our decision in Darby v. Schley, 8 So. 3d 1011, 1013 (Ala. Civ. App. 2008),

to be instructive in this matter.

 In Darby, the plaintiff initiated an unlawful-detainer action in the

Shelby District Court. That court transferred the action to the Shelby

Circuit Court based on assertions made in the defendant's motion to

dismiss. Id. at 1013. The Shelby Circuit Court entered a summary

judgment in the defendant's favor on the unlawful-detainer claim, and

the plaintiff appealed. Id. This court vacated the Shelby Circuit Court's

judgment and dismissed the appeal, stating, in relevant part:

 "By statute, original jurisdiction over unlawful-detainer
 actions lies in the district courts. § 6-6-330, Ala. Code 1975
 ('The forcible entry upon and detainer, or the unlawful
 detainer, of lands, tenements and hereditaments is cognizable
 before the district court of the county in which the offense is
 committed.'). A circuit court may not exercise jurisdiction
 over an unlawful-detainer action until the district court has
 adjudicated the unlawful-detainer action and one of the
 parties has appealed to the circuit court. See § 6-6-350, Ala.
 Code 1975 ('Any party may appeal from a judgment entered
 against him or her [in an unlawful-detainer action] by a
 district court to the circuit court at any time within seven days
 after the entry thereof, and [the] appeal and the proceedings
 thereon shall in all respects, except as provided in this article,
 be governed by this code relating to appeal from district
 courts.'). Accordingly, [the plaintiff's] unlawful-detainer

 5
 CL-2026-0393

 action was not an action 'within the exclusive jurisdiction of
 the circuit court,' § 12-11-9, [Ala. Code 1975], and, therefore,
 the Shelby District Court did not have the authority to
 transfer that action to the Shelby Circuit Court pursuant to §
 12-11-9. Moreover, because the Shelby District Court had not
 adjudicated [the plaintiff's] unlawful-detainer action and no
 appeal from such an adjudication had been taken, the
 unauthorized transfer of [the plaintiff's] unlawful-detainer
 action could not transfer jurisdiction over that action to the
 Shelby Circuit Court. Furthermore, after the transfer of the
 action to the Shelby Circuit Court, [the plaintiff] did not
 amend his complaint to assert another claim that was within
 the circuit court's original jurisdiction.

 "Because the Shelby Circuit Court lacked jurisdiction
 over [the plaintiff's] unlawful-detainer action, the purported
 judgment it entered in that action is void and, therefore, will
 not support an appeal. See, e.g., State Dep't of Revenue v.
 Arnold, 909 So. 2d 192, 193 (Ala. 2005)."

8 So. 3d at 1013-14 (footnote omitted).

 Smith's unlawful-detainer claim, which was the sole claim Smith

raised, was within the exclusive jurisdiction of the district court, see Ala.

Code 1975, § 6-6-330, and, pursuant to Ala. Code 1975, § 12-11-9

(providing that district courts must transfer cases within the "exclusive

jurisdiction of the circuit court" to the appropriate circuit court), it was

not subject to being transferred to the circuit court. Hood's equitable

defense to that claim is similarly within the district court's jurisdiction,

as is his compulsory counterclaim that Smith had violated the terms of

 6
 CL-2026-0393

the alleged purchase agreement. Ala. Code 1975, § 12-12-30. Because

the district court did not adjudicate Smith's unlawful-detainer claim or

Hood's compulsory counterclaim, neither party could have appealed that

adjudication to the circuit court.3 Ala. Code 1975, § 6-6-350. Thus, the

district court's unauthorized transfer of the action to the circuit court did

not transfer jurisdiction over the action to the circuit court. As was the

case in Darby, because the circuit court lacked jurisdiction over Smith's

unlawful-detainer action, the circuit court's judgment in the action is void

and will not support this appeal. Darby, 8 So. 3d at 1014. Accordingly,

we dismiss Hood's appeal, albeit with instructions to the circuit court to

vacate its void judgment and to transfer the unlawful-detainer action

back to the district court.4 See Rimpsey Agency, Inc. v. Johnston, 218 So.

3d 1242, 1245-46 (Ala. Civ. App. 2016).

 3Hood's "statement of the facts" section in his brief on appeal
suggests that he appealed an adjudication of the district court. However,
the record contains no such adjudication. Instead, the record clearly
indicates that the district court purported to transfer the case to the
circuit court pursuant to Ala. Code 1975, § 12-11-9.

 4We note that Smith sought $53,000 in her application and affidavit

for the entry of a default judgment, which exceeds the district court's
$20,000 jurisdictional limit. See Ala. Code 1975, § 12-12-30. Upon return
to the district court, Smith must either waive the excess damages that is
seeking from Hood or initiate a separate action in the circuit court for the
 7
 CL-2026-0393

 APPEAL DISMISSED WITH INSTRUCTIONS.

 Moore, P.J., and Hanson, Fridy, and Bowden, JJ., concur.

portion of her monetary claim exceeding the jurisdictional limits of the
district court. Nest Two Ventures, LLC v. Capps, 295 So. 3d 1066, 1072
n.2 (Ala. Civ. App. 2019).
 8

leads.caseName: Maynard Nexsen, PC v. Cadence Bank
leads.text:
Rel: November 6, 2026 

Notice: This opinion is subject to formal revision before publication in the advance sheets of Southern 
Reporter. Readers are requested to notify the Reporter of Decisions, Alabama Appellate Courts, 
300 Dexter Avenue, Montgomery, Alabama 36104-3741 ((334) 229-0650), of any typographical or other 
errors, in order that corrections may be made before the opinion is printed in Southern Reporter. 

SUPREME COURT OF ALABAMA 

OCTOBER TERM, 2026-2027 

_________________________ 

SC-2025-0419 
_________________________ 

Maynard Nexsen, PC 

v. 

Cadence Bank 

 Appeal from Jefferson Circuit Court 
(CV-24-902787) 

SELLERS, Justice.
1 

1This case was originally assigned to another Justice on this Court. 
It was reassigned to Justice Sellers on August 27, 2026. 
SC-2025-0419 
2 

 In this permissive interlocutory appeal filed pursuant to Rule 5, 
Ala. R. App. P., Maynard Nexsen, PC ("Maynard"), appeals from a 
judgment of the Jeffer son Circuit Court denyin g Maynard's motion to 
dismiss or for a summary judgment in a legal-malpractice action 
commenced against it by Cadence Ba nk ("Cadence"). According to 
Maynard, Cadence's claims are barred by the statute of limitations set 
forth in the Alabama Legal Services Liability Act ("the ALSLA"), Ala. 
Code § 6-5-570 et seq. We answer the questions certified by the trial 
court, reverse the trial court's judg ment, and direct the trial court to 
grant Maynard's motion. 
The trial court certified the following questions: 
"Are Cadence's claims against Maynard time-barred under 
the [ALSLA]? More specifically , when did Cadence's claims 
against Maynard accrue under th e [ALSLA] so as to trigger 
the [ALSLA's] two year limitations period, and if the claim 
accrued more than two years before Cadence filed this 
lawsuit, does the [ALSLA's] six month ameliorative period or 
some other tolling or legal prin cip[le] save Cadence's claims 
against Maynard from being time-barred in consideration of 
the information contained in Maynard's evidentiary 
submissions?" 

 In October 2020, Cadence enga ged Maynard to provide legal 
services to Cadence in connection with an $8 million loan Cadence 
proposed to make to Assure Hold ing Company ("AHC"). Adams and 
SC-2025-0419 
3 

Reese, LLP, served as AHC's counsel. The loan closing took place on 
November 18, 2020. To secure re payment of the loan, AHC and its 
subsidiaries granted Cadence a secu rity interest in bank accounts and 
other assets. 
One of those subsidiaries was property and casualty insurer 
American Insurance Company ("AIC"). AIC insured properties in various 
states, including Louisiana. In August 2021, a hurricane caused 
substantial property damage in Louisiana. Determining that AIC did not 
have the capital to pay insurance clai ms that were made in the wake of 
the hurricane, the Louisiana Insurance Commissioner ("the LIC") sought 
to place AIC into receivership. Am ong other things, the LIC sought an 
order enjoining the enforcement of a ll liens on AIC's assets and sought 
the right to terminate or modify contracts entered into by AIC. In 
January 2022, a Louisiana court grante d the LIC's request, placed AIC 
into receivership, and enjoined cre ditors, including Cadence, from 
enforcing liens on AIC's assets. 
At some point, the LIC took the position that Cadence's claimed 
security interest in AIC's assets is invalid, or at least not entitled to 
priority, because certain government authorities had not approved the 
SC-2025-0419 
4 

loan from Cadence. Emails from a Cadence representative dated March 
16, 2022, indicate that Cadence was made aware of the LIC's position 
regarding Cadence's security interest at least by that date.2 
After the March 2022 emails we re sent, Cadence promptly 
intervened in the receivership action in Louisiana, specifically to protect 
its security interest in AIC's assets. Two days later, on March 25, 2022, 
Cadence commenced a separate action ag ainst the LIC, also in an effort 
to protect its security interest. Cadence's action against the LIC 
eventually was consolidated with the LIC's receivership action. In June 
2022, the Louisiana court entered a consent decree whereby 
approximately $6.2 million of AIC' s assets was set aside pending 
resolution of the dispute between the LIC and Cadence regarding 
Cadence's security interest. 
On January 13, 2023, the LIC filed what has been referred to as a 
counterclaim against Cadence, pursuant to which the LIC formally 
pleaded that Cadence had failed to acquire necessary regulatory approval 

2Unredacted versions of the referenced emails were filed with this 
Court under seal. Although, according to Cadence, the LIC has never 
formally pleaded that Cadence does no t hold a priority security interest 
in AIC's assets, the emails and other materials in the record make clear 
that the LIC had taken that position. 
SC-2025-0419 
5 

of the loan to AHC and, in additi on, that Cadence should be held 
responsible for insurance claims th at AIC was unable to pay. With 
respect to that particular claim, the LIC has theorized that, had 
regulatory approval been sought for the loan from Cadence to AHC, the 
loan would not have been approved , the appropriate authorities would 
have been made aware of AIC's financial condition, and AIC would have 
been placed in receivership sooner . This, the LIC has suggested, would 
have mitigated AIC's inability to pay the insurance claims resulting from 
hurricane damage. 
On July 16, 2024, Cadence commenced its legal-malpractice action 
against Maynard, alleging in general that Maynard should have advised 
Cadence to seek regulatory approval of the loan to AHC and the security 
interest granted by its subsidia ries. Cadence later amended its 
complaint to allege that Maynard fraudulently suppressed its alleged 
inability to handle the insurance-rela ted loan transaction. The trial 
court denied Maynard's motion fo r a dismissal or for a summary 
judgment, and Maynard filed this appeal. 
Maynard's dispositive motion in the trial court was styled as a 
motion to dismiss or, alternatively, for a summary judgment. It appears 
SC-2025-0419 
6 

that the parties submitted materials outside the complaint for the trial 
court's consideration in ruling on Maynard's motion. Among those 
materials are the above-referenced em ails relevant to the timing of 
Cadence's acquisition of knowledge of the LIC's position regarding 
Cadence's failure to obtain regulatory approval of the loan transaction. 
The parties do not expressly discu ss whether the trial court treated 
Maynard's dispositive motion as a motion to dismiss or as a motion for a 
summary judgment. See generally Rule 12(b), Ala. R. Civ. P. ("If, on a 
motion asserting … failure of the pl eading to state a claim upon which 
relief can be granted, matters outsid e the pleading are presented to and 
not excluded by the court, the motion shall be treated as one for summary 
judgment …."). The trial court did not expressly exclude any materials 
submitted outside the complaint, and both parties discuss the referenced 
emails in their respective appellate br iefs to this Court, although they 
differ on their interpretation of thos e emails. Part of the trial court's 
questions certified under Rule 5 asks if Cadence's claims are subject to 
tolling principles "in consideration of the information contained in 
Maynard’s evidentiary submissions." Based on everything before us, in 
answering the questions certified by the trial court for this permissive 
SC-2025-0419 
7 

appeal, we consider the material s submitted in connection with 
Maynard's motion. 
 Section 6-5-574(a), Ala. Code 1975, part of the ALSLA, provides: 
"(a) All legal service liabili ty actions against a legal 
service provider must be comme nced within two years after 
the act or omission or failure giving rise to the claim, and not 
afterwards; provided, that if the cause of action is not 
discovered and could not reas onably have been discovered 
within such period, then the action may be commenced within 
six months from the date of su ch discovery or the date of 
discovery of facts which woul d reasonably lead to such 
discovery, whichever is earlier; provided, further, that in no 
event may the action be comme nced more than four years 
after such act or omi ssion or failure; except, that an act or 
omission or failure giving rise to a claim which occurred before 
August 1, 1987, shall not in any event be barred until the 
expiration of one year from such date." 

 There is uncertainty in our casela w with respect to the statute of 
limitations in actions brought under the ALSLA. Specifically, the Court 
has not settled on a clear standard as to when the limitations period 
begins to run. According to the Co urt in Fox v. Hughston, 382 So. 3d 
1207, 1212 (Ala. 2023): 
"[T]here is a split of authority in our caselaw concerning when 
the statute-of-limitations period for a legal-malpractice action 
will begin to run. On the on e hand, our caselaw has applied 
the 'damage' approach, under which the limitations period 
begins to run from the date on which the client bringing the 
legal-malpractice action first su stained an injury or damage. 
On the other hand, our case law also has applied the 
SC-2025-0419 
8 

'occurrence' approach, under which the limitations period 
begins to run from the date on which the ac t or omission 
giving rise to the claim occurred and not when the client first 
suffered damage."3 

The Court in Fox concluded that, under either the occurrence rule 
or the damage rule, the limitations period applicable to the plaintiff's 
ALSLA claim in Fox had expired. S ee also Ex parte Seabol, 782 So. 2d 
212, 214 (Ala. 2000) ("Under § 6-5-574, 'a legal-malpractice cause of 
action accrues, and the statute-of-limitations period begins to run, when 
"the act or omission or failure giving rise to the claim" occurs, and not 
when the client first suffers ac tual damage.' Ex parte Panell, 756 So. 2d 
862, 868 (Ala. 1999)."); Floyd v. Massey & Stotser, P.C., 807 So. 2d 508 
(Ala. 2001) (applying both the occurren ce rule and the damage rule in 
concluding that the limitations period had expired); Dennis v. Northcutt, 
887 So. 2d 219 (Ala. 2004) (plurality op inion) (applying the occurrence 
rule); Denbo v. DeBray, 968 So. 2d 983 (Ala. 2006) (applying both the 
occurrence rule and the damage rule in concluding that the limitations 

3The "damage" rule might also be re ferred to as the "accrual" rule. 
See Fox v. Hughston, 382 So. 3d 1207, 1218 (Ala. 2023) (Parker, C.J., 
concurring in part and concurring in the result) (noting that the two 
terms have been used interchangeably). 

SC-2025-0419 
9 

period had expired); Coilplus-Alabama, Inc. v. Vann, 53 So. 3d 898 (Ala. 
2010) (same). 
 "To discern the legislative intent, the Court must first look to the 
language of the statute. If, giving the statutory language its plain and 
ordinary meaning, we conclude that the language is unambiguous, there 
is no room for judicial construction." City of Bessemer v. McClain, 957 
So. 2d 1061, 1074 (Ala. 2006). The language of 6-5-574(a) is clear that a 
claim under the ALSLA must be commenced "within two years after the 
act or omission or failure giving rise to the claim." In Fox, supra, two 
Justices wrote specially to urge the Court to adopt the occurrence rule as 
faithfully applying the plain language of § 6-5-574(a). 382 So. 3d at 1218 
(Mitchell, J., concurring in the resu lt) ("[T]he Court should clarify this 
area of the law and definitively hold that the occurrence approach, not 
the damage approach, is required by the statute's text."); id. (Parker, C.J., 
concurring in part and concurring in the result) (noting that the damage 
rule "directly contradicts" the lang uage in § 6-5-574(a) and stating that 
"this Court should establish, without further delay, that the occurrence 
rule is the only correct interpretation of the two-y

leads.caseName: Huset v. EIS Ultimate Holding, LP
leads.text:
SUMMARY 
November 5, 2026 

2026 COA 81 

No. 25CA1935, Huset v. EIS Ultimate Holding, LP — Labor and 
Industry — Covenants Not to Compete — Attempt to Enforce 
Covenant That is Void 

Section 8-2-113, C.R.S. 2026, governs covenants not to 
compete between an employer and an employee. The statute 
generally provides, subject to certain exceptions, that “a covenant 
not to compete that restricts the right of an individual to receive 
compensation for performance of labor is void.” § 8-2-113(2)(a). 
In 2022 the General Assembly adopted H.B. 22-1317. It 
added section 8-2-113(8)(a), which now states that “[a]n employer 
shall not enter into, present to a worker or prospective worker as a 
term of employment, or attempt to enforce any covenant that is void 
under this section.” H.B. 22-1317 stated, “This act applies to 
covenants not to compete entered into or renewed on or after the 
The summaries of the Colorado Court of Appeals published opinions 
constitute no part of the opinion of the division but have been prepared by 
the division for the convenience of the reader. The summaries may not be 
cited or relied upon as they are not the official language of the division. 
Any discrepancy between the language in the summary and in the opinion 
should be resolved in favor of the language in the opinion. 

applicable effective date of this act.” Ch. 441, sec. 2(2), 2022 Colo. 
Sess. Laws 3099. 
Section 8-2-113(8)(b), which was also created by H.B. 22-
1317, states that “[a]n employer that violates subsection (8)(a) of 
this section is liable for actual damages and a penalty of five 
thousand dollars per worker or prospective worker harmed by the 
conduct.” For the first time in a published Colorado opinion, a 
division of the court of appeals addresses whether the bar against 
attempting “to enforce any covenant that is void under this section” 
applies to an effort to enforce a restrictive covenant that was 
entered into before the adoption of section 8-2-113(8)(a) and (b) and 
was void under the statute as it existed before and after the 2022 
amendments. The division concludes that the clause of section 8-2-
113(8)(a) prohibiting an “attempt to enforce any covenant that is 
void under this section” and the remedies contained in section 8-2-
113(8)(b) apply to a covenant not to compete that was void when 
adopted if the employer attempts to enforce the void covenant after 
the act’s effective date. 

COLORADO COURT OF APPEALS 2026 COA 81 

Court of Appeals No. 25CA1935 
Weld County District Court No. 23CV30661 
Honorable Shannon Lyons, Judge 

Scott Huset and Impact Industrial Services, LLC, a Colorado limited liability 
company, 

Plaintiffs-Appellees, 

v. 

EIS Ultimate Holding, LP, a Delaware limited partnership; EIS Operating 
Enterprises, LLC, a Delaware limited liability company; and Earth Services & 
Abatement, LLC, a Colorado limited liability company, 

Defendants-Appellants. 

JUDGMENT AFFIRMED AND CASE 
REMANDED WITH DIRECTIONS 

Division III 
Opinion by JUDGE SCHUTZ 
Dunn and Berger*, JJ., concur 

Announced November 5, 2026 

Venable LLP, Emily F. Keimig, Carissa J. Davis, Denver, Colorado, for 
Plaintiffs-Appellees 

Kutak Rock LLP, Thomas W. Snyder, Reid A. Page, Denver, Colorado, for 
Defendants-Appellants 

*Sitting by assignment of the Chief Justice under provisions of Colo. Const. art. 
VI, § 5(3), and § 24-51-1105, C.R.S. 2026. 

1 
¶ 1 Defendants, EIS Ultimate Holding, LP and EIS Operating 
Enterprises, LLC (collectively, EIS) and Earth Services & Abatement, 
LLC (ESA), appeal the trial court’s entry of a declaratory judgment 
requested by plaintiffs, Scott Huset and Impact Industrial Services, 
LLC (Impact). Defendants contend that the trial court erred by 
denying their motion to dismiss and compel arbitration, by denying 
their motion to dismiss the case as moot, and by making various 
factual findings, evidentiary rulings, and legal conclusions. We 
affirm. 
I. Factual Background 
¶ 2 The factual and procedural history of this case is lengthy. We 
begin with a brief description of the parties’ organizational 
structures and their relationships. 
¶ 3 Brothers Kory and Kristian Mitchell founded ESA in 2006; 
they each owned 50% of the company. ESA provided asbestos 
abatement, demolition, and soil and water remediation services. 
¶ 4 Huset began working for ESA in 2009 when it was still a small 
business. He started as a project manager for soil remediation 
projects and then became a superintendent, project manager, 
senior project manager, and — beginning in July 2021 — 

2 
operations manager. However, the court determined that Huset’s 
job duties were most closely aligned with that of a senior project 
manager. 
¶ 5 In 2019, the Mitchell brothers sold their majority interest in 
ESA to EIS (or its predecessor), a holding company owned by the 
Mitchells and several other investors and small business owners. 
Kory Mitchell testified that, aside from ownership, “nothing really 
changed at that point from a corporate structure” for ESA. 
¶ 6 EIS continued to own and control ESA. EIS also owned and 
oversaw several environmental service companies across the 
country. The trial court noted that there was some uncertainty 
regarding the particular subsidiaries that are held under the EIS 
umbrella. 
¶ 7 Huset did not work for any EIS entities other than ESA. While 
working for ESA, Huset signed a “Management Incentive Unit Grant 
Agreement” (agreement), which contains both trade secret and 
related noncompete provisions, as well as an arbitration 
requirement. 

3 
¶ 8 These lengthy provisions are set forth in section six of the 
agreement (the restrictive covenants). Section 6(a) contains a 
confidentiality restriction that provides as follows: 
During the course of [Huset’s] employment 
with or other service to the Partnership 
Group[1], [Huset] has learned and will continue 
to learn confidential information of the 
Partnership Group. [Huset] acknowledges the 
time and expense incurred by the Partnership 
Group in connection with developing 
proprietary and confidential information in 
connection with the Partnership Group’s 
business and operations. [Huset] agrees that 
[Huset] will not, whether during [Huset’s] 
service as an employee or service provider of 
the Partnership Group or at any time 
thereafter, divulge, communicate, or use to the 
detriment of any member of the Partnership 
Group or any of its Affiliates or any other 
person, firm or entity, confidential information 
or trade secrets relating to any member of the 
Partnership Group or its Affiliates, including, 
without limitation, business strategies, 
operating plans, acquisition strategies 
(including the identities of (and any other 
information concerning) possible acquisition 
candidates), financial information, market 
analyses, acquisition terms and conditions, 
personnel information, know-how, customer 
lists and relationships, supplier lists and 
relationships, or other non-public proprietary 

1 The agreement defines Partnership Group as “collectively, the 
Partnership and each of its Subsidiaries.” It uses Partnership to 
refer to EIS Ultimate Holding, LP; but does not define 
“Subsidiaries.” 

4 
and confidential information relating to any 
member of the Partnership Group or its 
Affiliates. The foregoing confidentiality 
agreement shall not apply if [Huset] can show 
that the communication (i) is required in the 
course of performing [Huset’s] duties as an 
employee or service provider of the Partnership 
Group, (ii) is made with the General Partner’s 
written consent, (iii) relates to information that 
is or becomes generally known by the public 
other than as a result of a breach hereof, or (iv) 
is required by law or judicial or administrative 
process. 
¶ 9 Section 6(a)(iv) of the agreement provides that Huset, for the 
duration of his employment at ESA and the following two years, 
shall not 
directly or indirectly engage in, or serve as a 
principal, partner, joint venturer, member, 
manager, trustee, agent, stockholder, equity 
holder, director, officer, or employee of, advisor 
to, or in any other capacity or in any other 
manner, own, control, manage, operate, or 
otherwise participate, invest, or have any 
interest in, or be connected with, any person, 
firm, or entity that engages in any activity 
which competes directly or indirectly with any 
business of the Partnership Group anywhere 
within the United States, or in any other 
country where the Partnership group conducts 
or actively proposes to conduct business at 
any time within the two-year period 
immediately preceding the termination of 
[Huset’s] service as an employee . . . if in 
connection with any of the foregoing, [Huset] 
has been or would be required to (or does) 

5 
employ, reveal, or otherwise utilize trade 
secrets used by the Partnership Group before 
Huset’s termination. 
¶ 10 In March 2023, Huset, along with his business partner, Jeff 
Wright, started Impact. Wright owned 65% of Impact; Huset owned 
the remaining 35% and was Impact’s only other employee. Impact 
began as a trucking brokerage company; the trial court found that 
ESA is not a trucking broker and that Huset and Impact’s work 
does not compete with the defendants’ interests.2 In May 2023, 
Huset left ESA to work full-time for Impact. Shortly after Huset’s 
resignation from ESA, the defendants sent him three demand 
letters stating their intent to enforce the restrictive covenants. The 
third letter was also sent to Wright.3 
II. Procedural History 
¶ 11 The plaintiffs filed suit against the defendants in August 2023, 
two days after receiving the third demand letter. The complaint 
included a request that the trial court declare the restrictive 

2 The terms “trucking brokerage” and “trucking broker” appear 
throughout the record but are not precisely defined. The trial court 
ultimately found that Impact’s services do not compete with those 
provided by ESA. 
3 Wright was not a party to the underlying litigation and thus is not 
a party to this appeal. 

6 
covenants void under section 8-2-113(7), C.R.S. 2026, which states, 
“A worker who is a party to a covenant not to compete, or a 
subsequent employer that has hired or is considering hiring the 
worker, may seek a declaratory judgment from a court of competent 
jurisdiction or an arbitrator that the covenant not to compete is 
unenforceable.” In addition to declaratory relief, the plaintiffs 
requested an award of damages, prejudgment interest, penalties, 
and their attorney fees and costs under section 8-2-113(8)(b). The 
plaintiffs also asserted a claim, and requested the same relief, 
under section 8-2-113(1.5)(a), which states, “It is unlawful to use 
force, threats, or other means of intimidation to prevent any person 
from engaging in any lawful occupation at any place the person 
sees fit.” 
¶ 12 In September 2023, the defendants filed suit against the 
plaintiffs in the United States District Court for the District of 
Colorado. Contemporaneously, the defendants also filed a 
complaint against the plaintiffs with the American Arbitration 
Association (AAA), asserting claims for breach of the restrictive 
covenants along with various tort and statutory claims. 

7 
¶ 13 The defendants then filed a motion to dismiss the plaintiffs’ 
complaint and to compel arbitration in the trial court. The court 
denied the motion on two grounds: first, that Impact had no 
arbitration agreement with the defendants; and second, because the 
factual allegations could plausibly support the conclusion that the 
state court was the appropriate forum for resolution of the 
enforceability of the noncompete clause. 
¶ 14 The defendants did not pursue an interlocutory appeal of the 
order denying the motion to compel arbitration. They then 
answered the complaint, without asserting any counterclaims or 
affirmative defenses. 
¶ 15 The defendants next filed their first motion for summary

leads.caseName: Sherilyn Hart v. North Waverly LLC
leads.text:
If this opinion indicates that it is “FOR PUBLICATION,” it is subject to 
revision until final publication in the Michigan Appeals Reports. 

-1- 
S T A T E O F M I C H I G A N 

C O U R T O F A P P E A L S 

SHERILYN HART, 

 Plaintiff-Appellee, 

and 

ANTHONY MCCARTY, 

 Plaintiff, 

UNPUBLISHED 
November 05, 2026 
10:37 AM 
v No. 373806 
Ingham Circuit Court 
NORTH WAVERLY LLC, 

LC No. 22-000089-CH 
 Defendant-Appellant. 

Before: WALLACE, P.J., and CAMERON and KOROBKIN, JJ. 

PER CURIAM. 
 This action arises from a property dispute between adjoining residential and commercial 
properties. Plaintiffs, Sherilyn Hart and her husband Anthony McCarty, with Hart having title to 
a residential property (1324 Property) they were endeavoring to rehabilitate and rent, brought 
claims for trespass, nuisance in fact, nuisance per se , and to quiet title against defendant, North 
Waverly LLC, the owner of the commercial property next door to the south (1300 Property) . 
Plaintiffs’ complaint contended that defendant altered the drainage of its property to unnaturally 
increase and concentrate the flow of such drainage onto their neighboring property, which increase 
in volume and velocity of water caused them and their property significant damages, including 
significantly interfering with their right to the use and quiet enjoyment of their property. The 
complaint likewise contend ed that defendant, by way of its employees and agents, entered onto 
the 1324 Property and constructed and altered certain landscaping at the property line between 
their two parcels (a border and retaining wall comprised variously of poured concrete, cinder block 
and railroad ties) that intrudes and encroaches onto the 1324 Property. Defendant, in turn, filed a 
counterclaim to quiet title based upon adverse possession as to that portion of property where the 
retaining wall is constructed and located to the extent it intrudes upon the 1324 Property. 
-2- 
 The trial court held a four -day bench trial during which it granted defendant’s motion to 
dismiss Anthony McCarty, based upon lack of standing because he was not a record title holder or 
a person in possession of the property (e. g., a tenant). 1 The trial court entered a judgment and 
order finding for plaintiff on her trespass and nuisance claims and dismissing defendant’s quiet 
title claim.2 It awarded “[a]ctual damages consisting of the reasonable expenses of necessary 
repairs to the property and remediation of the retainer wall for $150,000; noneconomic damages 
for emotional distress and mental anguish awarded in the amount of $50,000; and attorney fees of 
$40,000 for a total award of $240,000.” 
 The trial court then denied in part and granted in part defendant’s subsequent motion to 
amend judgment and for new trial. It granted the motion as to its award of attorney fees, vacating 
that award, and, based on its finding that defendant was 80% responsible for those damages under 
the doctrine of comparative negligence , it reduced its award of economic damages by 20%, 
resulting in an amended judgment of $170,000. 
 Defendant then brought this timely appeal of right. For the reason s set forth herein, w e 
affirm in part, reverse in part, and remand for the trial court’s entry of an amended judgment 
modifying its award of economic damages and clarif ying its equitable award of nuisance 
abatement as set forth herein. 
I. FACTUAL BACKGROUND AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY 
Hart and McCarty, husband and wife, purchased the property at 1324 N. Waverly Rd. in 
2013, intending to rehabilitate and make use of it as a rental property. Their primary residence is 
located next door to the north at 1400 N. Waverly Road. Both the 1324 Property and their primary 
residence are marital assets, but only Hart’s name is on the title for the 1324 Property. Defendant, 
North Waverly, purchased the commercial property next door to the south of the 1324 Property at 
1300 N. Waverly Rd. in March 2015. Hart and McCarty’s trial testimony was that there was no 
water damage to the 1324 Property when they purchased it in 2013 and they had no water damage 
or problems with excess water run-off or flooding on the 1324 Property in 2014-2015.3 Plaintiff 
and McCarty each testified that they first noticed excess water drainage in mid-May 2016. Starting 
at that time, they noticed the grass and soil was very wet and saturated with water and it was more 
difficult to mow the lawn with their tractor in the section of the back and side yard next to the 1300 
Property. 
McCarty went over to meet with the managing member and an owner of North Waverly , 
Eric Stevenson, for the first time on June 1, 2016 to address a truckload of asphalt and broken up 

1 In light of this dismissal, unless otherwise noted, hereafter, references to “plaintiff” in this opinion 
will be to Sherilyn Hart. 
2 The trial court made no express ruling as to plaintiff’s quiet title claim , which is likewise not 
addressed on appeal. 
3 McCarty testified that he mowed the backyard to the 1324 Property in 2011 -2012 while it was 
bank-owned and was very familiar with it and likewise noticed no water damage or issues with 
excess water drainage during that time. 
-3- 
concrete that contractors for the 1300 Property left in the middle of the 1324 Property driveway, 
and noticed black plastic corrugated piping 4 running over the ground up to and over the 1300 
Property’s property line and retaining wall with the 1324 Property at that time. 
McCarty and plaintiff each testified that, in mid-May of 2016, North Waverly made 
changes to the drainage from the downspouts on the 1300 Property, removing their extensions and 
causing them to “plug into” one of two long pieces of uncapped black plastic corrugated pipe. The 
collector pipe from the front downspouts laid over the retaining wall between the 1300 Property 
and 1324 Property and emptied onto the 1324 Property. There were two such collector pipes and 
the “back one” (to which the black corrugated pipes at the end of the back downspouts connected) 
“came all the way to the property line where they dug a small hole” and stuck the uncapped end 
of the black plastic corrugated pipe into the hole “[s]o it’s just under the surface of the ground, just 
across the property line” onto the 1324 Property. 
While talking to Stevenson and his “real estate partner” on June 1, 201 6, McCarty asked 
about the front collector pipe he observed running up to and over the retaining wall between their 
properties. Stevenson said that it was just there temporarily while they were having the parking 
lot worked on and that it was going to run under the parking lot. McCarty said, “Okay, if you’re 
sure that’s what’s going on because if it rains, there is going to be a lot of water here.” Until then, 
McCarty had no idea that this was reason that the grass and soil in the back and side yard of the 
1324 Property had been so wet and saturated starting in mid-May 2016. 
McCarty testified that that front collector pipe Stevenson said was “temporary” remained 
in its place there for nearly six years, until 2021. He testified that, after those two collector drains 
were put in place, because the back collector drain was “slipped just under the surface of the dirt,” 
water “would back flow out from where it was plugged in the ground, . . . bubble up at the top and 
spill over,” onto the 1324 Property and “flow[] and pool[] all at the back of the house on the east 
wall of the house. Because the front collector drain “was just a big black pipe that emptied right 
onto” the 1324 Property, that drainage water “ran down and flowed into the garage, around the 
garage,” and if it was a really big rain it would flow through the garage and reach the house. 
McCarty testified that he informed Ste venson that his changes to the 1300 Property 
drainage system caused concentrated, excessive water drainage onto the 1324 Property if it rained, 
and he repeatedly called Stevenson to find out when the two collector pipes draining at and over 
the retaining wall between their two properties would be removed . Stevenson gave McCarty 
multiple stories as to what was going on, the last of which was “that pipe [was] in the ground, and 
that no more water should come from it,” and he stopped taking McCarty’s calls in the Fall of 
2016. 

4 This piping was also referred to as “black plastic drain tile” at trial due to it being perforated for 
drainage purposes. While plaintiff contested that there was never any evidence at trial that the 
black plastic corrugated piping was perforated, McCarty later testified in the context of his capping 
the collector pipes: “These pipes have tiny, tiny little holes in them ever so often. So that if you 
cap it, and it’s holding water in there, it’s what’s called seep holes. It’ll slowly allow that water to 
seep out under the ground. That’s how it’s designed to work.” 
-4- 
At some point starting in June 2021, defendant rebuilt the eastern portion of the retaining 
wall between the 1324 Property and 1300 Property . Constructed of stacked railroad ties, it was 
reset further south by defendant (but still over the property line onto the 1324 Property ), and the 
front black plastic corrugated collector pipe w as buried in the ground behind the railroad tie 
retaining wall with pea gravel at the same east-west location along the retaining wall where it 
terminated previously. But this action did not resolve the problem with the focused excessive 
water draining onto the 1324 Property. A Summer 2021 video taken after this work was performed 
was shown at trial depicting water pouring out of a hole at the base of the railroad tie retaining 
wall where the front collector pipe was buried, causing the pea gravel to wash out along with the 
water onto the 1324 Property and onto its driveway 100 feet from the border between the two 
properties. That same video likewise depicts water seeping through the soil where the black plastic 
corrugated collector pipe was burie d in the ground with pea gravel , right at the property line 
between the 1300 Property and the 1324 Property , and is actively streaming out of the soil onto 
the 1324 Property. Prior to 2021, plaintiff testified that this back collector pipe was not even 
buried. 
Prior to filing this lawsuit , McCarty had many conversations (and many attempts at 
conversations) with Stevenson regarding the concentrated, increased water drainage from the 1300 
Property, called the Township and County many times, and testified that he contacted the EPA in 
2019. McCarty testified that, in 2018, he rented earth-moving machinery, dug a trench, installed 
a larger sump line, and bought and installed a large sump pump meant for commercial buildings 
to pump away the water seeping into their basement from the 1300 Property. He also employed 
this rented earth-moving machinery to shave down portions of the backyard so that some of the 
concentrated water drainage from the 1300 Property’s collector pipes would drain around the 
house and garage rather than down to them. 
In June 2020, McCarty testified that he capped the ends of the front and back black plastic 
corrugated collector pipes when: the property was already saturated, the 1324 Property’s basement 
had previously and repeatedly flooded, a significant rainstorm was forecast, he and his wife could 
not find an attorney to take on this case, and they were “fed up.” The caps remained in place for 
approximately 11 months, and McCarty testified that , after he capped them, the saturated soil in 
the back and side of the 1324 Property near its border with the 1300 property began to noticeably 
dry out over time. McCarty later noticed that the caps were removed and “thrown onto his yard.” 
As already noted, commencing around mid-June 2021, defendant performed work on the 
railroad tie portion of the retaining wall, rebuilding and resetting it further south (closer to but still
