TO BE PUBLISHED IN THE OFFICIAL REPORTS

 OFFICE OF THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
 State of California

 ROB BONTA
 Attorney General

 _______________

 :
 OPINION :
 : No. 25-1102
 of :
 : November 5, 2026
 ROB BONTA :
 Attorney General :
 :
 ZACHARY W. SORENSON :
 Associate Deputy Solicitor General :
 :

 The HONORABLE TOM LACKEY, ASSEMBLYMEMBER, has requested an
opinion on questions relating to the Housing Crisis Act of 2019.

 QUESTIONS PRESENTED AND CONCLUSIONS

 1. Government Code section 66300(b)(1) prohibits urban cities and counties
from imposing restrictions on residential development capacity. If a locality passes a law
to allow more housing, can a referendum rejecting that change violate subdivision (b)(1)?

 Yes. A referendum rejecting a legislative enactment that would allow additional
housing can constitute a prohibited moratorium-like restriction on housing development
within the meaning of section 66300(b)(1).

 2. Can a locality unilaterally invalidate a referendum that violates section
66300(b)(1)?

 No. A city or county cannot deem a referendum void without a court order.

 1
 25-1102
  3. What statute of limitations governs private section 66300(b)(1) actions?

 It depends. A three-year limitations period applies to challenges to referenda,
while a 90-day limitations period applies to land use decisions by a local legislative body.

 BACKGROUND

 The Housing Crisis Act of 2019 was enacted to address California’s “housing
supply crisis.” 1 The Legislature found that “housing demand [was] far outstripping
supply,” resulting in “very expensive” housing and “rapid” rent increases. 2 Despite high
demand, homebuilders were “unable to meet that demand because of local rules that limit
the number of units or simply prohibit building altogether.” 3 So the Housing Crisis Act
declared a “statewide housing emergency” and “[s]uspend[ed] certain restrictions on the
development of new housing.” 4 The Act includes several provisions to ease limits on
homebuilding. Relevant here is Government Code section 66300, which restricts local
authority to modify land use regulations in ways that limit housing development.

 1. Local land use authority derives from California’s Planning and Zoning Law. 5
Under this statute, every city and county is required to “adopt a comprehensive, long-
term general plan for [its] physical development.” 6 The general plan must “comprise an
integrated, internally consistent and compatible statement of policies” for local planning. 7

 As relevant here, a general plan must include a “land use element.” The land use
element “designates the proposed general distribution and general location and extent of
the uses of the land for housing, business, industry, open space, . . . education, public
buildings and grounds, . . . and other categories of public and private uses of land.” 8

1
 Sen. Bill No. 330 (2019-2020 Reg. Sess.) § 2, subd. (a)(1) (S.B. 330).
2
 Id., § 2, subd. (a).
3
 Off. of Sen. Floor Analyses, Sen. Rules Com., analysis of S.B. 330, Sept. 5, 2019, p. 7.
4
 S.B. 330, § 2, subds. (b), (c)(1) (declaring “housing emergency” until Jan. 1, 2025);
Sen. Bill No. 8 (2021-2022 Reg. Sess.) § 13, subd. (b) (S.B. 8) (extending emergency
until Jan. 1, 2030).
5
 This law is codified as title 7 of the Government Code (sections 65000-66499.58).
6
 Gov. Code, § 65300. This requirement also applies to every charter city. (Ibid.)
7
 Id., § 65300.5, subd. (a).
8
 Id., § 65302, subd. (a).

 2
 25-1102
  The general plan, including its land use element, functions “as the ‘constitution for
all future developments’ within the city or county.” 9 Specific plans and zoning
ordinances implement the applicable general plan and must be consistent with that plan. 10

 Specific plans are not required, but can be adopted by cities and counties “for the
systematic implementation of the general plan.” 11 Specific plans are commonly used for
“a particular development site or sub-area.” 12 A specific plan must “specify . . . [t]he
distribution, location, and extent of the uses of land” within its area. 13

 Zoning ordinances implement and must follow the general plan and any specific
plans that apply. Zoning ordinances “divide” the jurisdiction “into zones” to dictate the
“intensity of land use” in each zone, as well as development attributes such as “location,
height, bulk, number of stories, and size of buildings.” 14

 General plans, specific plans, and zoning ordinances each operate by defining
categories within which uniform standards apply. General plan categories can be broad,
while zoning offers more detail. 15 Once defined, categories are mapped to specific areas
or parcels. A general plan must show “the proposed general distribution and general
location” for categories. 16 Zoning ordinances are more precise; zones must have definite
boundaries so that property owners know what rules apply. 17

 Any parcel’s residential capacity is a product of several attributes of the applicable
land use categories. Some rules cap the number of dwelling units per acre or per lot.
Others—like limits on height, floor area ratio, or setbacks—restrict capacity indirectly.

9
 Citizens of Goleta Valley v. Board of Supervisors (1990) 52 Cal.3d 553, 570, quoting
O’Loane v. O’Rourke (1965) 231 Cal.App.2d 774, 782.
10
 See Gov. Code, §§ 65454 (specific plans), 65860 (zoning ordinances).
11
 Id., § 65450.
12
 California Department of Real Estate, Reference Book: Information Relating to Real
Estate Practice, Licensing and Examinations (2010) p. 476.
13
 Gov. Code, §§ 65451, 65454.
14
 Id., §§ 65850, 65851.
15
 Id., §§ 65302, subd. (a), 65852; see, e.g., San Diego Municipal Code, ch. 13, pp. 35-50
(33 residential zones).
16
 Gov. Code, § 65302, subd. (a).
17
 See United Outdoor Advertising Co. v. Business, Transportation & Housing Agency
(1988) 44 Cal.3d 242, 249.

 3
 25-1102
  Cities and counties must follow special procedures to adopt or amend general
plans, specific plans, and zoning ordinances. 18 Among other requirements, these
procedures include steps like written recommendations from planning agencies,
consultation with affected institutions, and public hearings. Under Government Code
section 65858, however, localities are permitted to adopt temporary “interim” ordinances
(also referred to as moratorium ordinances) to protect safety, health, and welfare, without
following the usual procedures; unless renewed, these ordinances can last up to 45 days.

 2. Local land use regulation is subject to the constitutional referendum power. 19
The procedures governing city and county referenda are set out in the Elections Code. 20
A referendum is possible only after final enactment of an ordinance by a legislative body.
To allow voters to weigh in, most ordinances cannot “become effective” until 30 days
after “final passage.” 21 During this 30-day period, voters can “petition protesting the
adoption of an ordinance.” 22 If enough voters join the petition, “the ordinance shall be
suspended.” 23 Unless the legislative body repeals the ordinance on its own, a “measure”
must be placed on the ballot “submit[ting] the ordinance to the voters.” 24 The enacted
ordinance remains suspended while the voters make their decision.

 If the voters opt to approve the ordinance, the suspension is lifted, so the ordinance
“become[s] effective.” 25 If the voters reject the ordinance, there are two consequences.
First, “the temporary suspension becomes permanent by operation of law.” 26 Second, the
city or county is temporarily prohibited from reenacting the same measure. For cities,
that prohibition lasts for one year (by statute). 27 Counties are prohibited from reenacting

18
 See, e.g., Gov. Code, §§ 65350-65362 (general plans), 65853-65857 (zoning).
19
 Cal. Const., art. II, § 11; Dwyer v. City Council of Berkeley (1927) 200 Cal. 505.
20
 Elec. Code, §§ 9140-9147 (counties), 9234-9247 (cities).
21
 Id., §§ 9141 (counties), 9235 (cities).
22
 Id., §§ 9144 (counties), 9237 (cities).
23
 Id., §§ 9144 (counties), 9237 (cities).
24
 Id., §§ 9145, 9147 (counties); see also id., § 9241 (cities).
25
 Id., §§ 9145 (counties), 9241 (cities).
26
 County of Kern v. T.C.E.F., Inc. (2016) 246 Cal.App.4th 301, 319; see Elec. Code,
§§ 9144, 9145 (counties), 9237, 9241 (cities).
27
 Elec. Code, § 9241.

 4
 25-1102
 an “essential feature” of the measure until there is “a material change in
circumstances.” 28

 3. Government Code section 66300 restricts the authority of certain urban cities
and counties to limit housing development. 29 The statute also expressly applies to the
electorate’s “referendum power.” 30 Relevant here, subdivision (b)(1) prohibits
“enact[ing]” land use measures that would have the “effect[]” of imposing a moratorium-
like restriction on housing development or reducing the amount of housing permitted in
certain other ways.

 Our requestor asks three questions about this statute: (1) whether a referendum
rejecting a measure that authorizes additional housing can violate section 66300(b)(1);
(2) whether a locality can declare such a referendum void on its own, without a court
order; and (3) what limitations period applies to private-party actions under this statute. 31

 ANALYSIS

1. Section 66300(b) Applies to Referenda Rejecting Legislative Enactments that
 Would Allow Additional Housing

 Our requestor asks whether certain kinds of referenda violate section 66300(b)(1).
The question envisions the following sequence of events: First, a city or county
legislative body enacts a “general plan amendment or specific plan for housing
development” that would “increase[] the ‘intensity of land use’” or “permit[] housing on
land where it would otherwise not be allowed.” Second, voters then reject that enactment
via referendum.

 a. Our requestor first asks whether such a referendum would constitute a
moratorium-type restriction prohibited by subdivision (b)(1)(B)(i), which provides:

 [W]ith respect to land where housing is an allowable use, an affected
 county or an affected city shall not enact a development policy, standard, or
 condition that would have . . . the following effect[]: . . .

28
 County of Kern v. Alta Sierra Holistic Exchange Service (2020) 46 Cal.App.5th 82, 85,
97; see Elec. Code, §§ 9140-9147.
29
 Gov. Code, § 66300, subd. (b)(1).
30
 Id., subd. (a)(3).
 Assemblymember Tom Lackey, letter requesting opn. to Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta, Opn.
31

Unit, Dept. of J., June 25, 2026, pp. 2-3.

 5
 25-1102
  Imposing a moratorium or similar restriction or limitation on housing
 development, including mixed-use development, within all or a portion of
 the jurisdiction of the affected county or city . . . . 32

The terms “affected county” and “affected city” are defined to “include[] the electorate
. . . exercising its local initiative or referendum power.” 33 A “development policy,
standard, or condition” includes a “provision of, or amendment to” “a general plan,” “a
specific plan,” or “a zoning ordinance.” 34

 i. We begin with the text of subdivision (b)(1)(B)(i). This provision is written
expansively. Its key term is “moratorium,” but it also extends to any “similar restriction
or limitation on housing development.” Additionally, section 66300 directs that its
provisions are to be “broadly construed so as to maximize the development of housing.” 35

 Here is how dictionaries define the relevant terms: A “moratorium” is a
“suspension of a specific activity.” 36 A “restriction” is “a regulation that restricts or
constrains.” 37 Similarly, a “limitation” is “a restriction or restraint imposed from
without,” including “by law.” 38 (“Restrict” and “limit” both mean “set bounds or limits
to.” 39)

32
 Gov. Code, § 66300, subd. (b)(1)(B)(i), italics added. Although not at issue here, the
provision excludes restrictions enacted “to specifically protect against an imminent threat
to the health and safety of persons residing in, or within the immediate vicinity of, the
area subject to the moratorium or for project

leads.text:
Deutsche Bank Trust Co. Ams. v Leis 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06498 
 November 5, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Third Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Deutsche Bank Trust Company Americas, as Trustee, Appellant, 
 v 
 Marie Leis et al., Defendants. 

 Decided and Entered:November 5, 2026 
 CV-25-0694 
 Calendar Date: September 8, 2026 
 Before: Pritzker, J.P., Ceresia, Powers, Corcoran And Ryba, JJ. 

 McCabe, Weisberg & Conway, LLC, Port Chester (Robert Yusko of counsel), for appellant. 

 [*1] 
 Ryba, J. 
 Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court (Meagan Galligan, J.), entered April 4, 2025 in Sullivan County, which denied plaintiff's motion to, among other things, vacate a prior order. 
 This appeal arises from a mortgage foreclosure action commenced by plaintiff following an alleged default on a promissory note executed by David A. Leis (hereinafter decedent) and secured by a mortgage executed by decedent and his wife, defendant Marie Leis, on residential property in Sullivan County. Following mandatory settlement conferences, Supreme Court (Meddaugh, J.) issued an order in March 2017 directing plaintiff to file a motion for an order of reference no later than December 31, 2017. The order expressly advised that the specified date constituted a scheduled call of the calendar and that, should plaintiff fail to timely file the required motion, the matter would be marked off the calendar and thereafter dismissed if plaintiff failed to timely move to restore the action within one year. Plaintiff failed to submit the required motion by the court-imposed deadline. In January 2018, Supreme Court notified plaintiff that the action had been marked off the calendar based upon its failure to comply with the court's directive. Thereafter, plaintiff failed to move to restore the matter within one year, and, by order dated January 7, 2019, Supreme Court dismissed the action without prejudice pursuant to 22 NYCRR 202.27. More than six years later, plaintiff moved pursuant to CPLR 5015 (a) (1) to vacate the dismissal and restore the matter to the active calendar, together with other related relief. Supreme Court (Galligan, J.) denied the motion, finding that plaintiff failed to establish a reasonable excuse for its prolonged delay in seeking to vacate the default. Plaintiff appeals. 
 We affirm. We have consistently held that 22 NYCRR 202.27 permits dismissal of an action as abandoned where a plaintiff fails to timely comply with a court directive to move the litigation forward ( see Nadler v County of Albany , 237 AD3d 1461 , 1461 [3d Dept 2025]; U.S. Bank N.A. v Hartquist , 227 AD3d 1149 , 1150 [3d Dept 2024]; Bank of N.Y. v Wells , 222 AD3d 1237, 1239 [3d Dept 2023]; Bank of N.Y. Mellon v Vaiana , 218 AD3d 1094, 1096 [3d Dept 2023]). A plaintiff seeking to vacate a dismissal entered pursuant to 22 NYCRR 202.27 must demonstrate both a reasonable excuse for the default and a potentially meritorious cause of action ( see U.S. Bank N.A. v Hartquist , 227 AD3d at 1151; Bank of N.Y. Mellon v Vaiana , 218 AD3d at 1096 ; Hayes v Village of Middleburgh , 140 AD3d 1359, 1361 [3d Dept 2016]). Whether those requirements have been satisfied is a determination that rests within the sound discretion of the court ( see Nadler v County of Albany , 237 AD3d at 1462; U.S. Bank N.A. v Hartquist , 227 AD3d at 1151). 
 Here, Supreme Court (Meddaugh, J.) expressly advised plaintiff of the consequences of failing to timely comply with its directive and plaintiff neither adhered to the deadline nor sought [*2] an extension of time. After the matter was marked off the calendar in January 2018, plaintiff once again failed to take timely action to restore the matter, resulting in dismissal of the complaint in January 2019. Thereafter, plaintiff inexplicably allowed the matter to remain dormant for more than six years before seeking to vacate the dismissal in February 2025. Despite this prolonged period of inactivity, plaintiff submitted no affidavit from counsel or other individual with personal knowledge explaining the missed motion deadline, the failure to respond to the court's notification that the matter had been marked off the calendar, or the subsequent six-year delay in seeking to vacate the dismissal. Although plaintiff cited legal authority for the general proposition that law office failure may, under appropriate circumstances, constitute a reasonable excuse for a default, plaintiff's submissions were devoid of any factual allegations to warrant invoking the doctrine. Indeed, plaintiff identified no specific calendaring error, office miscommunication or other facts demonstrating that its default was due to law office failure, nor did plaintiff offer any explanation whatsoever for the lengthy delay in moving to vacate the dismissal. 
 To the extent that plaintiff contends that defendants' alleged failure to file a notice of entry constitutes a reasonable excuse for the delay, we disagree. The filing of a notice of entry bears only upon the timeliness of a CPLR 5015 (a) (1) motion, not upon whether a reasonable excuse for a default has been established. Under these circumstances, Supreme Court (Galligan, J.) acted well within its discretion in concluding that plaintiff failed to demonstrate a reasonable excuse for its default. Because plaintiff failed to establish a reasonable excuse, Supreme Court was not required to determine whether plaintiff had otherwise demonstrated a potentially meritorious foreclosure action ( see U.S. Bank N.A. v Hartquist , 227 AD3d at 1151; Bank of N.Y. Mellon v Vaiana , 218 AD3d at 1096 ). 
 Plaintiff's remaining contentions, including its assertion that Supreme Court should have exercised its inherent authority to vacate the dismissal in the interest of justice, have been examined and found to be unpersuasive. 
 Pritzker, J.P., Ceresia, Powers and Corcoran, JJ., concur. 
 ORDERED that the order is affirmed, without costs.

J-S32036-26 

NON-PRECEDENTIAL DECISION - SEE SUPERIOR COURT O.P. 65.37 

DENIYA N. SMITH 

 Appellant 

 v. 

CARRINGTON MORTGAGE SERVICES, 
LLC 
: 
: 
: 
: 
: 
: 
: 
: 
: 
: 
IN THE SUPERIOR COURT OF 
 PENNSYLVANIA 

No. 209 EDA 2026 

Appeal from the Order Entered December 23, 2025 
In the Court of Common Pleas of Philadelphia County Civil Division at 
No(s): 250800663 

BEFORE: BOWES, J., OLSON, J., and STEVENS, P.J.E.* 
MEMORANDUM BY STEVENS, P.J.E.: FILED NOVEMBER 5, 2026 
Plaintiff/Appellant, Deniya N. Smith, appeals pro se from the trial court’s 
order sustaining preliminary objections filed by Defendant/Appellee 
Carrington Mortgage Services, LLC, (“Carrington”) in response to Ms. Smith’s 
complaint that sought to quiet title in her favor to real property that Carrington 
purchased at sheriff’s sale after it prevailed in its mortgage foreclosure action 
and secured judgment against her and her co-defendant, Ase Family Trust. 
Specifically, the trial court agreed with Carrington that Ms. Smith was 
prohibited from collaterally attacking the foreclosure action and default 
judgment. We agree and, accordingly, affirm. 
The trial court provides a pertinent account of the relevant facts and 
procedural history of the case: 
____________________________________________ 
* Former Justice specially assigned to the Superior Court. 
J-S32036-26 
- 2 - 

In April 2021, Deniya Nekeidra Smith purchased 5324 W. 
Columbia Ave (the “Property”) and executed a promissory note 
secured by a mortgage. On March 27, 2023, Ms. Smith 
purportedly transferred title of the Property to the “Ase Family 
Trust” to which Ms. Smith claims she is a trustee.fn1 On May 18, 
2023, Carrington [] assumed responsibility for the mortgage 
through an assignment. 

Fn.1: Ms. Smith filed this action individually and “in 
her representative capacity as Trustee of the Ase 
Family Trust.” Ms. Smith is not an attorney, so she is 
not permitted to legally represent a trust in [the trial 
court], as is discussed infra. 

In June 2023, Carrington commenced a foreclosure action (June 
Term 2023 No. 14420 (2306034989), naming both Ms. Smith 
individually and the Ase Family Trust as defendants. The trial 
court eventually entered a default judgment in the foreclosure 
action, and the Property was sold at Sheriff’s Sale.fn2 Carrington 
purchased the Property at the sale on May 13, 2025, and recorded 
the deed. 

Fn.2: [At the time of the trial court opinion, Ms. Smith 
was] appealing an Order entered in the foreclosure 
action, 1047 EDA 2025. 

On August 7, 2025, Carrington initiated an ejectment action 
(August Term No. 2025 No. 0830) against Ms. Smith. At the same 
time, Ms. Smith initiated this quiet title action on behalf of herself 
and in her representative capacity as Trustee of the Ase Family 
Trust, arguing that the foreclosure judgment was defective. [The 
trial court] consolidated the actions on October 23, 2025. 
Carrington filed Preliminary Objections in this quiet title action, 
arguing that Ms. Smith is barred by collateral estoppel from 
relitigating the foreclosure issue. [The trial court] sustained the 
J-S32036-26 
- 3 - 
Preliminary Objections and dismissed this quiet title action with 
prejudice. 

Following [the trial court’s] Order, Ms. Smith filed this timely 
appeal with the Superior Court claiming inter alia that the [trial 
court] erred in dismissing the case without assessing it on the 
merits. 
TCO, 3/9/2026, at 1-2. 
Ms. Smith’s pro se “Brief for Appellant” raises the following issues for 
this Court’s consideration: 

1. Whether the trial court erred in dismissing Appellant’s quiet 
title action by treating it as an impermissible collateral attack 
on a foreclosure judgment. 

2. Whether the trial court erred in sustaining preliminary 
objections and dismissing the complaint with prejudice. 

3. Whether the trial court erred in concluding that Appellant 
lacked standing as a matter of law. 
Brief of Appellant, at 4 (unpaginated). 
Our well-settled standard of review of an order sustaining or denying 
preliminary objections is as follows: 

“Our standard of review of an order of the trial court overruling or 
granting preliminary objections is to determine whether the trial 
court committed an error of law. When considering the 
appropriateness of a ruling on preliminary objections, the 
appellate court must apply the same standard as the trial court.” 
De Lage Landen Fin'l Servs., Inc., v. Urban P'ship, LLC, 903 
A.2d 586, 589 (Pa. Super. 2006). 

“Preliminary objections in the nature of a demurrer 
test the legal sufficiency of the complaint.” When 
considering preliminary objections, all material facts 
set forth in the challenged pleadings are admitted as 
true, as well as all inferences reasonably deducible 
therefrom. Preliminary objections which seek the 
J-S32036-26 
- 4 - 
dismissal of a cause of action should be sustained only 
in cases in which it is clear and free from doubt that 
the pleader will be unable to prove facts legally 
sufficient to establish the right to relief. If any doubt 
exists as to whether a demurrer should be sustained, 
it should be resolved in favor of overruling the 
preliminary objections. 
Hykes v. Hughes, 835 A.2d 382, 383 (Pa. Super. 2003) (citations omitted). 
Haun v. Comm. Health Sys., Inc., 14 A.3d 120, 123 (Pa. Super. 2011) 
(citations modified). 
When an ejectment action is brought by the purchaser of a title obtained 
from a sheriff's sale in a mortgage foreclosure, the grounds on which the 
underlying judgment of foreclosure can be collaterally attacked are strictly 
limited. 

Initially, we note that an attack on a sheriff's sale usually cannot 
be made in a collateral proceeding. An ejectment action is a 
proceeding collateral to that under which the land was sold. Thus, 
where it is claimed that the underlying default judgment is merely 
voidable, that claim will not be entertained because such a 
judgment cannot be reached collaterally. However, in an 
ejectment action[,] it may be alleged that the judgment is void. 
A void decree can be attacked at any time. Where a judgment is 
void, the sheriff's sale [that] follows is a nullity. A judgment is 
void when the court had no jurisdiction over the parties, or the 
subject matter, or the court had no power or authority to render 
the particular judgment. A judgment [that] is void cannot support 
an ejectment action and may be asserted as a defense in the 
ejectment proceeding. 
Dime Savings Bank, FSB v. Greene, 813 A.2d 893, 895 (Pa. Super. 2002) 
(citations omitted); see also Fannie Mae v. Ferreri, (non-precedential 
decision) 339 A.3d 437 (Pa. Super. 2025). 
J-S32036-26 
- 5 - 
Here, Ms. Smith alleges not that the trial court’s decree was void for 
want of jurisdiction over the parties or subject matter or for lack of power or 
authority to render the judgment but, instead, that Carrington’s interest in the 
property was invalid. Specifically, she advanced a quiet title action in which 
she “challenges the validity of [Carrington’s] asserted interest in the 
property.” Brief of Appellant, “Argument I.” p. 7 (unpaginated). It is well-
settled, however, that such a “defect of title”-based collateral challenge to a 
sheriff’s sale and delivery of sheriff’s deed may not prevail. 

[A]n attack on a sheriff's sale usually cannot be made in a 
collateral proceeding. In Caplan v. Kent, 76 A.2d 764 (Pa. 
1950), it was held that a sheriff's return, regular on its face, 
could not be attacked collaterally in a bill in equity to quiet 
title. “Confirmation of a sheriff's deed cures irregularities and 
defects, which make the sale voidable * * *.” McLanahan v. 
Goodman, 108 A. 206, 208 (Pa.1919). In Mencke v. 
Rosenberg, 51 A. 767, 769 (Pa.1902), the court said in reference 
to an ejectment action: “This is a proceeding collateral to that 
under which the land was sold. The acknowledgment of the 
sheriff's deed passed a valid title to the purchaser, unless there 
was fraud or want of authority in the sale.” After reiterating this 
rule in Knox v. Noggle, 196 A. 18 (Pa. 1938), the court added: 
“(T)he distinction is * * * between irregularities in the 
proceedings, misdescriptions of the property, the sale of several 
tracts as an entirety, defect of title, and similar objection, on the 
one hand, all of which are foreclosed as defenses by delivery 
of the sheriff's deed, and, on the other, attacks upon the sale 
on the ground that it was unauthorized, or vitiated by fraud, in 
which cases the right of redress survives such delivery.” 196 A. at 
19–20. 
Roberts v. Gibson, 251 A.2d 799, 800-01 (Pa. Super. 1969) (citations 
modified; emphasis added). 
J-S32036-26 
- 6 - 
As the trial court observes, Ms. Smith is attempting to use a quiet title 
action as an impermissible collateral attack to relitigate the default judgment 
entered in the foreclosure action, and it did not permit her to do so.1 Under 
our jurisprudence, we agree the present quiet title action is an improper 
collateral attack on the sheriff’s sale and thus conclude the trial court 
appropriately sustained Carrington’s preliminary objections and dismissed the 
action. As our resolution of this issue is dispositive of the appeal, we affirm 
the order entered below. 
Order affirmed. 

Date: 11/5/2026 

____________________________________________ 
1 The trial court explains further that Ms. Smith has filed a separate appeal 
challenging the trial court’s default judgment in the foreclosure action on the 
merits.

leads.caseName: Columbus v. Ohio Wholesale Auto Sales, L.L.C.
leads.text:
[Cite as Columbus v. Ohio Wholesale Auto Sales, L.L.C., 2026-Ohio-4386.] 

IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF OHIO 

TENTH APPELLATE DISTRICT 

City of Columbus, Ohio, : 
a municipal corporation, 
 : 
 Petitioner-Appellee, 
 : No. 25AP-467 
v. (C.P.C. No. 21CV-5236) 
 : 
Ohio Wholesale Auto Sales, LLC et al., (REGULAR CALENDAR) 
 : 
 Respondents-Appellees, 
 : 
Wiltshire Capital Partners, LP, 
 : 
 Respondent-Appellant. 
 : 

D E C I S I O N 
Rendered on November 5. 2026 

On brief: Haynes, Kessler, Myers & Postalakis, and 
Christopher T. Cline, for appellee, Ohio Wholesale Auto Sales, 
LLC. Argued: Christopher T. Cline. 

On brief: Joquetta S. Wells , for appellant. Argued: 
Joquetta S. Wells. 

APPEAL from the Franklin County Court of Common Pleas 
DINGUS, J. 
{¶ 1} Respondent-appellant, Wiltshire Capital Partners, LP (“Wiltshire”), appeals 
from a judgment of the Franklin County Court of Common Pleas, in this eminent domain 
action, vesting title in certain real property to petitioner-appellee, City of Columbus, upon 
the city’s $4,014 payment to respondent-appellee, Ohio Wholesale Auto Sales, LLC (“Ohio 
Wholesale Auto Sales”). For the following reasons, we reverse and remand. 
No. 25AP-467 2 

I. Facts and Procedural History 
{¶ 2} In August 2021, the City of Columbus filed a petition for appropriation of real 
property declaring its intention to use eminent domain to appropriate a fee simple interest 
and a temporary easement for a 0.082 -acre parcel of land in Clinton Township and to 
appropriate a temporary construction easement for a 0.016-acre parcel of land in Clinton 
Township. The eminent domain proceedings were initiated “for the purposes of making, 
constructing, repairing or improving a state, U.S. or interstate highway which shall be open 
to the public, without charge ” as part of the Hudson Street Sidewalks Project. (Aug. 17, 
2021 Petition at ¶ 7.) In its appropriation petition, the City of Columbus named nine 
entities who have, claim to have, or may have, the following estate interest or right in the 
real property: (1) Ohio Wholesale Auto Sales, fee simple interest; (2) Doug Davis and 
Marilyn Bernard, mortgage of record; (3) William L. Bowersock, mo rtgage of record; (4) 
Florence Odita, mortgage of record; (5) Wiltshire, mortgage of record; (6) State of Ohio, 
Department of Taxation, judgment of record; (7) Don’s Garage, Inc., judgment of record; 
(8) City of Columbus, notice of lis pendens; and (9) Franklin County Treasurer, property 
taxes and assessments. Based on various dismissals and default judgments, only three 
respondents remained as of April 18, 2022: Wiltshire, Ohio Wholesale Auto Sales, and the 
Franklin County Treasurer. 
{¶ 3} On August 2, 2022, the trial court held a status conference and, based on the 
parties’ representations at that conference, set the matter for an evidentiary hearing “to 
determine Defendant Wiltshire Capital Partners’ LP’s standing in this matter.” (Aug. 3, 
2022 Order.) Before the scheduled hearing, the trial court issued an August 11, 2022 order 
vacating the hearing order and directing the parties to submit briefing and any evidence 
regarding Wiltshire’s “standing,” stating it would “rule on the issue without oral 
arguments.” (Aug. 11, 2022 Order.) The court ordered the parties to submit their briefs 
and any evidence by August 26, 2022. Ohio Wholesale Auto Sales timely filed a brief 
indicating that Wiltshire had filed a complaint for foreclosure in 2017, under Franklin C.P. 
case No. 17CV-7723, involving Wiltshire’s same mortgage interest at issue in the current 
eminent domain action. Conversely, Wiltshire submitted an untimely brief on September 1, 
2022, along with a motion for leave to file it. The court denied Wiltshire’s motion for leave 
No. 25AP-467 3 

and did not consider Wiltshire’s brief. Neither the City of Columbus nor the Franklin 
County Treasurer submitted a brief. 
{¶ 4} On July 24, 2023, the trial court issued a “Decision and Entry Regarding 
Status of Defendant Wiltshire Capital Partners LP. ” In the decision and entry, the trial 
court determined that because Wiltshire had its claim decided adversely against it in a 
separate foreclosure action involving the same mortgage interest at issue here, res judicata 
applied and Wiltshire “no longer has a stake in any matter relating to the mortgage and 
cannot claim some real interest in the subject matter of the action to fulfill its jurisdictional 
requirement.” (Decision & Entry at 5.) Based on this finding, the trial court determined 
that Wiltshire “has no standing and its claim is barred by res judicata” and, thus, ordered 
that Wiltshire “is barred from presenting any claims based on the mortgage and promissory 
note which it first advanced in the 2017 Foreclosure.” Id. Wiltshire timely appealed, but 
this court did not reach the merits because it dismissed the appeal for lack of a final, 
appealable order. Columbus Mun. Corp. v. Wiltshire Capital Partners, LP, 2024-Ohio-
2180, ¶ 19 (10th Dist.).1 
{¶ 5} On April 2, 2025, the trial court reinstated the matter to active status and 
scheduled a status conference “to discuss the procedural posture of [the] litigation.” (Apr. 
2, 2025 Order to Reinstate & Notice of Status Conference.) At the status conference , 
counsel for the City of Columbus indicated that a settlement had been reached with Ohio 
Wholesale Auto Sales , but that Wiltshire had objected to that settlement based on its 
asserted interest in the property. Counsel for Ohio Wholesale Auto Sales argued that, for 
multiple reasons, Wiltshire ha d no valid mortgage interest in the property and that, 
therefore, the matter should move forward to final judgment, with approval of the 
settlement agreement and transfer of title with payment to Ohio Wholesale Auto Sales . 
Opposing this resolution, Wiltshire’s counsel argued that the status conference should have 
been limited to the case’s procedural posture, not substantive issues. 

1 Although this court did not reach the merits of the appeal, this court noted that the trial court’s purported 
determination of Wiltshire’s lack of “standing” was contrary to general notions of standing , as the City of 
Columbus named Wiltshire as a defendant in the appropriation action. See Columbus Mun. Corp. at ¶ 17 
(“An assertion of lack of standing is typically understood as a challenge to the capacity of party to bring an 
action.”) (Emphasis deleted.). Whether res judicata precludes Wiltshire from claiming a mortgage interest 
in the subject property is not a standing issue. 
No. 25AP-467 4 

{¶ 6} On May 2, 2025, the trial court filed an entry noting that “[a]t issue in this 
case is Wiltshire’s contention that it possesses a mortgage interest in the property sought 
to be taken through eminent domain by” the City of Columbus. (May 2, 2025 Entry at 1.) 
It also noted that on July 24, 2023, it “determined that Wiltshire’s right to assert a mortgage 
interest in the premises has been foreclosed and terminated by an earlier mortgage 
foreclosure filed by Wiltshire that the Court dismissed, pursuant to Civil Rule 41(B)(1), for 
failure to prosecute.” Id. In addition to this determination, the trial court agreed with Ohio 
Wholesale Auto Sales’ contention that Wiltshire was “precluded from asserting its alleged 
interest in the premises because of its failure to set forth an interest in the premises and 
apparent assignment of the note that underlies its mortgage.” Id. at 2. Consequently, the 
trial court filed an agreed judgment entry on settlement and an entry vesting title in the real 
property in the City of Columbus. 
{¶ 7} Wiltshire timely appeals. 
II. Assignments of Error 
{¶ 8} Wiltshire assigns the following six assignments of error for our review: 
I. The trial court erred by ruling, contrary to law, that a Civ.R. 
41(B)(1) dismissal for failure to prosecute a foreclosure action 
in which service of process on the defendant(s) has not been 
obtained, constitutes an adjudication on the merits and, 
therefore, (a) bars the plaintiff from refiling the foreclosure 
action and (b) by vitiation of the mortgage related to the 
foreclosure action, precludes a mortgagee from the status of 
“owner” within the meaning of R.C. 163.01 (E) and from the 
status of Defendant/Respondent in an appropriation 
proceeding brought pursuant to Chapter 163 of the Ohio 
Revised Code. 

II. The trial court erred in ruling that Appellant Wiltshire does 
not have standing to participate in any manner in an eminent 
domain proceeding that seeks to appropriate property that is 
encumbered by a mortgage lien held by Wiltshire. 

III. The trial court abused its discretion to Wiltshire’s 
substantial prejudice by denying Appellant Wiltshire, the 
Mortgagee of specific property sought for appropriation, leave 
to file its brief and thereby be meaningfully heard during the 
trial court’s determinations on the issue of Wiltshire status in 
the proceeding for appropriation of the mortgaged property, 
and further abused its discretion by also denying Appellant 
No. 25AP-467 5 

Wiltshire’s Motion For Reconsideration made on the grounds 
of excusable neglect. 

IV. The trial court’s actions of entering an Order barring 
respondent-appellant Wiltshire from presenting claims based 
on Wiltshire’s mortgage interest on the property sought for 
appropriation, then subsequently entering an Order adverse 
to Wiltshire based on a rationale of Wiltshire’s failure to 
present claims advancing its mortgage interest constitutes an 
unreasonable abuse of discretion. 

V. The trial court erred as a matter of law and to respondent -
appellant Wiltshire’s substantial prejudice by imposing on 
Wiltshire an Order barring Wiltshire from presenting claims 
based on his mortgage in the eminent domain case. 

VI. The trial court erred by proceeding on a hearing of an oral 
R.C. 163.18 motion for distribution at a hearing event 
docketed as a “status conference” to discuss the “procedural 
posture” of the litigation in Case Number 21CV-5236. 
III. Discussion 
{¶ 9} Because they involve interrelated issues, we discuss together Wiltshire’s first, 
second, fourth, and fifth assignments of error. Wiltshire’s first assignment of error 
contends that the trial court erred in ruling that the Civ.R. 41(B)(1) dismissal in case No. 
17CV-7723 was an adjudication on the merits and precluded Wiltshire from claiming the 
status of owner under R.C. 163.01(E) for the purpose of the City of Columbus’ appropriation 
action. Wiltshire’s second assignment of error alleges that the trial court erred in ruling 
that Wiltshire lacked standing to participate in the appropriation action. And in both its 
fourth and fifth assignments of error, Wiltshire contends that the trial court erred in barring 
it from presenting any claims based on its mortgage interest in the property. Thus, each 
assignment of error challenges the trial court’s determination that res judicata barred 
Wiltshire from asserting its claimed interest in the property in the appropriation action. 
These assignments of error have merit. 
{¶ 10} The doctrine of res judicata encompasses both claim preclusion, also known 
as res judicata or estoppel by judgment, and issue preclusion, also known as collateral 
estoppel. State v. C.L.H ., 2019-Ohio-3786, ¶ 15 (10th Dist.). At issue here is whether 
Wiltshire was precluded, in the appropriation action, from asserting a mortgage interest in 
the property based on the previous dismiss al, pursuant to Civ.R. 41(B)(1) , for failure to 
No. 25AP-467 6 

prosecute the mortgage foreclosure action filed by Wiltshire. The trial court found that the 
dismissal of the foreclosure action precluded Wiltshire from asserting its interest in the 
appropriation action. We disagree. 
{¶ 11} In August 2017, Wiltshire filed a mortgage foreclosure complaint, which was 
assigned case No. 17CV-7723. In that action, on March 5, 2018, the trial court filed a notice 
of intent to dismis

UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS 

FOR THE TENTH CIRCUIT 
_________________________________ 
In re: LINN W. JENSEN, 

 Debtor. 

------------------------------ 

LINN W. JENSEN, 

 Plaintiff - Appellant, 

v. 

THE BANK OF NEW YORK MELLON, 
f/k/a The Bank of New York, as Trustee for 
the Certificate Holders of CWMBS, Inc., 
CHL Mortgage Pass-Through Trust 
2005-1, Mortgage Pass-Through 
Certificates, Series 2005-1; NEWREZ 
LLC, d/b/a Shellpoint Mortgage Servicing, 

 Defendants - Appellees. 

No. 25-1430 
(D.C. No. 1:22-CV-00837-RM) 
(D. Colo.) 
_________________________________ 
ORDER AND JUDGMENT* 
_________________________________ 
Before HARTZ, TYMKOVICH, and McHUGH, Circuit Judges. 
_________________________________ 

* After examining the briefs and appellate record, this panel has determined 
unanimously that oral argument would not materially assist in the determination of 
this appeal. See Fed. R. App. P. 34(a)(2); 10th Cir. R. 34.1(G). The case is therefore 
ordered submitted without oral argument. This order and judgment is not binding 
precedent, except under the doctrines of law of the case, res judicata, and collateral 
estoppel. It may be cited, however, for its persuasive value c onsistent with 
Fed. R. App. P. 32.1 and 10th Cir. R. 32.1 . 
FILED 
United States Court of Appeals 
Tenth Circuit 

November 5, 2026 

Christopher M. Wolpert 
Clerk of Court 
Appellate Case: 25-1430 Document: 34 Date Filed: 11/05/2026 Page: 1 
2 
Linn Jensen, proceeding pro se 1, appeals a dist rict court order that affirmed an 
order by a b ankruptcy court permitting a proof of claim to real property she owned 
(the “Property”) filed by Bank of New York Mellon (the “Bank”) and overruling her 
statute -of-limitations -based objections thereto. We have jurisdiction under 
28 U.S.C. § 1291, and we affirm. 
BACKGROUND 
In 2004, the Property was owned by Mark and Sonya Ashmore, who 
mortgaged it. The Bank came to hold the note secured by a deed of trust on the 
Property. The note required monthly payments through 2035. By June 2010, the 
Ashmores were in default on the note. The Bank sent Mr. Ashmore a notice of intent 
to accelerate and, a year later, filed a “Notice of Election and Demand for Sale” 
(“NED”) with the Boulder County Public Trustee. But, ultimately, the Bank 
withdrew the NED and did not proceed with the sale. 
The Bank restarted foreclosure proceedings in January 2013 with a second 
NED. The Property was auctioned to Resurgent Capital Services, LP, which paid 
Mr. Ashmore $2,000 to get him to move out but then set aside the sale and reinstated 
the note and deed of trust. The Bank then withdrew its second NED. In 2015, the 
Bank filed and then withdrew a third NED. 

1 Because Ms. Jensen proceed s pro se, we construe her arguments liberally, but 
we “cannot take on the responsibility of serving as [her] attorney in constructing 
arguments and searching the record.” Garrett v. Selby Connor Maddux & Janer , 
425 F.3d 836, 840 (10th Cir. 2005). 
Appellate Case: 25-1430 Document: 34 Date Filed: 11/05/2026 Page: 2 
3 
In 2017, the Ashmores quitclaimed their interests in the Property to 
Ms. Jensen. In 2019, the Bank filed a fourth NED and obtained from the Boulder 
County District Court an order authorizing a foreclosure sale. But before it could 
complete the sale, Ms. Jensen filed for Chapter 13 bankruptcy. 
In the bankruptcy court, t he Bank filed a proof of claim related to the Property , 
and Ms. Jensen initiated an adversary proceeding objecting on statute- of-limitations 
grounds. She argued the statute of limitations ran six years after the Bank filed the 
first NED. The bankruptcy court rejected Ms. Jensen’s argument, finding after a trial 
that the Bank abandoned acceleration of the note when it withdrew the 2011, 2013, 
and 2015 NEDs , which reinstated the original maturity date of the note for statute -of-
limitations -accrual purposes . Ms. Jensen appealed to the district court, which 
affirmed, and thereafter to this court. 
DISCUSSION 
“In an appeal in a bankruptcy case, we independently review the bankruptcy 
court’s decision, applying the same standard as the . . . district court.” Miller v. Bill 
and Carolyn Limited P’ship (In re Baldwin ), 593 F.3d 1155, 1159 (10th Cir. 2010). 
“In doing so, we treat the . . . district court as a subordinate appellate tribunal whose 
rulings are not entitled to any deference . . . .” Aviva Life & Annuity Co. v. White (In 
re Millennium Multiple Emp. Welfare Ben efit Plan), 772 F.3d 634, 638 
(10th Cir. 2014) (internal quotation marks omitted). So, like the district court, “[w]e 
review findings of fact pursuant to a clearly erroneous standard and conclusions of 
Appellate Case: 25-1430 Document: 34 Date Filed: 11/05/2026 Page: 3 
4 
law de novo.” Stillwater Nat. Bank & Tr. Co. v. CIT Grp./Equip. Fin., Inc. , 
383 F.3d 1148, 1150 (10th Cir. 2004). 
Because the Property was located in Colorado, we apply Colorado law to this 
dispute. See Lindsay v. Beneficial Reins. Co. (In re Lindsay) , 59 F.3d 942, 948 
(9th Cir. 1995) (“Texas law controls in this case, because the real estate foreclosed 
on is in Texas. . . . The security of land title in Texas should not be compromised by 
applying the law of a different state to Texas foreclosure sales.”); see also id. at 948–
49 (“The deed of trust said that any foreclosure sale should follow Texas law. No 
serious argument can be made for applying the law of any state but Texas to the 
Texas real estate foreclosure.”); R. vol. 1 at 211 (d eed of trust, stating “[t]his 
Security Instrument shall be governed by federal law and the law of the jurisdiction 
in which the Property is located .” (emphasis added)). 
When applying Colorado law, “[i ]f the Colorado Supreme Court has not 
decided an issue, our task is to predict how it would rule.” Evanston Ins. Co. v. L aw 
Off. of Michael P. Medved, P.C. , 890 F.3d 1195, 1198 (10th Cir. 2018). And in so 
doing, “we follow the opinions of an intermediate state appellate court unless 
convinced by other persuasive data that the highest court of the state would decide 
otherwise.” Id. at 1200 (internal quotation marks omitted). 
Under Colorado law, the statute of limitations to foreclose is six years. 
Colo. Rev. Stat. § 38-39-207 (“The lien created by any instrument shall be 
extinguished, regardless of any other provision in this article to the contrary, at the 
same time that the right to commence a suit to enforce payment of the indebtedness 
Appellate Case: 25-1430 Document: 34 Date Filed: 11/05/2026 Page: 4 
5 
or performance of the obligation secured by the lien is barred by any statute of 
limitation of this state.”); id . § 13-80-103.5(1)(a) (setting six- year statute of 
limitations for “all actions for the enforcement of rights set forth in any instrument 
securing the payment of or evidencing any debt”). When a lender exercises its right 
under a note repayable in installments to accelerate amounts due because of a 
debtor’s default, “the entire remaining balance of the loan becomes due immediately 
and the statute of limitations is triggered for all installments that had not previously 
become due.” Hassler v. Acct. Brokers of Larimer Cnty., Inc. , 274 P.3d 547, 553 
(Colo. 2012). 
Colorado’s intermediate appellate courts , following the “great weight of 
authority,” have held that “in Colorado, a lender may abandon the acceleration of a 
note.” Bank of N .Y. Mellon v. Peterson , 442 P.3d 1006, 1011 (Colo. App. 2018), 
modified on reh’g (Jan. 10, 2019); see also Igou v. Bank of Am., N.A. , 459 P.3d 776, 
780 (Colo. App. 2020) (“[A] creditor may abandon . . . acceleration. To do so, the 
creditor must manifest its intent to abandon acceleration by a clear affirmative act. 
Abandoning the acceleration restores the [note’s] original maturity date for purposes 
of accrual of the statute of limitations.” (internal quotation marks and citations 
omitted)). This holding follows the Colorado Supreme Court’s holding “that the 
doctrine of waiver applies to acceleration.” See Peterson, 442 P.3d at 1011 (citing 
Goodwin v. Dist. Ct ., 779 P.2d 837, 843 -44 (Colo. 1989)). 
Ms. Jensen argues this court should apply New York law to determine when 
the statute of limitations began to run, see Aplt. Opening Br. at 3–4, but she provides 
Appellate Case: 25-1430 Document: 34 Date Filed: 11/05/2026 Page: 5 
6 
no reason New York law would control here, nor does she provide any basis to 
conclude the Colorado Supreme Court would be more likely to apply New York 
common law than to apply the rule set forth in Peterson and Igou. 
The Bank manifested its intent to abandon acceleration of its security interest 
in the Property when it withdrew the NEDs in 2011, 2013, and 2015. That 
abandonment restored the note’s original maturity date for purposes of when the 
statute of limitations accrued. So the statute of limitations had not run when it 
foreclosed on Ms. Jensen. The bankruptcy court did not err in so ruling. 2 
CONCLUSION 
We affirm the judgment of the district court. 
Entered for the Court 

Timothy M. Tymkovich 
Circuit Judge 

2 Ms. Jensen also asserts, in passing, that proceedings in the bankruptcy court 
were “hobbled by . . . a Covid Era Zoom Trial which posed many challenges for a 
fair and manageable trial ” Aplt. Opening Br. at 2. But she does not develop this 
argument any further, including an explanation of whether the court reached any 
adverse findings due to its being so “hobbled” or an explanation as to why the trial 
was unfair or mismanaged Because the statement is conclusory and undeveloped, we 
conclude she has waived any argument on th ese points, and consider them no further. 
See United States v. Woodmore, 135 F.4th 861, 877 (10th Cir. 2025) (“Under the 
doctrine of appellate- briefing waiver, a litigant may waive appellate review of an 
issue by not arguing it —or arguing it in an inadequate manner —in one’ s opening 
brief. This rule applies to arguments that are advanced in an opening brief only in a 
perfunctory manner.” (internal quotation marks and citation omitted)). 
Appellate Case: 25-1430 Document: 34 Date Filed: 11/05/2026 Page: 6

Third District Court of Appeal
 State of Florida

 PER CURIAM.

leads.caseName: Blue Castle (Cayman), Ltd. v. Dacosta
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Blue Castle (Cayman), Ltd. v Dacosta 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06409 
 November 4, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Blue Castle (Cayman), Ltd., respondent, 
 v 
 Andrea Dacosta, et. al., appellants, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on November 4, 2026 
 2025-04477, 2025-10291, (Index No. 64323/24) 
 Colleen D. Duffy, J.P. 
 Betsy Barros 
 Barry E. Warhit 
 Lisa S. Ottley, JJ. 

 Alice A. Nicholson, Brooklyn, NY, for appellants. 
 Hasbani & Light, P.C., New York, NY (Danielle P. Light of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the defendants Andrea Dacosta and Simone Pimentel-Ortiz appeal from (1) an order of the Supreme Court, Westchester County (Robert S. Ondrovic, J.), dated February 24, 2025, and (2) an order and judgment of foreclosure and sale (one paper) of the same court dated July 25, 2025. The order, insofar as appealed from, granted those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against those defendants and to strike their affirmative defense alleging the expiration of the statute of limitations and denied the cross-motion of those defendants for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them. The order and judgment of foreclosure and sale granted the plaintiff's unopposed motion to confirm a referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale, confirmed the referee's report, and directed the sale of the real property at issue. 
 ORDERED that the appeal from the order is dismissed; and it is further, 
 ORDERED that the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale is affirmed; and it is further, 
 ORDERED that one bill of costs is awarded to the plaintiff. 
 In 2013, LoanCare, a division of FNF Servicing, Inc., commenced an action (hereinafter the first action) against the defendants Andrea Dacosta and Simone Pimentel-Ortiz (hereinafter together the defendants), among others, to foreclose a mortgage encumbering certain real property located in Yonkers (hereinafter the property). In the complaint, LoanCare elected to accelerate the entire mortgage debt. In an order dated April 29, 2016, the complaint in the first action was dismissed for failure to prosecute pursuant to CPLR 3215(c). 
 Thereafter, in October 2018, a subsequent assignee commenced a second foreclosure action (hereinafter the second action) against the defendants, among others, to foreclose the same mortgage. In an order and judgment dated November 30, 2023, after a hearing, the complaint in the second action was dismissed insofar as asserted against the defendants for failure to properly serve the defendants. 
 In June 2024, the plaintiff commenced this action against the defendants, among [*2] others, to foreclose the same mortgage. In their answer, the defendants alleged, among other affirmative defenses, that the action was time-barred. The plaintiff moved, inter alia, for summary judgment on the complaint and to strike the defendants' affirmative defense alleging the expiration of the statute of limitations on the ground, inter alia, that no state statute of limitations applied since prior to the plaintiff's ownership, a note and the mortgage were held by the Government National Mortgage Association (hereinafter GNMA) as one of several predecessors in interest to LoanCare. The plaintiff alleged that GNMA is immune from the application of New York's statute of limitations and that after GNMA held the note and the mortgage, and after several subsequent assignments, the note and the mortgage were assigned to the plaintiff. The defendants opposed the plaintiff's motion and cross-moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them as time-barred, contending that the statute of limitations began to run in 2013, when the first action was filed. 
 In an order dated February 24, 2025 (hereinafter the February 2025 order), the Supreme Court, among other things, granted those branches of the plaintiff's motion and, in effect, denied the defendants' cross-motion. In an order and judgment of foreclosure and sale dated July 25, 2025, the court granted the plaintiff's unopposed motion to confirm a referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale, confirmed the referee's report, and directed the sale of the property. The defendants appeal from the February 2025 order and the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale. 
 The appeal from the February 2025 order must be dismissed because the right of direct appeal therefrom terminated with the entry of the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale in the action ( see Matter of Aho , 39 NY2d 241, 248 ). The issues raised on the appeal from the February 2025 order are brought up for review and have been considered on the appeal from the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale ( see CPLR 5501[a][1]; Matter of Aho , 39 NY2d at 248 ). 
 Although the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale was entered upon the default of the defendants in opposing the plaintiff's motion to confirm the referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale, the defendants may obtain review of "matters which were the subject of contest" before the Supreme Court ( James v Powell , 19 NY2d 249 ; see Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Harrison , 188 AD3d 1298 , 1299). Since the defendants opposed the plaintiff's motion, inter alia, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendants and cross-moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them as time-barred, appellate review of the February 2025 order is permitted. 
 An action to foreclose a mortgage is governed by a six-year statute of limitations ( see CPLR 213[4]). "[E]ven if a mortgage is payable in installments, once a mortgage debt is accelerated, the entire amount is due and the statute of limitations begins to run on the entire debt" ( Bank of N.Y. Mellon v Mor , 201 AD3d 691, 694 ). The entire mortgage debt will be deemed to have been accelerated by the commencement of a mortgage foreclosure action in which the complaint seeks payment of the full outstanding loan balance ( see U.S. Bank N.A. v Connor , 204 AD3d 861, 863 ). 
 Nevertheless, "[t]here is no federal statute of limitations applicable to mortgage foreclosure actions brought by the United States or its federal agencies" ( Fleet Natl. Bank v D'Orsi , 26 AD3d 898, 899 ; see RCR Servs. v Herbil Holding Co. , 229 AD2d 379, 380 ). "That rule applies equally to an assignee of a federal agency, including a commercial lender, and includes the benefit of immunity from a state limitations period" ( Fleet Natl. Bank v D'Orsi , 26 AD3d at 899 ; see RCR Servs. v Herbil Holding Co. , 339 AD2d at 380). 
 Here, the plaintiff established, prima facie, that the mortgage was previously held by GNMA, which is a federal government entity ( see 12 UCS § 1717[a][2][A]; RCR Servs. v Herbil Holding Co. , 229 AD2d at 380 ). In support of its motion and in opposition to the defendants' cross-motion, the plaintiff submitted, inter alia, the note, which was endorsed to the Secretary of the United States Department of Housing and Urban Development, the mortgage assignment to GNMA dated April 4, 2012, and recorded on April 5, 2013, and the subsequent assignment of the mortgage to the plaintiff dated February 1, 2022, and recorded on February 18, 2022. Therefore, the plaintiff, as an assignee of a federal agency, demonstrated that New York's statute of limitations was inapplicable and, thus, established its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law dismissing the defendants' affirmative defense alleging the expiration of the statute of limitations. 
 The defendants failed to raise a triable issue of fact in opposition to those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendants and to strike their affirmative defense alleging the expiration of the statute of limitations or to establish their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them. Contrary to the defendants' contention, GNMA had a right, as set forth in the note, to foreclose the mortgage, which was subsequently assigned to the plaintiff ( see RCR Servs. v Herbil Holding Co. , 229 AD2d at 380 ). 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted those branches of plaintiff's motion which were for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendants and to strike the defendants' affirmative defense alleging the expiration of the statute of limitations and denied the defendants' cross-motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them as time-barred. 
 DUFFY, J.P., BARROS, WARHIT and OTTLEY, JJ., concur.

leads.caseName: Desrosiers v. U.S. Bank Natl. Assn.
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Desrosiers v U.S. Bank Natl. Assn. 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06414 
 November 4, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Samuel Desrosiers, respondent, 
 v 
 U.S. Bank National Association, etc., et al., appellants, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on November 4, 2026 
 2024-01471, 2024-04280, (Index No. 615476/22) 
 Betsy Barros, J.P. 
 Barry E. Warhit 
 Janice A. Taylor 
 Susan Quirk, JJ. 

 Friedman Vartolo LLP, Garden City, NY (Stephen J. Vargas of counsel), for appellants. 
 Charles Wallshein, Melville, NY, for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4) to cancel and discharge of record a mortgage, the defendants U.S. Bank National Association and Mortgage Electronic Registration Systems, Inc., appeal from (1) an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Christopher Modelewski, J.), dated February 8, 2024, and (2) a judgment of the same court dated May 14, 2024. The order granted the plaintiff's motion for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendants U.S. Bank National Association and Mortgage Electronic Registration Systems, Inc., and, in effect, for summary judgment dismissing the counterclaim of the defendant U.S. Bank National Association and denied those branches of those defendants' cross-motion which were for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them and on the counterclaim of the defendant U.S. Bank National Association. The judgment, upon the order, is in favor of the plaintiff and against those defendants and directed the Suffolk County Clerk to discharge of record the subject mortgage. 
 ORDERED that the appeal from the order is dismissed; and it is further, 
 ORDERED that the judgment is affirmed; and it is further, 
 ORDERED that one bill of costs is awarded to the plaintiff. 
 The appeal from the order must be dismissed because the right of direct appeal therefrom terminated with the entry of the judgment in the action ( see Matter of Aho , 39 NY2d 241, 248). The issues raised on the appeal from the order are brought up for review and have been considered on the appeal from the judgment ( see CPLR 5501[a][1]; Matter of Aho , 39 NY2d at 248). 
 In October 2006, Samuel Desrosiers (hereinafter the borrower) executed a note in the sum of $340,000 in favor of Lehman Brothers Bank, FSB (hereinafter Lehman). The note was secured by a mortgage on certain real property located in Amityville. The borrower allegedly defaulted on his obligations under the note and mortgage by failing to make the monthly payments [*2] due April 1, 2008, and thereafter. 
 On July 30, 2008, Mortgage Electronic Registration Systems, Inc. (hereinafter MERS), as nominee for Lehman, commenced an action against the borrower, among others, to foreclose the mortgage (hereinafter the 2008 action). A judgment of foreclosure and sale was entered on February 18, 2010. 
 In an order dated March 7, 2011, the Supreme Court vacated the judgment of foreclosure and sale and directed dismissal of the complaint based upon a finding that service of process was not properly effected upon the borrower. 
 On August 8, 2022, the borrower commenced this action pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4) to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage and, after issue was joined, moved for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against U.S. Bank National Association (hereinafter U.S. Bank), the current holder of the mortgage loan, and MERS and, in effect, for summary judgment dismissing the counterclaim of U.S. Bank alleging unjust enrichment. U.S. Bank and MERS cross-moved, inter alia, for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them and on the counterclaim of U.S. Bank alleging unjust enrichment. Those defendants argued, among other things, that the statute of limitations had not expired because MERS lacked standing to commence the 2008 action and, thus, the statute of limitations had not begun to run. 
 In an order dated February 8, 2024, the Supreme Court granted the borrower's motion and denied those branches of the cross-motion of U.S. Bank and MERS which were for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them and on the counterclaim of U.S. Bank. 
 In a judgment dated May 14, 2024, the Supreme Court, upon the order, directed the Suffolk County Clerk to discharge of record the mortgage. U.S. Bank and MERS appeal. 
 RPAPL 1501(4) provides that "[w]here the period allowed by the applicable statute of limitation for the commencement of an action to foreclose a mortgage . . . has expired, any person having an estate or interest in the real property subject to such encumbrance may maintain an action . . . to secure the cancellation and discharge of record of such encumbrance, and to adjudge the estate or interest of the plaintiff in such real property to be free therefrom" ( see Bank of Am., N.A. v Scher , 205 AD3d 985, 987-988). An action to foreclose a mortgage is governed by a six-year statute of limitations ( see CPLR 213[4]). "[E]ven if a mortgage is payable in installments, once a mortgage debt is accelerated, the entire amount is due and the statute of limitations begins to run on the entire debt" ( Bank of N.Y. Mellon v Mor , 201 AD3d 691, 694; see Cohen v Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. , 229 AD3d 758, 760-761). "An acceleration of a mortgage debt can occur when a creditor commences an action to foreclose upon a note and mortgage and seeks, in the complaint, payment of the full balance due" ( Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Lefkowitz , 171 AD3d 843, 844 [internal quotation marks omitted]). 
 "[S]ervice of a complaint is ineffective to constitute a valid exercise of the option to accelerate a debt where the plaintiff does not have the authority to accelerate the debt or to sue to foreclose at that time" ( U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Atedgi , 236 AD3d 707, 711 [internal quotation marks omitted]). However, CPLR 213(4), as amended by the Foreclosure Abuse and Prevention Act (FAPA) (L 2022, ch 821), provides, in relevant part, that in an action pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4) to cancel and discharge of record a mortgage, "a defendant shall be estopped from asserting that the period allowed by the applicable statute of limitation for the commencement of an action upon the instrument has not expired because the instrument was not validly accelerated prior to, or by way of commencement of a prior action, unless the prior action was dismissed based on an expressed judicial determination, made upon a timely interposed defense, that the instrument was not validly accelerated" (CPLR 213[4][b]; see Brennan v Deutsche Bank Trust Co. Ams. , 237 AD3d 1027, 1030). 
 Here, the borrower demonstrated, prima facie, that the statute of limitations began to run on July 30, 2008, when MERS, as nominee for Lehman, commenced the 2008 action and elected in the complaint to "accelerate the mortgage balance and declare the same to be immediately due and payable" ( see Citimortgage, Inc. v Gunn , 234 AD3d 922, 923). The borrower further demonstrated, prima facie, that the instant action was commenced on August 8, 2022, more than six years later ( see Cohen v Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. , 229 AD3d at 760). 
 In opposition, U.S. Bank and MERS failed to raise a triable issue of fact. Their contention that the complaint in the 2008 action did not constitute a valid acceleration of the debt because MERS lacked standing to commence that action is precluded by CPLR 213(4)(b) because the 2008 action was not dismissed "based on an expressed judicial determination, made upon a timely interposed defense, that the instrument was not validly accelerated" ( id. ; see Brennan v Deutsche Bank Trust Co. Ams. , 237 AD3d 1027, 1029). There is no merit to their contention that FAPA does not apply retroactively ( see Van Dyke v U.S. Bank, N.A. , 45 NY3d 461; Article 13 LLC v Ponce De Leon Fed. Bank , 45 NY3d 441). Their challenges to the constitutionality of the retroactive application of FAPA are also without merit ( see Van Dyke v U.S. Bank, N.A. , 45 NY3d 461; Article 13 LLC v Ponce De Leon Fed. Bank , 45 NY3d 441; FV-1, Inc. v Palaguachi , 234 AD3d 818, 822). 
 With respect to the counterclaim of U.S. Bank, "'[t]o prove unjust enrichment, a party must show that the other party was enriched at his or her expense, and [that] it is against equity and good conscience to permit that person to retain what is sought to be recovered'" ( Daniels v Ruggiero , 230 AD3d 563, 565, quoting Delidimitropoulos v Karantinidis , 186 AD3d 1489, 1491; see Daldan, Inc. v Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. , 188 AD3d 989, 991). However, the voluntary payment doctrine "bars recovery of payments voluntarily made with full knowledge of the facts, and in the absence of fraud or mistake of material fact or law" ( GITSIT Solutions, LLC v Azcuy , 242 AD3d 956, 959, quoting Dillon v U-A Columbia Cablevision of Westchester , 100 NY2d 525, 526; see Daldan, Inc. v Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. , 188 AD3d at 991). 
 Here, U.S. Bank made no showing that payments it made for real estate taxes, or other payments it made toward the upkeep of the premises, were made accidentally or mistakenly or that it was induced to make such payments by fraud ( see GITSIT Solutions, LLC v Azcuy , 242 AD3d at 959). Thus, it was barred by the voluntary payment doctrine from recovering such payments under the doctrine of unjust enrichment ( see id. at 959-960; Daldan, Inc. v Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. , 188 AD3d at 991-992). 
 The parties' remaining contentions either are without merit or need not be reached in light of our determination. 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the plaintiff's motion for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against U.S. Bank and MERS and, in effect, for summary judgment dismissing the counterclaim of U.S. Bank and denied those branches of those defendants' cross-motion which were for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them and on the counterclaim of U.S. Bank. 
 BARROS, J.P., WARHIT, TAYLOR and QUIRK, JJ., concur.
