leads.caseName: Nationstar Mtge., LLC v. Greenfeld
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Nationstar Mtge., LLC v Greenfeld 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06445 
 November 4, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Nationstar Mortgage, LLC, etc., appellant, 
 v 
 Jehoshea Greenfeld, respondent, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on November 4, 2026 
 2024-05843, (Index No. 520959/20) 
 Betsy Barros, J.P. 
 Barry E. Warhit 
 Janice A. Taylor 
 Susan Quirk, JJ. 

 McCarter & English, LLP, New York, NY (Adam M. Swanson and Timothy W. Salter of counsel), for appellant. 
 Berg & David, PLLC, Inwood, NY (Sholom Wohlgelernter and Abraham David of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Larry D. Martin, J.), dated February 6, 2024. The order, insofar as appealed from, granted the motion of the defendant Jehoshea Greenfeld for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him as time-barred and on his counterclaim pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4) to cancel and discharge of record the subject mortgage and denied those branches of the plaintiff's cross-motion which were for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against that defendant and dismissing that defendant's counterclaim pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4) to cancel and discharge of record the subject mortgage, to strike that defendant's affirmative defense alleging that the action was time-barred, and for an order of reference. 
 ORDERED that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs. 
 In July 2008, the defendant Jehoshea Greenfeld executed a note and mortgage agreement encumbering certain real property located in Brooklyn. In September 2010, CitiMortgage, Inc., as servicer of the note, commenced an action against Greenfeld, among others, to foreclose the mortgage (hereinafter the prior action). A provision of the complaint elected to call due the entire mortgage debt. Greenfeld failed to appear or answer the complaint. 
 In January 2016, after being substituted as the plaintiff in the prior action, Federal National Mortgage Association moved, inter alia, for leave to enter a default judgment against Greenfeld and for an order of reference. Greenfeld cross-moved, among other things, to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him or, in the alternative, to vacate his default in appearing or answering the complaint and for leave to serve a late answer. In an order dated August 15, 2016, the Supreme Court, inter alia, granted those branches of the motion and denied those branches of the cross-motion. 
 Greenfeld appealed from the order dated August 15, 2016. On May 6, 2020, this Court reversed the order insofar as appealed from, denied those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were for leave to enter a default judgment against Greenfeld and for an order of reference, and granted that branch of Greenfeld's cross-motion which was to dismiss the complaint insofar as [*2] asserted against him pursuant to CPLR 3215(c) ( see Federal Natl. Mtge. Assn. v Greenfeld , 183 AD3d 658). 
 Subsequently, in October 2020, the plaintiff, Nationstar Mortgage, LLC, commenced this action against Greenfeld, among others, to foreclose the mortgage. Greenfeld interposed an answer in which he asserted, inter alia, an affirmative defense alleging that this action was time-barred and a counterclaim pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4) to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage. 
 Thereafter, Greenfeld moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him as time-barred, based on the retroactive application of the Foreclosure Abuse Prevention Act (FAPA) (L 2022, ch 821 [eff Dec. 30, 2022]) to this action, and on his counterclaim pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4) to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage. The plaintiff opposed Greenfeld's motion and cross-moved, among other things, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against Greenfeld and dismissing Greenfeld's counterclaim pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4) to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage, to strike Greenfeld's affirmative defense alleging that the action was time-barred, and for an order of reference. Greenfeld opposed the plaintiff's cross-motion. In an order dated February 6, 2024, the Supreme Court, inter alia, granted Greenfeld's motion and denied those branches of the plaintiff's cross-motion. The plaintiff appeals. 
 An action to foreclose a mortgage is governed by a six-year statute of limitations ( see CPLR 213[4]; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Feurtado , 241 AD3d 499, 500; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Dagrin , 233 AD3d 1065, 1066). Pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4), a person who has "an estate or interest in real property subject to a mortgage may maintain an action to secure the cancellation and discharge of the encumbrance, and to adjudge the estate or interests free of it, if the applicable statute of limitations for commencing a foreclosure action has expired" ( U.S. Bank N.A. v Medianik , 223 AD3d 935, 938; see Pryce v U.S. Bank, N.A. , 226 AD3d 711, 712). 
 Even where a mortgage is payable in installments, once the mortgage debt is accelerated, the entire amount is due and the statute of limitation begins to run on the entire debt ( see Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Feurtado , 241 AD3d at 500; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Dagrin , 233 AD3d at 1066). Acceleration occurs, among other ways, by the commencement of a foreclosure action wherein the noteholder elects in the complaint to call due the entire amount secured by the mortgage ( see Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Feurtado , 241 AD3d at 500; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Dagrin , 233 AD3d at 1066-1067). 
 Here, the six-year statute of limitations began to run on the entire mortgage debt in September 2010, with the commencement of the prior action, wherein a provision of the complaint elected to call due the entire mortgage debt. The instant action was commenced in October 2020, more than four years after the statute of limitations expired. 
 Nonetheless, the plaintiff contends that because the dismissal of the prior action in May 2020 was not for "neglect to prosecute" within the meaning of CPLR 205(a), this action was timely commenced pursuant to the six-month savings provision of that statute. However, the plaintiff's contention that it was entitled to rely on the savings provision of CPLR 205(a), notwithstanding the dismissal of the prior action pursuant to CPLR 3215(c), is precluded by FAPA, which replaced the savings provision of CPLR 205(a) with CPLR 205-a in actions, like here, upon instruments described in CPLR 213(4) ( see CPLR 205-a; Nationstar Mtge., LLC v Oliveri , 243 AD3d 579, 580; Bank of N.Y. Mellon Trust Co. v Kyung Lee , 242 AD3d 1163, 1165; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Vista Holding, LLC , 239 AD3d 830, 832). FAPA specifically defines a dismissal pursuant to CPLR 3215(c) as a type of neglect that precludes a plaintiff from taking advantage of the six-month savings provision of CPLR 205-a ( see Nationstar Mtge., LLC v Oliveri , 243 AD3d at 580; Bank of N.Y. Mellon Trust Co. v Kyung Lee , 242 AD3d at 1165; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Vista Holding, LLC , 239 AD3d at 832). 
 Contrary to the plaintiff's contention, the Supreme Court correctly determined that CPLR 205-a applies retroactively to this action and that such retroactive application does not violate [*3] the plaintiff's due process rights under the United States and New York State Constitutions ( see HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v St. Hillaire , 251 AD3d 17; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Vista Holding, LLC , 239 AD3d at 833). 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted Greenfeld's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him as time-barred and on his counterclaim pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4) to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage and denied those branches of the plaintiff's cross-motion which were for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against Greenfeld and dismissing Greenfeld's counterclaim pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4) to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage, to strike Greenfeld's affirmative defense alleging that the action was time-barred, and for an order of reference. 
 In light of our determination, we need not reach Greenfeld's remaining contention. 
 BARROS, J.P., WARHIT, TAYLOR and QUIRK, JJ., concur. 
 ENTER: 
 Darrell M. Joseph 
 Clerk of the Court

leads.caseName: U.S. Bank N.A. v. Rahman
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
U.S. Bank N.A. v Rahman 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06481 
 November 4, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 U.S. Bank National Association, appellant, 
 v 
 Sharmina X. Rahman, et al., defendants, 153 Pulaski Street, LLC, respondent. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on November 4, 2026 
 2025-00786, (Index No. 535025/22) 
 Francesca E. Connolly, J.P. 
 Deborah A. Dowling 
 Lillian Wan 
 Susan Quirk, JJ. 

 Robertson, Anschutz, Schneid, Crane & Partners, PLLC, Westbury, NY (Joseph F. Battista of counsel), for appellant. 
 Bronstein, Gewirtz & Grossman, LLC, New York, NY (Edward N. Gewirtz of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Larry D. Martin, J.), dated July 9, 2024. The order granted the motion of the defendant 153 Pulaski Street, LLC, for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it as time-barred. 
 ORDERED that the order is affirmed, with costs. 
 In January 2010, the plaintiff commenced an action against the defendant Sharmina X. Rahman, among others, to foreclose a mortgage encumbering certain real property located in Brooklyn (hereinafter the 2010 action), electing in the complaint to accelerate the mortgage debt. By order dated August 15, 2013, the Supreme Court directed dismissal of the 2010 action as abandoned pursuant to CPLR 3215(c). In November 2015, the plaintiff allegedly sent Rahman a letter to revoke the acceleration of the mortgage debt (hereinafter the de-acceleration letter). At or around the same time, Rahman transferred her entire interest in the property to the defendant 153 Pulaski Street, LLC (hereinafter the defendant). 
 In November 2022, the plaintiff commenced the instant action to foreclose the same mortgage against the defendant, among others. The defendant interposed an answer in which it asserted various affirmative defenses, including that the action was barred by the statute of limitations. Thereafter, the defendant moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it as time-barred. The plaintiff opposed the motion. In an order dated July 9, 2024, the Supreme Court granted the defendant's motion. The plaintiff appeals. 
 An action to foreclose a mortgage is governed by a six-year statute of limitations ( see CPLR 213[4]). Where the mortgage debt is accelerated, the entire balance of the debt accrues and the statute of limitations begins to run on the full amount due ( see U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Miele , 243 AD3d 718 , 720; Citibank, N.A. v Horan , 230 AD3d 1216 , 1217). The entire mortgage debt will be deemed to have been accelerated, as relevant here, by the commencement of a mortgage foreclosure action in which the complaint seeks payment of the full outstanding loan balance ( see Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Mayer , 244 AD3d 686 , 688; U.S. Bank N.A. v Connor , 204 AD3d 861, 863 ). 
 Here, the defendant demonstrated, prima facie, that the six-year statute of limitations began to run in January 2010, when the plaintiff commenced the 2010 action and elected in the complaint to call due the entire amount secured by the mortgage ( see Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Mayer , 244 AD3d at 688; Citimortgage, Inc. v Gunn , 234 AD3d 922 , 923). The defendant further demonstrated that the instant action was commenced in November 2022, more than six years later, and is, therefore, time-barred ( see Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Vista Holding, LLC , 239 AD3d 830 , 832; U.S. Bank N.A. v Doura , 204 AD3d 721, 723 ). 
 In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact as to whether the statute of limitations was tolled or otherwise inapplicable, or whether the plaintiff had actually commenced this action within the applicable limitations period. 
 Contrary to the plaintiff's contention, the de-acceleration letter did not revoke the prior election to accelerate the debt. After the enactment of the Foreclosure Abuse Prevention Act (FAPA) (L 2022, ch 821), a noteholder can no longer unilaterally revoke a prior election to accelerate the debt ( see CPLR 203[h]; FV-I, Inc. v Samuels , 240 AD3d 757 , 759; Bank of N.Y. Mellon v Stewart , 216 AD3d 720, 723 ). The plaintiff's arguments challenging FAPA's retroactive application and constitutionality are without merit ( see Van Dyke v U.S. Bank, N.A. , 45 NY3d 461 , 474; Article 13 LLC v Ponce De Leon Fed. Bank , 45 NY3d 441 , 452-453; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Feurtado , 241 AD3d 499 , 501). 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it as time-barred. 
 The plaintiff's remaining contentions are either improperly raised for the first time on appeal or without merit. 
 CONNOLLY, J.P., DOWLING, WAN and QUIRK, JJ., concur.

 Darrell M. Joseph 
 Clerk of the Court

leads.caseName: U.S. Bank N.A. v. Walker
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
U.S. Bank N.A. v Walker 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06482 
 November 4, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 U.S. Bank National Association, etc., respondent, 
 v 
 Michael Walker, et al., appellants, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on November 4, 2026 
 2024-07262, 2024-07263, (Index No. 607402/17) 
 Angela G. Iannacci, J.P. 
 Deborah A. Dowling 
 Carl J. Landicino 
 Laurence L. Love, JJ. 

 Ronald D. Weiss, P.C., Melville, NY (Rosemarie Klie of counsel), for appellants. 
 McCalla Raymer Leibert Pierce, LLP, New York, NY (Harold L. Kofman of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the defendants Michael Walker and Lisa C. Walker appeal from two orders of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (James P. McCormack, J.), both dated May 7, 2024. The first order, insofar as appealed from, granted those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendants Michael Walker and Lisa C. Walker and for an order of reference and denied that branch of the cross-motion of the defendants Michael Walker and Lisa C. Walker which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them. The second order, insofar as appealed from, granted the same relief to the plaintiff and referred the matter to a referee to compute the amount due to the plaintiff. 
 ORDERED that the first order is modified, on the law, by deleting the provision thereof granting those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendants Michael Walker and Lisa C. Walker and for an order of reference, and substituting therefor a provision denying those branches of the motion; as so modified, the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, without costs or disbursements, and so much of the second order as granted those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendants Michael Walker and Lisa C. Walker and for an order of reference and referred the matter to a referee to compute the amount due to the plaintiff is vacated; and it is further, 
 ORDERED that the appeal from the second order is dismissed as academic in light of our determination on the appeal from the first order, without costs or disbursements. 
 In June 2008, the defendants Michael Walker and Lisa C. Walker (hereinafter together the defendants) executed a note in favor of Mortgage Lenders Network USA, Inc. The note was secured by a mortgage on certain residential property located in Valley Stream. The defendants allegedly defaulted on their obligations under the note and mortgage, as modified by a modification agreement dated April 11, 2016. In July 2017, the plaintiff commenced this action against the defendants, among others, to foreclose the mortgage. The defendants interposed an answer asserting various affirmative defenses, including lack of standing. In January 2024, the plaintiff moved, inter [*2] alia, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendants and for an order of reference. The defendants opposed the motion and cross-moved, among other things, for summary judgement dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them for failure to comply with RPAPL 1304 and lack of standing. In an order dated May 7, 2024, the Supreme Court granted the plaintiff's motion and denied the defendants' cross-motion. In a second order also dated May 7, 2024, the court granted the same relief to the plaintiff and referred the matter to a referee to compute the amount due to the plaintiff. The defendants appeal. 
 Where, as here, the plaintiff's standing has been placed in issue by the defendant's answer, "'the plaintiff must prove its standing as part of its prima facie showing on a motion for summary judgment'" ( LNV Corp. v Almberg , 246 AD3d 896 , 899, quoting Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Kingsbury , 171 AD3d 871 , 872). "'A plaintiff has standing to commence a foreclosure action where it is the holder or assignee of the underlying note, either by physical delivery or execution of a written assignment prior to the commencement of the action with the filing of the complaint'" ( LNV Corp. v Allison , 206 AD3d 710, 712 , quoting Nationstar Mtge., LLC v Weisblum , 143 AD3d 866, 868 ). "The plaintiff can establish standing by attaching a copy of the properly endorsed note to the complaint when commencing the action" ( Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Garland , 219 AD3d 962, 963 ). However, "'[w]here there is no allonge or note that is either endorsed in blank or specially endorsed to the plaintiff, mere physical possession of a note at the commencement of a foreclosure action is insufficient to confer standing or to make a plaintiff the lawful holder of a negotiable instrument for the purposes of enforcing the note'" ( LNV Corp. v Allison , 206 AD3d at 712 , quoting U.S. Bank N.A. v Moulton , 179 AD3d 734, 737 ). 
 Here, contrary to the plaintiff's contention, it failed to establish its standing based on its attachment of the note to the complaint. The copy of the note attached to the complaint was not endorsed in blank and did not reflect that it was specially endorsed to the plaintiff, given that the name of the entity to whom the note was specifically endorsed did not exactly reflect the name of the plaintiff in this action ( see Residential Mtge. Loan Trust 2013-TT2 v Kaodichimma , 212 AD3d 742, 743 ). The assignments of mortgage in the record were also insufficient to establish the plaintiff's standing, as, according to those documents, the mortgage was not assigned to the plaintiff until December 2019, after the commencement of this action in July 2017. 
 Moreover, an affidavit of Talya Harris submitted in support of the plaintiff's motion was insufficient to establish, prima facie, the plaintiff's standing. Harris stated that she was an employee of Nationstar, the plaintiff's loan servicer. However, Harris did not state that Nationstar, as agent for the plaintiff, was in possession of the note at the time that the action was commenced ( see Bank of N.Y. Mellon v Ettinger , 176 AD3d 1152 , 1155), and she failed to annex any business records establishing that Nationstar, as agent for the plaintiff, possessed the note at the time that the action was commenced ( see Star201, LLC v Duran , 233 AD3d 726 , 728). 
 The evidence submitted in support of the plaintiff's motion also failed to establish that the plaintiff strictly complied with RPAPL 1304 prior to the commencement of the action. RPAPL 1304(1) provides that "at least ninety days before a lender, an assignee or a mortgage loan servicer commences legal action against the borrower, . . . including mortgage foreclosure, such lender, assignee or mortgage loan servicer shall give notice to the borrower." "Strict compliance with RPAPL 1304 notice to the borrower or borrowers is a condition precedent to the commencement of a foreclosure action" ( Citibank, N.A. v Conti-Scheurer , 172 AD3d 17 , 20; see Bank of Am., N.A. v Gonzalez , 219 AD3d 433, 434 ). "By requiring the lender or mortgage loan servicer to send the RPAPL 1304 notice by registered or certified mail and also by first-class mail, the Legislature implicitly provided the means for the plaintiff to demonstrate its compliance with the statute, i.e., by proof of the requisite mailing, which can be established with proof of the actual mailings, such as affidavits of mailing or domestic return receipts with attendant signatures, or proof of a standard office mailing procedure designed to ensure that items are properly addressed and mailed, sworn to by someone with personal knowledge of the procedure" ( Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Dennis , 181 AD3d 864, 866 [internal quotation marks omitted]). 
 Here, the plaintiff failed to submit an affidavit of mailing or proof of mailing by the United States Postal Service evidencing that it properly mailed notice to the defendants pursuant to [*3] RPAPL 1304. Instead, the plaintiff relied on the affidavit of Harris, copies of the purported notices, and a spreadsheet purportedly showing that the notices were mailed. Although the notices contained the statement "Sent Via Certified Mail," with a 22-digit number below it, no receipt or corresponding document issued by the United States Postal Service was submitted proving that the notices were actually sent by certified mail more than 90 days prior to commencement of the action ( see Green Tree Servicing, LLC v Helmsorig , 227 AD3d 1053 , 1055; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Dennis , 181 AD3d at 866 ). Further, the plaintiff failed to demonstrate the admissibility of the spreadsheet, as it did not demonstrate that a record, which was created by an entity that was never identified, was incorporated into the plaintiff's or its servicer's records and relied upon in the regular course of their business ( cf. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Kohli , 241 AD3d 1402 , 1404; U.S. Bank N.A. v Romano , 231 AD3d 1079 , 1081). Harris's affidavit was also insufficient to establish a standard office mailing procedure designed to ensure that items are properly addressed and mailed. Although Harris averred that the 90-day notices were mailed "by and through [the plaintiff's] agents," she then stated that she was familiar with the plaintiff's practice and procedure, not the servicer's practice and procedure, for mailing the 90-day notices. Harris did not aver that she was familiar with the mailing practices of the servicer which purportedly sent the notices and failed to otherwise demonstrate familiarity with a standard office practice and procedure designed to ensure that items are properly addressed and mailed ( see Wilmington Trust, N.A. v Singh , 241 AD3d 1404 , 1407; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Dennis , 181 AD3d at 866 ). 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have denied those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendants and for an order of reference without regard to the sufficiency of the defendants' opposition papers ( see Winegrad v New York Univ. Med. Ctr. , 64 NY2d 851, 853 ). 
 However, the Supreme Court properly determined that the defendants were not entitled to summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them on the ground of lack of standing. On a cross-motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint based upon the plaintiff's alleged lack of standing, "the burden is on the moving defendant to establish, prima facie, the plaintiff's lack of standing, rather than on the plaintiff to affirmatively establish its standing in order for the motion to be denied" ( Deutsche Bank Trust Co. Ams. v Vitellas , 131 AD3d 52, 59-60 ). "To defeat a defendant's motion, the plaintiff has no burden of establishing its standing as a matter of law" ( id. at 60 ; see Phoenix Grantor Trust v Exclusive Hospitality, LLC , 172 AD3d 923 , 926). Here, the defendants' submissions failed to eliminate triable issues of fact as to the plaintiff's standing as the holder of the note at the time of the commencement of the action ( see U.S. Bank N.A. v Smith , 221 AD3d 1043, 1045 ). 
 The Supreme Court also properly determined that the defendants were not entitled to summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them on the ground that the plaintiff failed to comply with RPAPL 1304. "[E]ven in the face of a plaintiff's failure to establish, prima facie, that a notice was properly mailed on a motion for summary judgment on the complaint . . . a defendant still has to meet its burden, on a

UMB Bank, N.A. v 68 Colonial, LLC 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06483 
 November 4, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 UMB Bank, National Association, etc., respondent, 
 v 
 68 Colonial, LLC, et al., appellants, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on November 4, 2026 
 2025-05717, (Index No. 612041/23) 
 Lara J. Genovesi, J.P. 
 Deborah A. Dowling 
 Lillian Wan 
 Susan Quirk, JJ. 

 Manmohan K. Bakshi, P.C., New York, NY, for appellants. 
 Vallely Mitola Ryan PLLC, Syosset, NY (Ryan D. Mitola and Margarita Gaitas of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the defendants 68 Colonial, LLC, Audra Juliano, and Michael Cholowsky appeal from an amended order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (Eileen C. Daly-Sapraicone, J.), entered April 7, 2025. The amended order granted the plaintiff's motion pursuant to CPLR 3217(b) to discontinue the action and cancel the notice of pendency and denied, as academic, the motion of the defendants 68 Colonial, LLC, Audra Juliano, and Michael Cholowsky, inter alia, pursuant to CPLR 3211(a) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against them. 
 ORDERED that the amended order is affirmed, with costs. 
 In 2023, the plaintiff commenced this action to foreclose a mortgage against the defendants 68 Colonial, LLC, Audra Juliano, and Michael Cholowsky (hereinafter collectively the defendants), among others. The defendants interposed an answer, asserting various affirmative defenses and counterclaims. In August 2024, the defendants moved, inter alia, pursuant to CPLR 3211(a) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against them. The plaintiff opposed the motion. In October 2024, the plaintiff moved pursuant to CPLR 3217(b) to discontinue the action and cancel the notice of pendency. The defendants opposed the motion. In an amended order entered April 7, 2025, the Supreme Court granted the plaintiff's motion and denied, as academic, the defendants' motion. The defendants appeal. 
 CPLR 3217(b) permits a voluntary discontinuance of an action by court order "upon terms and conditions, as the court deems proper" ( see Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Starr , 245 AD3d 888, 890). In general, absent a showing of special circumstances, including prejudice to a substantial right of the defendant or other improper consequences, a motion for a voluntary discontinuance should be granted without prejudice ( see CPLR 3217[c]; U.S. Bank N.A. v Narain , 223 AD3d 856, 857; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Holcomb , 178 AD3d 773, 774). The determination of whether, and upon what terms and conditions, to grant a motion to discontinue an action pursuant to CPLR 3217(b) lies within the sound discretion of the court ( see Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Starr , 245 AD3d at 890). 
 Under the particular circumstances of this case, the Supreme Court providently [*2] exercised its discretion in granting the plaintiff's motion to discontinue the action, as there was no showing that the defendants would be prejudiced by the discontinuance ( see U.S. Bank N.A. v Narain , 223 AD3d at 857; HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v Kone , 188 AD3d 836, 838; Green Tree Servicing LLC v Shiow Fei Ju , 182 AD3d 840, 842). In light of the foregoing, the court properly denied, as academic, the defendants' motion, inter alia, to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against them ( see HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v Kone , 188 AD3d at 838). 
 The parties' remaining contentions either need not be reached in light of our determination or are without merit. 
 GENOVESI, J.P., DOWLING, WAN and QUIRK, JJ., concur.

 Darrell M. Joseph 
 Clerk of the Court

leads.caseName: Wilmington Sav. Fund Socy., FSB v. Kogan
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Wilmington Sav. Fund Socy., FSB v Kogan 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06485 
 November 4, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Wilmington Savings Fund Society, FSB, etc., respondent, 
 v 
 Alexander Kogan, appellant, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on November 4, 2026 
 2019-13983, (Index No. 507379/15) 
 Angela G. Iannacci, J.P. 
 Paul Wooten 
 Laurence L. Love 
 Elena Goldberg Velazquez, JJ. 

 Justin F. Pane, P.C., Bohemia, NY, for appellant. 
 Day Pitney LLP, New York, NY (Christina A. Livorsi of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the defendant Alexander Kogan appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Noach Dear, J.), dated November 4, 2019. The order denied that defendant's motion pursuant to CPLR 3211(a)(5) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him as time-barred. 
 ORDERED that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the motion of the defendant Alexander Kogan pursuant to CPLR 3211(a)(5) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him as time-barred is granted. 
 In 2007, New Century Mortgage Corporation (hereinafter New Century) commenced an action against the defendant Alexander Kogan (hereinafter the defendant), among others, to foreclose a mortgage on certain real property located in Brooklyn (hereinafter the 2007 action). The defendant failed to answer the complaint. In an order dated August 29, 2011 (hereinafter the dismissal order), the Supreme Court directed dismissal of the 2007 action for failure to comply with a prior order. New Century thereafter moved, inter alia, to vacate the dismissal order. In an order dated January 14, 2013, the court denied New Century's motion. 
 In 2015, New Century's alleged successor in interest, which was later substituted by the plaintiff, commenced this action against the defendant, among others, to foreclose the mortgage. The defendant moved pursuant to CPLR 3211(a)(5) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him as time-barred in light of the commencement of the 2007 action. The plaintiff opposed the motion, arguing that the debt was not validly accelerated because New Century lacked standing to commence the 2007 action. In an order dated November 4, 2019, the Supreme Court denied the defendant's motion. The defendant appeals. 
 An action to foreclose a mortgage is governed by a six-year statute of limitations ( see id. § 213[4]; Federal Natl. Mtge. Assn. ["Fannie Mae"] v Brach , 247 AD3d 849 , 850). Once a mortgage debt is accelerated, such as by the commencement of a mortgage foreclosure action in which the complaint seeks payment of the full outstanding loan balance, the entire amount becomes due and the statute of limitations begins to run on the entire debt ( see Federal Natl. Mtge. Assn. [*2] ["Fannie Mae"] v Brach , 247 AD3d at 850). 
 "[S]ervice of a complaint is ineffective to constitute a valid exercise of the option to accelerate a debt where the plaintiff does not have the authority to accelerate the debt or to sue to foreclose at that time" ( U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Atedgi , 236 AD3d 707 , 711 [internal quotation marks omitted]). However, CPLR 213(4), as amended by the Foreclosure Abuse Prevention Act (FAPA) (L 2022, ch 821), provides, in relevant part, that in any action to foreclose a mortgage, "if the statute of limitations is raised as a defense, and if that defense is based on a claim that the instrument at issue was accelerated prior to, or by way of commencement of a prior action, a plaintiff shall be estopped from asserting that the instrument was not validly accelerated, unless the prior action was dismissed based on an expressed judicial determination, made upon a timely interposed defense, that the instrument was not validly accelerated" (CPLR 213[4][a]; see U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Atedgi , 236 AD3d at 711; MTGLQ Invs., L.P. v Lila , 226 AD3d 889 , 890-891). 
 Here, the defendant demonstrated, prima facie, that the debt was accelerated when New Century commenced the 2007 action, electing in the complaint to call due the entire amount secured by the mortgage ( see MTGLQ Invs., L.P. v Kovaleva , 246 AD3d 719 ; MTGLQ Invs., L.P. v Lila , 226 AD3d at 890). The defendant further demonstrated, prima facie, that this action, commenced in 2015, more than six years later, was time-barred ( see MTGLQ Invs., L.P. v Kovaleva , 246 AD3d 719 ; MTGLQ Invs., L.P. v Lila , 226 AD3d at 890). 
 In opposition to the defendant's prima facie showing, the plaintiff failed to raise a question of fact. Contrary to the plaintiff's contention, the 2007 action was not "dismissed based on an expressed judicial determination, made upon a timely interposed defense, that the instrument was not validly accelerated" (CPLR 213[4][a]). Rather, the 2007 action was dismissed for failure to comply with a prior court order. Thus, the plaintiff is estopped from asserting in this action that the debt was not validly accelerated by the commencement of the 2007 action ( see U.S. Bank, N.A. v Bookspan , 247 AD3d 955 ; MTGLQ Invs., L.P. v Lila , 226 AD3d at 891). 
 The plaintiff's contention that FAPA should not apply retroactively, as well as its challenges to the constitutionality of the retroactive application of FAPA, are without merit ( see Van Dyke v U.S. Bank, N.A. , 45 NY3d 461 ; Article 13 LLC v Ponce De Leon Fed. Bank , 45 NY3d 441 ; FV-1, Inc. v Palaguachi , 234 AD3d 818 , 822; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Dagrin , 233 AD3d 1065 , 1069-1071; 97 Lyman Ave., LLC v MTGLQ Invs., L.P. , 233 AD3d 1038 , 1043). 
 The parties' remaining contentions need not be reached in light of our determination. 
 IANNACCI, J.P., WOOTEN, LOVE and GOLDBERG VELAZQUEZ, JJ., concur. 
 ENTER: 
 Darrell M. Joseph 
 Clerk of the Court

leads.caseName: Ameream LLC v. Borough of East Rutherford
leads.text:
NOT FOR PUBLICATION WITHOUT THE APPROVAL OF THE TAX COURT
 COMMITTEE ON OPINIONS

 AMEREAM LLC, TAX COURT OF NEW JERSEY

 Plaintiff, DOCKET NO. 007852-2025

 v.

 BOROUGH OF EAST RUTHERFORD,

 Defendant.

 Decided: October 30, 2026

 Romal D. Bullock, for plaintiff
 (McManimon, Scotland, & Baumann LLC, attorneys).

 Kenneth A. Porro, for defendant
 (Brach Eichler LLC, attorneys).

 David J. Shipley, for amicus curiae
 (Stevens & Lee, attorneys).

GILMORE, J.T.C.

 In the State of New Jersey, when a tax appeal results in a judgment reducing the assessment,

N.J.S.A. 54:51A-8 (the “Freeze Act”) precludes the taxing district from raising the assessment for

the following two years, subject to specific exceptions. This case asks whether that protection

extends to the American Drean Mall, whose developer makes payments in lieu of taxes (“PILOT”)

and would not otherwise be subject to conventional property taxes. It does. This case also asks

whether any of the statute’s exceptions apply. They do not.

 Background

 Plaintiff Ameream LLC (“Plaintiff”) is the owner and developer of the American Dream

Mall in East Rutherford, New Jersey. After a July 2025 trial, this court reduced the properties’
 cumulative 2025 assessments to $1,653,960,000. For tax year 2026, defendant, Borough of East

Rutherford (“Borough”), increased the cumulative assessments to $1,899,992,100, resulting in

Plaintiff’s present motion to freeze the court’s 2025 judgment into tax year 2026. The court is

urged to deny the motion by the Borough and amicus curiae US Bank and Trust Company (“US

Bank”).1 They argue that the properties’ PILOT status, the Borough’s yearly reassessment for the

2026 tax year, and a substantial change in value each bar application of the Freeze Act.

 Availability of the Freeze Act to Properties Subject to PILOT Agreements

 The first question is whether the Freeze Act even applies to the court’s 2025 judgment,

given that Plaintiff operates under a PILOT agreement. Traditional PILOT agreements set

payments on a fixed schedule. The subject PILOT is different; its payments equal 90% of the

conventional property taxes that would otherwise be due based on the properties’ assessments.

Thus, the assessments drive the calculation of the payments. Section 4.02(b) of the PILOT

agreement accordingly provides that

 the Borough covenants to maintain current property assessments for
 the Leasehold Estate and Improvements in accordance with
 Applicable Law, and as applicable, to reassess such interests in the
 same manner and at the same time as other real property within the
 Borough is reassessed, as if the same were subject to conventional
 property taxes in the Borough . . . . To the extent that such
 provisions set forth herein conflicts with generally applicable
 principles of conventional property taxation, the principles of
 conventional property taxation shall control, including but not
 limited to, the determination of the assessment by the Tax Assessor
 in the exercise of his or her sound discretion under Applicable Law
 and rights of the Developer to contest any assessment so determined.

1
 US Bank serves as the trustee for the bondholders. The bonds financed the subject development,
and the majority of funds from the PILOT are used to repay the bonds. Given this interest, the
court permitted US Bank to appear as amicus curiae, brief the issues, present limited testimony,
and participate in argument.
 2
  Nothing in the agreement bars application of the Freeze Act. Rather, the agreement

explicitly requires the Borough to assess the properties as if they were subject to conventional

property taxes, and preserves Plaintiff’s right to contest those assessments under principles of

conventional property taxation.2

 US Bank argues that Plaintiff cannot seek Freeze Act protection because it is not a

“taxpayer,” meaning that Plaintiff does not pay conventional property taxes. But the relevant

portion of the Freeze Act does not mention taxpayers or taxes, instead focusing on the

conclusiveness of a Tax Court judgment:

 Where a judgment not subject to further appeal has been rendered
 by the Tax Court involving real property, the judgment shall be
 conclusive and binding upon the municipal assessor and the taxing
 district . . . for the assessment year and for the two assessment years
 succeeding the assessment year covered by the final judgment . . . .

 [N.J.S.A. 54:51A-8(a).]

 For tax year 2025, the Borough assessed the properties pursuant to principles of

conventional property taxation, the Plaintiff challenged the assessments pursuant to principles of

conventional property taxation, and the court entered judgment reducing the assessments pursuant

to principles of conventional property taxation. The court therefore finds no basis to deny Plaintiff

the right to seek application of the Freeze Act simply because the properties are subject to a PILOT

agreement. Plaintiff did not challenge the PILOT; it challenged the assessments, as the agreement

expressly contemplates. That being settled, the court turns to whether any of the statute’s

exceptions require denial of relief.

2
 Plaintiff’s right to appeal the assessment is not precluded by N.J.S.A. 54:3-21(b) as the Financial
Agreement governing the development is not subject to the provisions of the Long Term Tax
Exemption Law.
 3
  Change in Value and Other Exceptions under the Freeze Act

 The Freeze Act is a statute of mandatory and automatic application. Fifth Roc Jersey

Assocs., L.L.C. v. Town of Morristown, 26 N.J. Tax 212, 222 (Tax 2011). However, it does not

apply where there have been “changes in value occurring after the assessment date[,] . . . a

complete revaluation or complete reassessment of all real property within the district has been put

in effect . . . [or] the property in question has been the subject of an . . . added assessment . . .

condominium or cooperative conversion, a subdivision or a zoning change.” N.J.S.A. 54:51A-

8(a). When an assessment is increased in contravention of the statute, the Freeze Act places the

burden of proving an exception upon the taxing district. N.J.S.A. 54:51A-8(b).

 Here, neither the Borough nor US Bank presented substantive evidence of a change in

value, of improvements supporting an added assessment, or of a conversion, subdivision, or zoning

change. US Bank offered testimony and news articles about previously dark storefronts reopening,

related tenant improvements, an improving economy, and declining market capitalization rates.

None of this was quantified. Regardless, neither bare evidence of increased tenant occupancy nor

general changes in the market serve to defeat the Act. See 160 Chubb Props., LLC v. Lyndhurst

Twp., 31 N.J. Tax 192, 202 (Tax 2019) (citing Union Minerals & Alloys Corp. v. Town of Kearny,

11 N.J. Tax 280, 285 (Tax 1990), aff’d, 13 N.J. Tax 114 (App. Div. 1992)); see also Cumberland

Arms Assocs. v. Burlington Twp., 10 N.J. Tax 255, 263, 268 (Tax 1988).

 Thus, the sole remaining issue is whether the Borough’s yearly reassessment program

constitutes a “complete reassessment of all real property within the district” under the Freeze Act.

 4
  Yearly and Annual Reassessments under the Freeze Act

 The Freeze Act was enacted in 1946, L. 1946, c. 161, to address “repeated yearly increases

in the assessed value of property . . . subjecting [the taxpayer] to the trouble and expenses of annual

appeals to the county tax board.” Newark v. Fischer, 8 N.J. 191, 199-200 (1951). In 1957, the

Legislature amended the Act to end a judgment’s binding effect when a program for a complete

revaluation of all real property in the district takes effect. L. 1957, c. 36. In 1999, the Legislature

added complete reassessments to this exception. L. 1999, c. 208.

 The reason for the exception is readily apparent. When the amendments were adopted,

district-wide revaluations and reassessments were infrequent, much less annual. They were

performed when needed, with subsequent regulations quantifying that need through statistical

markers such as a low average ratio, a high coefficient of dispersion, or more than ten years since

the last revaluation. N.J.A.C. 18:12A-1.14(b). The Borough’s witness testified that in his

experience, prior to the past 10 to 15 years, voluntary reassessments were conducted at most once

every five years. With assessments in many districts falling to a fraction of market value over

time, a revaluation or reassessment inevitably produced large increases in assessed values, offset

by a corresponding drop in the tax rate. Freezing a pre-revaluation or pre-reassessment judgment

through that kind of reset would create a disparity unfair to every other taxpayer in the district.

 Application of Chapter 123, L. 1973, c. 123 (now codified as amended at N.J.S.A. 54:51A-

6), makes the point even clearer. Consider a township with an average ratio of 50%. A property

assessed at $400,000, implying a market value of $800,000, is successfully appealed. The court

finds a market value of $650,000 and, applying the 50% ratio under Chapter 123, sets the

assessment at $325,000. The following year, the township completes a reassessment, and every

property is assessed at 100% of market value. Without the exception, the Freeze Act would keep

 5
 the appealed property assessed at 50% of its true value, while every other property in the township

is assessed at 100% of true value.

 While yearly and annual reassessments3 are a relatively recent phenomenon, our courts

have previously considered their interaction with the Freeze Act. In Tartivita v. Borough of Union

Beach, 31 N.J. Tax 335 (Tax 2019), aff’d, 33 N.J. Tax 16 (App. Div. 2021), the court carefully

and meticulously examined whether an annual reassessment under the Assessment Demonstration

Program (“ADP”) was procedurally sufficient to constitute a complete reassessment, concluding

that it was not. In Pella Realty, LLC v. City of Paterson, 31 N.J. Tax 474 (Tax 2020), the court

held that a non-ADP yearly reassessment program does not, by itself, preclude the Freeze Act, and

ordered a plenary hearing on whether the program satisfied the district-wide reassessment criteria

of N.J.A.C. 18:12A-1.14(c) and the Application for Full Reassessment, Form AFR.

 The Borough in this matter is not an ADP district; it conducts its yearly reassessments

through Form AFR using a five-year rolling inspection schedule. But this court need not decide

whether the Borough’s program satisfied the requisite procedural requirements. No matter the

answer, the complete reassessment exception turns on a more basic proposition: whether the

district-wide reassessment changed assessments enough that a frozen judgment would leave the

resulting assessment out of step with the rest of the district. The Freeze Act does not define

“complete,” but the word implies a true district-wide reset, not routine annual updating. The

Appellate Division’s affirmance in Tartivita points to the same conclusion. It looked not only at

procedure, but at how few assessments changed, and by how little.

3
 Typically, taxing districts operating under the ADP conduct “annual reassessments,” while
districts conducting reassessments every year outside the ADP describe their programs as “yearly
reassessments.” The difference in terminology does not affect the court’s reasoning.
 6
  In analyzing undefined terms in the Freeze Act, Judge Lario in Cumberland Arms looked

to the New Jersey Supreme Court:

 It is frequently difficult for a draftsman of legislation to anticipate
 all situations and to measure his words against them. Hence cases
 inevitably arise in which a literal application of the language used
 would lead to results incompatible with the legislative design. It is
 the proper function, indeed the obligation, of the judiciary to give
 effect to the obvious purpose of the Legislature, and to that end
 words us

not certified for publication or ordered published, except as specified by rule 8.1115(b). This opinion

COURT OF APPEAL, FOURTH APPELLATE DISTRICT 
DIVISION ONE 
STATE OF CALIFORNIA 
BLAINE MCLAUGHLIN, 
 Plaintiff and Appellant, 
 v. 
AERO PROPERTIES et al., 
 Defendants and Respondents. 
D085645 

(Super. Ct. No. 37-2021-
00029316-CU-PO-CTL) 
APPEAL from a judgment of the Superior Court of San Diego County, 
Carolyn M. Caietti, Judge. Affirmed. 
Lew-Stevens and Steven B. Stevens; Nguyen Lawyers and Minh T. 
Nguyen; Bates Law and Paul W. Bates for Plaintiff and Appellant. 
Horvitz & Levy, David M. Axelrad and Jeffrey Vides; Murchison 
& Cumming and Robert M. Scherk for Defendants and Respondents. 
Blaine McLaughlin was injured at his place of employment when he 
stepped into a hole in the floor created in connection with an ongoing 
bathroom renovation project. He filed suit against the contractor—Rogaciano 
Sanchez; the landlord—Aero Properties; the landlord’s General Partner—
William Gibbs; and the property managers—Strategic Property Management 

2 
Associates, Inc. and Victor Liong. The trial court granted Aero Properties 
and Gibbs (collectively, Respondents) summary judgment against 
McLaughlin on the grounds that Respondents did not owe McLaughlin a duty 
of care as a landlord with no actual knowledge of the allegedly hazardous 
condition (i.e., the hole). McLaughlin asks us to reverse the summary 
judgment and asserts that a triable issue of material fact remains as to 
whether Respondents retained control over the premises for purposes of the 
remodel. We conclude there is no triable issue of material fact and affirm the 
judgment. 
I. FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND 
A. McLaughlin’s Complaint 
In his complaint, filed July 21, 2021, McLaughlin asserted one cause of 
action for general negligence against Sanchez, and one for negligence based 
on premises liability against Respondents and the property manager 
defendants. 
McLaughlin alleged that, at all relevant times, he was an employee of 
VB MDS Auto Services, doing business as Midas Muffler (Midas). In July 
2019, Sanchez contracted with Respondents to do certain repairs and 
improvements at the Midas property. Midas remained open during the 
remodel, repairs and improvements.1 On or about July 20, 2019, during the 
remodel and repairs, Sanchez “cut a large square hole in the floor in front of 
the employee restroom sink.” McLaughlin entered the restroom to wash his 
hands on July 22, 2019, “and his leg dropped into the hole . . . causing [him] 
to sustain serious injuries.” 

1 According to the summary judgment pleadings, Aero owns the Midas 
property and leased it to Midas through a commercial auto center lease 
agreement executed in January 2019. Aero is a limited partnership. Gibbs is 
the general partner and the managing partner. 

3 
As to Respondents, McLaughlin alleged that they “were negligent in 
that, among other things, they failed to exercise due care in the inspection, 
ownership, construction, operation and maintenance, of [the Midas property] 
to ensure that occupants were not subject to any unreasonable risk of harm.” 
In addition, McLaughlin alleged that “each of them, knew, or in the exercise 
of reasonable diligence, should have known, of such dangerous conditions, 
and knew, or in the exercise of reasonable care, should have known that such 
conditions created an unreasonable risk of harm in sufficient time prior to the 
injury to have corrected it.” Despite this knowledge, Respondents 
“negligently failed to take steps to either make the condition safe or warn 
[McLaughlin] of the dangerous condition.” 
B. Respondents’ Motion for Summary Judgment 
In June 2024, Respondents moved for summary judgment. They 
asserted that Aero was an “out-of-possession landlord who had leased the 
entire premises” to Midas and, therefore, owed no duty of care to 
McLaughlin. Respondents asserted further that Sanchez was “acting at the 
direction of VB MDS’s owner, Victor Bagdasar” when he created the hole, 
because Bagdasar had asked Sanchez “to create a second floor drain in the 
employee restroom.” Although Respondents had contracted with Sanchez to 
complete certain restroom upgrades, the second drain was outside the scope 
of the agreed-upon repairs and was not approved by Respondents. 
Accordingly, they asserted that they did not have notice or actual knowledge 
of the drain (or the associated hole) and had no ability to cure any resulting 
dangerous condition. 
Respondents pointed to several clauses in the lease agreement. First, 
they noted that Midas was responsible for maintaining the premises and for 
all improvements, with the exception of structural elements like the roof and 
foundation. In the instance of a “non-monetary breach,” Midas would have 

4 
10 days to cure before Respondents could reenter the property. Second, they 
acknowledged that an addendum to the lease addressed the bathroom 
remodel and stated that “Aero would, at its sole cost and expense, upgrade 
the existing restrooms . . . to comply with the requirements of the Americans 
with Disabilities Act” (ADA), and that Midas agreed to provide reasonable 
access for that purpose. Respondents also agreed to provide “porta-potties” 
for use by Midas employees and customers “during any period the restroom 
area is out of service.” 
Respondents asserted that they contracted with Sanchez to complete 
the restroom repairs in accordance with the plans referenced in the 
addendum to the lease. Any changes to those plans required approval from 
Gibbs. Respondents alleged that “Sanchez went outside the scope of work 
approved by Gibbs by adding a second drain in the employee restroom at the 
request of Victor Bagdasar.”2 
Gibbs submitted a declaration in support of the motion for summary 
judgment and provided copies of the lease, the addendum, the associated 
architectural plans, and the contract with Sanchez for the bathroom remodel. 
Respondents also provided excerpts from the depositions of Sanchez and 
McLaughlin. 
Sanchez testified as follows: 
“Q: And any changes you made, it got approved by Mr. 
Gibbs, right? 
 [Objections.] 
A: There was no change in the process. None was made. 
Except the new drain. 

2 Respondents also filed a cross-complaint against Sanchez, Bagdasar, 
and VB MDS. 

5 
Q: And you got Mr. Gibb’s approval of putting in the new 
drain before you did that, right? 
 [Objections.] 
A: When [Bagdasar], the owner of Midas, asked me to 
please make him a new drain, I mentioned it to Mr. 
Gibbs. He told me, ‘No, don’t do it.’ Okay. I didn’t do 
it. [¶] The following week, [Bagdasar] continued to 
implore, ‘Please, I need another drain; make one for 
me.’ [¶] And since I knew how to do it, I did so as a 
favor to him since the completion of the work has been 
prolonged and delayed. I did so as a favor to him 
including that without charging for my time. That’s 
why I did that.” 
C. McLaughlin’s Opposition to the Motion for Summary Judgment 
McLaughlin opposed the motion for summary judgment. He asserted 
that Respondents had a nondelegable duty to maintain the property in a safe 
condition, and that they were vicariously liable for the negligence of Sanchez, 
the contractor that they hired. McLaughlin also argued that knowledge of 
the hole was imputed to Respondents for similar reasons, and that there was 
a triable issue of fact as to whether Gibbs approved installation of the second 
drain. 
McLaughlin alleged that Sanchez told Bagdasar that he would obtain 
approval from Gibbs for the second drain and then subsequently installed the 
drain without further discussion, raising at least an inference that Defendant 
Gibbs approved of the second drain. McLaughlin also alleged that Sanchez 
allowed Midas employees to use the restroom to wash their hands, in part 
because Gibbs informed him that the outdoor hand washing station that 
Sanchez had set up was inadequate. McLaughlin submitted deposition 
excerpts from Bagdasar, Sanchez, Gibbs, and himself as support for these 
allegations. 

6 
McLaughlin testified that he never saw any Midas employees using the 
outdoor hand washing station and that he was never told that he, or anyone 
else, needed to use that station and not the bathroom sink to wash their 
hands. Bagdasar testified that Sanchez had set up a temporary water line to 
the sink in the bathroom midway through the project, so that the mechanics 
could wash the grease off their hands. Gibbs was aware that the mechanics 
were using the sink for this purpose. Bagdasar asked Gibbs about the second 
drain in the bathroom and Gibbs said, “talk to [Sanchez].”3 Gibbs never said 
no to the request. When Bagdasar talked to Sanchez about the drain, 
Sanchez said that he would talk to Gibbs to get his approval. 
D. Respondents’ Additional Evidence 
Respondents submitted additional deposition excerpts in their reply. 
Gibbs testified that there were no formal documentation standards for 
change orders for the project, but that something like a drain would require a 
further submission to the City for permitting and that he did not know about 
the second drain until after the fact. Bagdasar testified that the employees 
had “no choice” but to use the outdoor, temporary sink to wash their hands. 
E. The Trial Court’s Ruling 
After reviewing the submissions and hearing argument, the trial court 
entered summary judgment in favor of Respondents. The trial court found 
that there was no triable issue of fact. The court explained: “The undisputed 
facts show Aero agreed to upgrade the existing restroom ‘consistent with the 
plans’, the drain was outside the scope of the plans and expressly not 
approved by Gibbs. There is no evidence for a trier of fact to determine Aero 
volunteered to repair a defective condition, specifically the second drain hole 

3 Bagdasar used the name “Rojas” but later confirmed that “Rojas” and 
“Sanchez” were the same person. 

7 
and the way it was left. Plaintiff tries to create a dispute by arguing an 
inference shows Sanchez received approval from Gibbs to construct the drain. 
This is directly refuted by Sanchez. For these same reasons, knowledge 
cannot be imputed to Aero because this work was done outside the scope of 
what Sanchez was tasked to do not just as reflected in the plans, but by 
Gibbs’ direct orders as well.” 
McLaughlin filed a timely notice of appeal. 
II. DISCUSSION 
McLaughlin asserts that the trial court should not have granted 
Respondents summary judgment. He argues that Respondents maintained 
control over the premises for the purposes of the bathroom remodel project, 
and that they therefore remained liable for any dangerous conditions created 
by their contractor. In addition, he asserts that there remains a disputed 
issue of material facts as to whether Sanchez created the second drain solely 
at the request and/or direction of Midas. 
A. Relevant Authority and Standard of Review 
We review an order granting a motion for summary judgment de novo, 
strictly construing the moving party’s evidence, and resolving evidentiary 
doubts in favor of the party who the trial court entered judgment against. 
(Aguilar v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (2001) 25 Cal.4th 826, 843 (Aguilar); Miller 
v. Department of Corrections (2005) 36 Cal.4th 446, 460.) 
“[T]he party moving for summary judgment bears [the] initial burden of 
production to make a prima facie showing of the nonexistence of any triable 
issue of material fact.” (Aguilar, supra, 25 Cal.4th at p. 850.) “A prima facie 
showing is one that is sufficient to support the position of the party in 
question.” (Id. at p. 851.) Among the ways in which a

Nancy Alanis appeals from the dismissal of her complaint, which

Antonio—one at 1040 Blanco Road (the “Blanco Property”) and another at 
13210 Hunters View (the “Hunters View Property”). The district court 
concluded that all of Alanis’s claims were barred by res judicata. That is 
because it determined that all her claims had already been , or could have 
been, raised in seven prior lawsuits she brought against the defendants or 
their privies. On appeal, however, Alanis has forfeited, by failing to brief, any 
argument that the district court erred by giving preclusive effect to the 
judgments in those prior cases. See Yohey v. Collins , 985 F.2d 222, 224– 25 
(5th Cir. 1993). Then, i nsofar as she argues that the district court lacked 
jurisdiction to rule on the defendants’ motions to dismiss based on the 
ripeness doctrine, that assertion lacks merit. See Abbott Lab’ys v. Gardner, 387 
U.S. 136, 148 (1967). 
She also challenges the district court’s denial of her Federal Rule of 
Civil Procedure 60(b)(4) motions . Through these motions, Alanis sought 
relief from two purportedly void state court orders that were entered in prior 
foreclosure proceedings. Under the circumstances presented here, Rule 
60(b)(4) does not provide an avenue for relief from the state court judgments 
at issue, and the district court did not err by declining to grant the requested 
relief. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 1; Callon Petroleum Co. v. Frontier Ins. Co. , 351 
F.3d 204, 208 (5th Cir. 2003). 
In light of the foregoing, the district court’s judgment is 
AFFIRMED. 
Finally, we note that Alanis has been declared a vexatious litigant in 
the Western District of Texas, and we have previously affirmed the dismissal 
of Alanis’s similar claims related to the Hunters View Property. See Alanis v. 
Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. , No. 22- 50246, 2022 WL 17844074, at *1 (5th Cir. 
Dec. 22, 2022) (per curiam) (unpublished). The instant action is at least the 
fourth lawsuit that Alanis has filed in state or federal court concerning the
