leads.caseName: B&D Investment Group, LLC v. Justice-Willow Springs Water Comm'n
leads.text:
2026 IL App (1st) 252649-U 
No. 1-25-2649 
Order filed November 4, 2026 
NOTICE: This order was filed under Illinois Supreme Court Rule 23 and is not 
precedential except in the limited circumstances allowed under Rule 23(e)(1). 

IN THE 
APPELLATE COURT OF ILLINOIS 
FIRST DISTRICT, THIRD DIVISION 

B&D INVESTMENT GROUP, LLC-8507-8527 S. 88th A VENUE SERIES, Plaintiff-Appellant 
v. 
JUSTICE-WILLOW SPRINGS WATER COMMISSION, an Illinois Municipal Corporation, 
Defendant-Appellee 
Appeal from the Circuit Court of Cook County. 
Honorable Joel Chupack, Judge, Presiding. 
No. 21-CH-3125 

JUSTICE ROCHFORD delivered the judgment of the court. 
Presiding Justice Quish and Justice Lampkin concurred in the judgment. 
ORDER 
¶ 1 Held: We affirm the grant of summary judgment for defendant on plaintiff’s amended 
complaint for declaratory and injunctive relief. 

¶ 2 Plaintiff, B&D Investment Group, LLC-8507-8527 S. 88th Avenue Series, is the owner of 
a strip mall in the Village of Justice (Village). Defendant, the Justice -Willow Springs Water 
Commission, is a municipal utility providing water service throughout the Village. In 2021, 
defendant notified plaintiff of its intention to reduce the number of water meters located at the strip 
mall so as to lower the administrative expenses relating to billing for water usage. Plaintiff filed 
an amended three-count complaint, seeking a declaration that defendant’s attempt to reduce only 

- 2 - 
the number of water meters at its strip mall, while not reducing the water meters at other similarly 
situated strip malls within the Village, violated the equal protection clause and was arbitrary and 
capricious. Plaintiff also sought injunctive relief. The circuit court granted summary judgment in 
favor of defendant. Plaintiff appeals. We affirm. 
¶ 3 Plaintiff’s strip mall contains eight commercial units consisting of seven stores and a day 
care center. Each store has its own water meter. The day care center has two additional water 
meters. There is a tenth water meter for the fire sprinkler system, which is not the subject of this 
appeal. Defendant uses specialized equipment to remotely read the water meters and determine the 
amount of water used by each commercial unit and then prepares a separate water bill for each 
such unit. In January 2021, defendant’s Executive Director, Colleen Kelly, told plaintiff’s manager 
and sole member, Dr. Mohamed Eldibany, that defendant wanted to consolidate seven of the water 
meters in the commercial units into one water meter, which would result in plaintiff receiving one 
total water bill for all the units. As a result of the consolidation, defendant no longer would prepare 
a separate water bill for each commercial unit, meaning that plaintiff would be required to 
determine each of the units’ water usage and then bill each unit accordingly. Eldibany objected to 
the consolidation as it would entail extra expenses for plaintiff. 
¶ 4 On January 28, 2021, defendant held a board meeting and directed its attorney to speak 
with Eldibany again about consolidating the water meters in plaintiff’s strip mall. On March 24, 
2021, defendant’s attorney sent Eldibany a letter informing him of defendant’s decision to 
consolidate the water meters in plaintiff’s strip mall. Eldibany continued to voice his objection. 
On June 17, 2021, defendant informed plaintiff that unless it made an appointment to consolidate 
the water meters within the next 14 days, defendant would “begin the process of terminating water 

- 3 - 
service” at the strip mall. Plaintiff contends that if defendant terminates the water service, five of 
its commercial tenants including the day care center would have to shut down. 
¶ 5 Plaintiff filed its initial complaint in this matter on June 25, 2021. In count I, plaintiff 
alleged that there were nine other strip malls located within the Village and receiving water from 
defendant. Those nine strip malls contained multiple commercial units, each of which was serviced 
by its own water meter. Defendant was not requiring any of those strip malls to consolidate or 
reduce their water meters. Plaintiff sought a declaration that defendant’s attempt to consolidate the 
water meters at its strip mall, while leaving the multiple water meters at the other nine strip malls 
intact, violated the equal protection clause. In count II, plaintiff sought a declaration that 
defendant’s attempt to consolidate the water meters at its strip mall was arbitrary and capricious. 
In count III, plaintiff sought a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction enjoining 
defendant from consolidating the water meters at its strip mall during the pendency of this action 
and a permanent injunction restraining the same conduct. 
¶ 6 The circuit court dismissed plaintiff’s complaint for failing to state a cause of action under 
section 2-615 of the Code of Civil Procedure (735 ILCS 5/2- 615 (West 2020)). Plaintiff filed an 
appeal from th at dismissal order (see B&D Investment Group, LLC -8507-8527 S. 88th Avenue 
Series v. Justice- Willow Springs Water Commission, 2022 IL App (1st) 211357-U ), which we 
proceed to discuss . First, plaintiff contended in the appeal from the dismissal order that its 
complaint stated a cause of action for an equal protection violation. Id. ¶ 13. We noted that an equal 
protection claim generally is concerned with governmental classifications affecting some groups 
of citizens differently than others. Id. Therefore an individual pursuing an equal protection 
challenge usually alleges that he has been arbitrarily classified as a member of an identifiable 

- 4 - 
group. Id. However, the equal protection clause is also understood to protect an individual (a so-
called “class of one”) against purely arbitrary governmental classifications. Id. 
¶ 7 We further noted that in the instant case, plaintiff was alleging such a class of one equal 
protection claim based on its being irrationally singled out for consolidation of its water meters. 
Id. ¶ 14. To state a cause of action under this theory, plaintiff must allege it was intentionally treated 
differently from others who were similarly situated. Id. To be similarly situated, plaintiff and its 
comparators must be prima facie identical in all relevant respects or directly comparable in all 
material respects. Id. Plaintiff must further allege that there is no rational basis for the different 
treatment. Id. 
¶ 8 We determined that “[u]ltimately, after discovery is completed,” the evidence may show 
some differentiation between plaintiff’s strip mall and the other strip malls in the Village which 
justifies the difference in treatment regarding the consolidation of the water meters. Id. ¶ 21. 
However, we found that “[f]or our purposes here at the pleading stage,” plaintiff’s complaint 
alleged facts sufficient to show that defendant intentionally treated it differently from other 
similarly situated strip malls for no rational reason and as such that defendant’ s consolidation 
decision contravened the equal protection clause and was arbitrary and capricious . Id. ¶¶ 21-24. 
Accordingly, we reversed the dismissal of counts I and II and remanded for further proceedings. 
Id. As counts I and II stated causes of action underlying count III’s claim for injunctive relief, we 
also reversed the dismissal of count III and remanded for further proceedings. Id. ¶ 26. 
¶ 9 On remand, plaintiff filed an amended complaint realleging that defendant’s attempt to 
consolidate only the water meters at its strip mall, while not reducing or consolidating the water 
meters at the comparator malls within the Village, violated the equal protection clause, was 
arbitrary and capricious, and merited injunctive relief. The difference between the original and 

- 5 - 
amended complaints is that the amended complaint now alleged that there are seven (not nine) 
comparator strip malls located within the Village which have not been required to consolidate their 
water meters. 
¶ 10 During discovery, Colleen Kelly, defendant’s E xecutive Director, gave a deposition in 
which she testified that she made the decision, on behalf of defendant, to consolidate the water 
meters at plaintiff’s strip mall. Kelly stated that her decision was based on the fact that “many” of 
plaintiff’s tenants were delinquent in making their water payments, thereby requiring defendant to 
shut off their water supply. Kelly also stated that a dispute between plaintiff and one of its tenants, 
J & J Fish & Chicken (J & J) regarding whether plaintiff had illegally tapped into J & J’s water 
line was an additional factor in the decision to consolidate plaintiff’s water meters. 
¶ 11 Kelly also filed an affidavit stating that consolidating the water meters in plaintiff’s strip 
mall would promote operating efficiencies for defendant and would result in lower administrative 
expenses for billing and collecting for water usage. Kelly further attested that multi-unit buildings 
with commercial tenants with a single consolidated water meter “have a lower number of 
delinquent payments, lower administrative expenses related to billing and collecting for water 
usage and require less servicing than buildings served by multiple meters.” 
¶ 12 Plaintiff filed interrogatories directed to defendant, asking it in pertinent part to state the 
factual basis for its decision to require plaintiff to consolidate the water meters at the strip mall. 
Defendant stated: 
“The Plaintiff’s Property had substantially more delinquent accounts than similarly situated 
properties from the period covering January 1, 2015, through December 31, 2020. 
Specifically, during the foregoing period, the Plaintiff’s property had the highest number 
of delinquent bills (i.e., bills issued which included a delinquent balance) in total and the 

- 6 - 
highest number of delinquent bills on a percentage basis of bills issued from January 1, 
2015 through December 31, 2020.” 
¶ 13 Defendant provided a chart prepared by its administrative assistant, Tabatha Sutera, 
showing that plaintiff’s strip mall had 477 delinquent water bills, whereas the comparator strip 
malls in the Village had between 31 and 296 delinquent bills. The chart further showed that 72% 
of the water bills for plaintiff’s strip mall were delinquent. The comparator strip malls in the Village 
had between 8% and 54% delinquent bills. 
¶ 14 In further response to plaintiff’s interrogatories, defendant also stated that it decided to 
consolidate the water meters in plaintiff’s strip mall, and not in the comparator strip malls, because 
water service for three of plaintiff ’s tenants was terminated for non-payment between January 1, 
2015, through December 31, 2020, whereas none of the tenants in the comparator strip malls had 
their water service terminated for non-payment during that same period; in 2020, one of plaintiff’s 
tenants, J & J, complained that plaintiff tapped into its water line, thereby causing it to be charged 
for water service attributable to another tenant, whereas no similar complaints were lodged by the 
tenants in the comparator strip malls; defendant has received requests from plaintiff to terminate 
its tenants’ water service for the non-payment of bills, whereas defendant has received no similar 
requests from the comparator strip malls; and fines and penalties were assessed against plaintiff 
on December 16, 2016, for cutting the lock off one of its water meters at its strip mall, whereas no 
similar fines and penalties were assessed against the comparator strip malls . Defendant further 
stated that consolidating plaintiff’s water meters will lower the number of delinquent payments 
and decrease defendant’s administrative expenses. 
¶ 15 Dr. Mohamed Eldibany, plaintiff ’s sole member, filed an affidavit attesting that plaintiff 
had never tapped into J & J’s water line. Eldibany also gave a deposition in which he stated that 

- 7 - 
d

leads.caseName: Steve Veysey, Kathy Carter, and Mary Powell v. Iowa Department of Natural Resources, Iowa Utilities Commission and Governor Kim Reynolds, in her official capacity
leads.text:
IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF IOWA
 _______________

 No. 25-1362
 Filed November 4, 2026
 _______________

 Steve Veysey, Kathy Carter, and Mary Powell,
 Plaintiffs–Appellants,
 v.
 Iowa Department of Natural Resources, Iowa Utilities Commission,
 and Governor Kim Reynolds, in her official capacity,
 Defendants–Appellees.
 _______________

 Appeal from the Iowa District Court for Polk County,
 The Honorable Michael Huppert, Judge.
 _______________

 AFFIRMED
 _______________

 Wallace L. Taylor (argued) of Law Offices of Wallace L. Taylor, Cedar
 Rapids, attorney for appellants.

Breana Bird, Attorney General, Eric Wessan, Solicitor General, Patrick C.
 Valencia, Deputy Solicitor General, and Ankit Pal (argued), and Halle
 Kissell (until withdrawal), Assistant Solicitors General, attorneys for
 appellees.

W. Charles Smithson, West Des Moines, attorney for Amicus Curiae Four
 Iowa State Senators.
 _______________

 1
  Heard at oral argument
by Schumacher, P.J., Sandy, J., and Telleen, S.J.
 Opinion by Sandy, J.

 2
 SANDY, Judge.

 In 2023, Governor Kim Reynolds issued Executive Order 10 (EO10),
which required in part for “all departments, agencies, boards, or
commissions” to review administrative rules and initiate rulemakings. Steve
Veysey, Kathy Carter, and Mary Powell (collectively, and as context requires,
“Veysey”) then sued the Iowa Department of Natural Resources (DNR),
Iowa Utilities Commission (IUC), and Governor Reynolds (collectively, the
“agencies”) as residents of Iowa who “have interests in Iowa land and water
that are affected by administrative rules adopted by [the DNR] and
[IUC],”—agencies subject to EO10’s requirements. Veysey requested a
declaratory judgment declaring EO10 illegal, invalid, and void.

 The agencies then moved to dismiss Veysey’s amended petition,
arguing Veysey and his co-plaintiffs lacked standing to bring their suit and
failed to state a claim upon which relief may be granted. The district court
agreed and dismissed Veysey’s petition. Veysey now appeals, arguing his
petition should not have been dismissed on either ground. Because Veysey
and each of his co-plaintiffs lack standing,1 we affirm.

 BACKGROUND FACTS AND PROCEEDINGS
 EO10 was issued in January 2023. The order contemplates that “the
proliferation of administrative rules and regulations at all levels of
government has imposed high costs on employers, inhibited job growth,
impeded private sector investment, and increased the complexity and
expense of economic life.” EO10 thus seeks to “reduc[e] this regulatory

 1
 Because we can affirm the district court on standing, we need not determine if
Versey has stated claims on which relief could be granted.

 3
 burden on Iowans” which “will promote citizens’ freedom to engage in
individual, family, and business pursuits.”

 With the aim of accomplishing that goal, EO10 requires that each
administrative agency, board, or commission review all of its respective Iowa
Administrative Code chapter through “a comprehensive evaluation and
rigorous cost-benefit analysis” by December 31, 2026. Following such
review, each agency, board, or commission must publish notice of its
intended action and either repeal the existing chapter or renew the chapter
through a new rulemaking consistent with the Iowa Administrative
Procedure Act. Agencies are not permitted to initiate new rulemakings prior
to the agency’s EO10 rule-chapter review.2 Under EO10, “[e]ach new rule
chapter finalized by the agency must reduce the overall regulatory burden, or
remain neutral, as compared to the previous rule chapter,” and “[a]ll
proposed amendments to an existing chapter must be contained within a
single rulemaking.”

 In March 2025, Veysey petitioned for entry of a declaratory judgment
finding “that Executive Order 10 is beyond the Governor’s authority and that
any agency rules adopted in compliance with Executive Order 10 are illegal
and invalid.” Veysey, individually, alleged that, as “an avid fly fisherman”
and “advocate for clean water,” EO10 diminishes the effectiveness of
Chapter 65 of the DNR rules, which are supposed to control pollution from
animal feeding operations. In addition, Executive Order 10 diminishes the
effectiveness of Chapters 50–55 of the DNR rules, which pertain to water

 2
 EO10 makes certain exceptions, including for promulgation of “emergency
rules” compliant with the process for new and amended rules and for rulemaking that is
directed by the Administrative Rules Coordinator.

 4
 withdrawal permits and the disposition of wastes from industrial, municipal
and agricultural operations, including large animal feeding operations.

 Carter alleged that, as an Iowan who “gets her drinking water from the
City of Rockford municipal water source, which draws its water from the
Devonian Limestone that was the subject of the water withdrawal permit
granted to an entity to capture carbon dioxide from an ethanol plant,” she is
also affected by EO10’s diminishing effects on chapter 50 through 55 of the
DNR rules, “which are supposed to control the amount of water that can be
withdrawn from Iowa’s aquifers.”

 Powell alleged that, as “an heir to a family farm in Shelby County over
which Summit Carbon Solutions has been granted eminent domain by the
Iowa Utilities Commission for a hazardous liquid pipeline,” EO10
“diminishes the effectiveness of Chapters 9 and 13 of the IUC rules, which
are supposed to protect landowners from the environmental and economic
damages caused by a pipeline.” She further claims that “[t]he new Chapter 9
and 13 rules, pursuant to Executive Order 10, will not effectively accomplish
[the chapters’] purposes.”

 The agencies then moved to dismiss Veysey’s petition in April for lack
of subject matter jurisdiction due to lack of standing and failure to state a
claim upon which any relief can be granted. On the issue of standing, the
agencies argued that Veysey only offered opinions relating to the executive
order’s effects and only presented “conjectural and hypothetical” allegations
rather than any injury-in-fact. Veysey resisted, contending his injuries were
not merely “conjectural or hypothetical, but . . . concrete and actual or
imminent,” such as through the governor’s office’s actions in “delet[ing]
protection from manure storage lagoons constructed in karst terrain.” Veysey
further restated his petition’s claims that EO10 “minimiz[es] the

 5
 effectiveness of [IUC] regulations,” which “affects Ms. Powell’[s] interest in
the land,” and diminishes the effects of chapters 50 through 55, which
negatively affect Carter’s interest in clean drinking water.

 Veysey then suggested that the standing requirements should be
relaxed for a couple reasons. First, he argued his petition raised “issues of
great importance” under Godfrey v. State, 752 N.W.2d 413 (Iowa 2008), as
his EO10 “strikes at the heart of the purpose and structure of the [Iowa]
Administrative Procedure Act,” and standing requirements can thus be
waived. Second, he claimed his action “is akin to a quo warranto action.” In
reply, the agencies observed that Veysey’s resistance merely restated the
opinions contained within his amended petition, failed to articulate how his
claims involved issues of great importance, and failed to describe how his
petition qualified as a quo warranto action under Iowa Rule of Civil
Procedure 1.1301.

 The district court agreed with the agencies and dismissed the petition
as lacking standing and failing to state a claim upon which relief may be
granted. The court found that “none of the plaintiffs have alleged that they
have incurred any of the damages they claim could flow from the issuance of
EO10” and “do not even allege that injury is likely or possible.” It also
declined to apply the issue-of-great-importance exception due to Veysey’s
failure to allege that EO10 “was inconsistent with the ordinary process
utilized by the executive branch” or presented a constitutional violation.

 Veysey now appeals.

 STANDARD OF REVIEW
 “We review a district court’s ruling on a motion to dismiss for the
correction of errors at law,” Mueller v. Wellmark, Inc., 818 N.W.2d 244, 253

 6
 (Iowa 2012) (citation omitted), including when the petition has been
dismissed for lack of standing, LS Power Midcontinent, LLC v. State, 988
N.W.2d 316, 329 (Iowa 2023). We “accept as true the petition’s well-pleaded
factual allegations, but not its legal conclusions.” Shumate v. Drake Univ.,
846 N.W.2d 503, 507 (Iowa 2014).

 DISCUSSION
 Under Iowa Rule of Civil Procedure 1.421(1)(a), a “[l]ack of
jurisdiction of the subject matter” may be raised in a pre-answer motion to
dismiss. Challenges to standing also may be raised in pre-answer motions to
dismiss, as standing is a “closely related doctrine[]” to subject matter
jurisdiction. Citizens for Responsible Choices v. City of Shenandoah, 686
N.W.2d 470, 473 (Iowa 2004). Under such motions, the petition’s well-
pleaded facts are admitted, and any ambiguity or uncertainty is waived.
O’Hara v. State, 642 N.W.2d 303, 305 (Iowa 2002).

 There are two requirements for a plaintiff to have standing, which
“must exist at the commencement of the litigation”: the plaintiff must
(1) possess “a specific personal or legal interest in the litigation”; and (2) “be
injuriously affected.” LS Power, 988 N.W.2d at 329 (citation omitted). A
specific or personal interest is one different than a general interest. See id.
And to be injuriously affected, the plaintiff must be able to show “an injury
in fact that is fairly traceable to the defendant’s conduct and is likely to be
remedied by a favorable decision.” Id. at 329–30. This means that “the injury
cannot be conjectural or hypothetical, but must be concrete and actual or
imminent.” Id. at 330 (cleaned up).

 In Godfrey, our supreme court crafted an exception to the traditional
standing requirement “to resolve certain questions of great public

 7
 importance and interest in our system of government.” 752 N.W.2d at 425.
But this consideration must be balanced with the “delicate and essential
judicial responsibility” of “exercis[ing] our power with the greatest of
caution.” See id. Thus, even when considering whether to apply an exception
to standing, we remain concerned with ensuring that “litigants are true
adversaries,” “a real concrete case exits,” and “the people most concerned
with an issue are in fact the litigants.” See id. at 425–26.

 The Godfrey court held “cases involving actions by private persons to
enforce public rights may be brought under the personal-interest alternative
to the first [standing] element.” Id. at 420. This permits a court to keep
primary focus on “the factual-injury element of standing,” which still
requires “some type of injury different from the population in general.” Id.

 In furtherance of his standing argument, Veysey reiterates his claims
below which, in turn, restated the factual claims in his amended petition. But
as the district court observed, Veysey has not asserted that he or the other
plaintiffs suffered any damages from the issuance of EO10. The potential
harm they do identify is vague and lacks explanation. For example, Veysey
simply states that “[EO10] diminishes the effectiveness of Chapter 50–55 of
the DNR rules,” without providing any further information such as
specifically which chapters or sections have been amended, how the
amendments negatively impact “water withdrawal permits and the
disposition of wastes from industrial, municipal and agricultural operations,
including large animal feeding operations,” or how those negative impacts
injure his ability to fly fish.

 The most concrete injury Veysey alleges can be found in his claim that
“new Chapter 9 and 13 rules, pursuant to [EO10], will not effectively
accomplish their purposes” of “requir[ing] a pipeline company to minimize

 8
 and repair damage to agricultural land resulting from the construction of the
pipeline.” But even this claim—that the newly amended chapters “will not

FOR PUBLICATION

 UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS
 FOR THE NINTH CIRCUIT

In re: VIKRAM SRINIVASAN, No. 26-577
 BAP No.
 Debtor.
 25-1122
_____________________________

VIKRAM SRINIVASAN, AKA
Vikram Srinivasan, OPINION

 Appellant,

 v.

MILESTONE FINANCIAL, LLC,

 Appellee.

In re: BEENA SRINIVASAN, No. 26-580

 Debtor. BAP No.
_____________________________ 25-1119

BEENA SRINIVASAN,

 Appellant,

 v.
 2 SRINIVASAN V. MILESTONE FINANCIAL, LLC

MILESTONE FINANCIAL, LLC,

 Appellee.

 Appeal from the Ninth Circuit
 Bankruptcy Appellate Panel
 Brand, Gan, and Corbit, Bankruptcy Judges, Presiding

 Argued and Submitted August 12, 2026
 San Francisco, California

 Filed November 4, 2026

 Before: Kenneth K. Lee, Salvador Mendoza, Jr., and Ana
 de Alba, Circuit Judges.

 Opinion by Judge de Alba

 SUMMARY *

 Bankruptcy

 In appeals from the Bankruptcy Appellate Panel by
Chapter 13 debtors Beena and Vikram Srinivasan, the panel:
(1) reversed the bankruptcy court’s dismissal of debtors’
cases for failure to comply with an order and instructed the
bankruptcy court instead to grant debtors’ requests for

*
 This summary constitutes no part of the opinion of the court. It has
been prepared by court staff for the convenience of the reader.
  SRINIVASAN V. MILESTONE FINANCIAL, LLC 3

voluntary dismissal; and (2) affirmed the bankruptcy court’s
imposition of one-year refiling bars on debtors.
 The panel reaffirmed court precedent holding that under
11 U.S.C. § 1307(b), a debtor has an absolute statutory right
to voluntarily dismiss a Chapter 13 bankruptcy case, even if
the debtor filed the Chapter 13 petition in bad faith. The
bankruptcy court therefore was required to consider debtors’
§ 1037(b) requests before other pending matters, including
orders requiring the filings of schedules and
statements. Accordingly, the bankruptcy court abused its
discretion by dismissing for failure to comply with a court
order. The panel reversed the bankruptcy court’s order and
instructed it to enter a new order of dismissal based on
debtors’ request pursuant to § 1307(b).
 The panel held, however, that the bankruptcy court acted
within its statutory authority, and did not abuse its discretion,
when it imposed the one-year refiling bars for cause under
11 U.S.C. § 105(a). The panel held that 11 U.S.C. § 109(g)
does not set the statutory maximum for such a sanction at
180 days, but rather provides a discrete sanction applicable
in certain, statutorily prescribed, circumstances. Agreeing
with the Third Circuit, the panel held that the bankruptcy
court had authority under 11 U.S.C. § 349(a) to impose a
refiling bar “for cause,” even in the context of debtors’
§ 1307(b) dismissal. The panel concluded that the
bankruptcy court’s refiling bar was reasonable, considering
debtors’ extensive history of multiple filings and repeated
failure to fully prosecute. In light of debtors’ bad faith
conduct, the record supported the bankruptcy court’s
imposition of a one-year bar and was an appropriate exercise
of its discretion.
 4 SRINIVASAN V. MILESTONE FINANCIAL, LLC

 COUNSEL

Joseph Boufadel (argued) and Gregory M. Salvato, Salvato
Boufadel LLP, Los Angeles, California, for Appellant.
Sarah L. Little (argued), Chris D. Kuhner, and Eric A.
Nyberg, Kornfield Nyberg Bendes Kuhner & Little PC,
Oakland, California, for Appellee.

 OPINION

DE ALBA, Circuit Judge:

 Chapter 13 debtors Beena and Vikram Srinivasan
(mother and son) appeal a bankruptcy court’s orders
imposing a one-year refiling bar following the court’s
dismissal of their cases for failure to comply with an order.
We hold that Appellants had an absolute right to dismiss
their Chapter 13 cases under 11 U.S.C. § 1307(b), and the
bankruptcy court erred by not honoring that right. We also
find, however, that the bankruptcy court acted within its
discretion in imposing a one-year refiling bar.
 I. Background
A. Factual Background
 Debtor – Appellants, Vikram Srinivasan and his mother
Beena Srinivasan, have filed for bankruptcy multiple times
before the instant case.
 Vikram filed bankruptcy petitions in December 2019,
December 2020, and August 2021. His first petition was
dismissed for failure to comply with an order requiring the
  SRINIVASAN V. MILESTONE FINANCIAL, LLC 5

filing of missing documents. Vikram’s second bankruptcy
petition was dismissed after he failed to appear at the
creditors’ meeting. His third bankruptcy petition was
dismissed with a finding of cause and a one-year bar to
refiling.
 Beena filed bankruptcy petitions in September 2019,
November 2019, July 2021, and September 2021. All four of
her bankruptcy petitions were dismissed for failure to
comply with an order requiring the filing of missing
documents.
 The facts of the instant petition began when Milestone
Financial, LLC (“Milestone”) financed a second mortgage
in December 2018 on a property Beena and her husband
owned. Vikram executed all loan documents as the
purported Attorney-in-Fact for his parents. Appellants never
made any payments on the mortgage.
 A Notice of Default was recorded and a trustee’s
foreclosure sale of the property was completed. Milestone
was the foreclosing beneficiary at the public auction and
afterwards attempted to evict Vikram and Beena Srinivasan.
 Alameda County’s eviction moratorium delayed
Milestone’s eviction attempt, and resulted in Milestone’s
commencement of an unlawful detainer action. Vikram and
Beena, as occupants of the real property, filed motions to
quash service but were denied. The unlawful detainer action
was approaching trial when Vikram and Beena each filed
Chapter 13 petitions on April 11, 2025, triggering an
automatic stay. 1

1
 Milestone filed a notice of related bankruptcy case with respect to
Appellants concurrently filed Chapter 13, Case Nos. 24-40627 and 24-
 6 SRINIVASAN V. MILESTONE FINANCIAL, LLC

B. Procedural History
 1. Bankruptcy court orders Appellants to provide
 missing documents
 Appellants filed their Chapter 13 bankruptcy petitions
incompletely; the petitions were filed without schedules and
other required documents. 2 Four days later, the bankruptcy
court issued orders requiring Appellants to file the missing
documents within fourteen days of the petition date.
 On April 25, 2025, the fourteenth day from the petition
date, Appellants filed a motion to extend time to file these
documents, “claiming good cause due to medical and health
related conflicts.” The bankruptcy court granted “an
extension until May 14, 2025,” but expressly warned that
“[i]f [Appellants] fail[ed] to comply with this Order, the
case[s] may be dismissed without further notice or hearing.”
 On May 7, 2025, Milestone filed a Motion for Relief
from the Automatic Stay to continue with its unlawful
detainer action against Appellants. In the same motion,
Milestone also requested the bankruptcy court exercise its
inherent authority pursuant to 11 U.S.C. § 105(a) 3 to bar
Appellants from refiling a bankruptcy petition for two years.

40628. The cases were deemed related and transferred to the Honorable
William J. Lafferty.
2
 Appellants represented themselves in pro per.
3
 11 U.S.C. § 105(a) states that “[t]he court may issue any order, process,
or judgment that is necessary or appropriate to carry out the provisions
of this title. No provision of this title providing for the raising of an issue
by a party in interest shall be construed to preclude the court from, sua
sponte, taking any action or making any determination necessary or
appropriate to enforce or implement court orders or rules, or to prevent
an abuse of process.”
  SRINIVASAN V. MILESTONE FINANCIAL, LLC 7

Milestone represented that Appellants acted in bad faith to
prevent them “from proceeding with the Unlawful Detainer
Action,” as demonstrated by Appellants’ failure to prosecute
multiple bankruptcy cases. Because Milestone’s motion
pertained only to relief from the automatic stay, the
bankruptcy court ordered it to file a separate motion for the
refiling bar. In the same order, the bankruptcy court granted
Milestone’s Motion for Relief from Stay.
 2. Appellants’ motions to voluntarily dismiss the
 bankruptcy petitions and reconsider grounds of
 dismissal
 As of the extension deadline, May 14, 2025, Appellants
had not yet filed the required documents with the bankruptcy
court. Instead, on the day of the deadline, they filed
applications to voluntarily dismiss their Chapter 13
bankruptcy petitions pursuant to 11 U.S.C. § 1307(b).
Section 1307(b) states that “[o]n request of the debtor at any
time, if the case has not been converted under section 706,
1112, or 1208 of this title, the court shall dismiss a case
under this chapter. Any waiver of the right to dismiss under
this subsection is unenforceable.” 11 U.S.C. § 1307(b). In
their motions, Appellants indicated the reason for filing the
case was now moot since they had renegotiated the terms of
their commercial lease and Beena was entering into
mediation with her husband regarding the marital estate. 4
 On May 16, 2025, the bankruptcy court dismissed
Appellants’ cases for failure to comply with the court order
granting their motion to extend time. Appellants moved for

4
 The Record shows Vikram’s application to voluntarily dismiss his
bankruptcy petition was filed on May 14, 2025, and entered at 5:03 PM
and Beena’s application to voluntarily dismiss her bankruptcy petition
was filed on May 14, 2025, and entered at 5:16 PM.
 8 SRINIVASAN V. MILESTONE FINANCIAL, LLC

reconsideration of the court’s dismissal orders, requesting
the grounds of dismissal be changed from failure to comply
with the court’s order to voluntary dismissal. Appellants did
not appear at the scheduled hearings on the motions. On
June 10, 2025, the bankruptcy court denied the motions for
reconsideration. In doing so, the court recognized
Appellants’ statutory right to request dismissal but
determined that their multiple filings, repeated failures to
fully prosecute, and the circumstances surrounding the
current filings made it appropriate to dismiss the cases for
failure to comply.
 3. Refiling bar and Appellants’ motion for
 reconsideration
 On June 3, 2025, Milestone moved to bar Appellants
from refiling a bankruptcy petition for two years, alleging a
pattern of bad faith filings. Appellants opposed the motion,
but the bankruptcy court ultimately imposed a one-year bar
after finding cause based on Appellants’ history of filings
and conduct in the instant case.
 Appellants moved for reconsideration of the refiling bar
orders, arguing that this type of sanction is statutorily capped
at 180 days pursuant to 11 U.S.C. § 349(a) and § 109(g). 11
U.S.C. § 349(a) states:

 Unless the court, for cause, orders otherwise,
 the dismissal of a case under this title does
 not bar the discharge, in a later case under this
 title, of debts that were dischargeable in the
 case dismissed; nor does the dismissal of a
 case under this title prejudice the debtor with
 regard to the filing of a subsequent petition
  SRINIVASAN V. MILESTONE FINANCIAL, LLC 9

 under this title, except as provided in section
 109(g) of this title.

11 U.S.C. § 349(a).
Section 109(g) then specifies that:

 Notwithstanding any other provision of this
 section, no individual or family farmer may
 be a debtor under this title who has been a
 debtor in a case pending under this title at any
 time in the preceding 180 days if-- (1) the
 case was dismissed by the court for willful
 failure of the debtor to abide by orders of the
 court, or to appear before the court in proper
 prosecution of the case; or (2) the debtor
 requested and obtained the voluntary
 dismissal of the case following the filing of a
 request for relief from the automatic stay
 provided by section 362 of this title.

11 U.S.C. § 109(g).
 Appellants again did not appear at the scheduled hearing
on their motions, and the bankruptcy court denied their
motions.
 Appellants timely appealed the bankruptcy court’s
orders issuing the refiling bar and

leads.text:
COURT OF APPEALS OF VIRGINIA 
Record No. 0736-24-4 
ELDRIDGE BOLLING, III 
v. 
CH REALTY VI–ALLIANCE MF ALEXANDRIA VAN DORN, L.L.C., ET AL. 
Present: Judges Beales, Causey and White 
Argued at Alexandria, Virginia 
Opinion Issued November 4, 2026* 
FROM THE CIRCUIT COURT OF THE CITY OF ALEXANDRIA 
Alfred D. Swersky, Judge Designate 
Richard S. Toikka (Wilt Toikka Kraft, LLP, on briefs), for appellant. 
Drew Marrocco (Denton US LLP, on brief), for appellee CH Realty VI–Alliance MF Alexandria 
Van Dorn, L.L.C. 
Amy M. Heerink (Leslie Paul Machado; O’Hagan Meyer, PLLC, on brief), for appellee 
Combined Van Dorn Towers, LLC. 
MEMORANDUM OPINION BY 
JUDGE DORIS HENDERSON CAUSEY 
 On April 1, 2024, a jury trial commenced on two claims brought by Eldridge Bolling, III 
against his former landlords, CH Realty VI–Alliance MF Alexandria V an Dorn, L.L.C. (CH Realty) 
and Combined V an Dorn Towers, L.L.C. (V an Dorn). Bolling had brought claims for retaliation 
under the Virginia Residential Landlord Tenant Act (VRLTA), Code § 55.1-1258, and racial 
discrimination under the Virginia Fair Housing Law (VFHL), Code § 36-96.3(A)(2). After the 
conclusion of Bolling’s presentation of evidence, both defendants moved to strike. The circuit court 
granted both motions. 

* This opinion is not designated for publication. See Code § 17.1-413(A). 
 - 2 - 
 On appeal, Bolling argues that the circuit court erred because he presented sufficient 
evidence to create a jury issue on his two claims. For the following reasons, we reverse and 
remand for further proceedings. 
BACKGROUND1 
 In February 2018, Bolling signed a residential lease for a unit in an apartment building in 
Alexandria, Virginia owned by CH Realty. Within months of moving in, Bolling learned of pest 
problems in the building, including an infestation of mice in his apartment and an infestation of 
bedbugs in the units of numerous fellow tenants. 
 Bolling raised concerns over the infestation with CH Realty’s building manager, Michelle 
Prasasouk. As Bolling testified, Prasasouk did “basically nothing” to fix the issue. Additionally, 
she responded by making comments to and about Bolling, referring to him as “you people” while 
“shak[ing] her head and laugh[ing].” Bolling, who is African American, informed her that he 
found these comments racist. In response, Prasasouk “switched up and would say ‘your kind.’” 
CH Realty did not fire or otherwise prevent Prasasouk from using these racial epithets, despite 
Bolling’s complaints. 
 Around September 2018, roughly two months after Bolling became aware of the 
infestation, Bolling contacted multiple governmental agencies to complain about the issue and 
CH Realty’s inaction. These agencies included the City of Alexandria’s Department of Code 
Administration, Housing Authority, and Health Department. Finally, on November 20, 2018, 

1 “According to well-settled principles of appellate review, when the evidence has been 
struck at the conclusion of the plaintiff’s case-in-chief, we will recite the facts in the light most 
favorable to the plaintiff.” Perdieu v. Blackstone Fam. Prac. Ctr., 264 Va. 408, 411 (2002) 
(citing Bryan v. Burt, 254 Va. 28, 30-31 (1997)). 
 - 3 - 
Bolling filed a Tenant’s Assertion lawsuit against CH Realty in general district court. In that suit, 
Bolling sought an abatement of rent, effective September 16, 2018.2 
Events During the Pendency of Bolling’ s Tenant’ s Assertion Suit 
 After filing his Tenant’s Assertion claim, Bolling began paying rent into escrow with the 
general district court. However, CH Realty soon began posting late payment notices3 on 
Bolling’s door. Bolling asked Prasasouk why CH Realty was issuing him these late notices 
despite his payments into escrow being legally required.4 CH Realty’s response to Bolling was 
that “[u]ntil it’s in the management office, you’re late.” 
 Bolling continued to have conversations with Prasasouk about the late payment notices. 
During one such conversation, less than one week after Bolling filed the Tenant’s Assertion, 
Prasasouk abruptly began “screaming” the words, “‘You’re threatening me,’ at the top of her 
lungs.” Bolling recalled that he was taken off guard by this and that other witnesses to the 
interaction appeared shocked. When Prasasouk reached for her phone, Bolling believed that she 
was going to call the police and, so, he went back to his unit and called the police himself. The 
police report confirmed that Bolling provided the same account to the police that he did at trial 
and that both parties were advised that the issue was civil in nature. 

2 One remedy in a Tenant’s Assertion suit is for the court to order “that the amount of 
rent, whether paid into the escrow account or paid to the landlord, be abated as determined by the 
court in such an amount as may be equitable to represent the existence of any condition found by 
the court to exist.” Code § 55.1-1244(D)(4). 

3 The record does not state whether these notices included language of lease termination 
under Code § 55.1-1245(F). Bolling does not argue that these notices, in themselves, made out a 
claim for retaliation under Code § 55.1-1258, so this omission in the record is not significant to 
our analysis. 

4 Under Code § 55.1-1244(B)(2), a tenant must pay rent into escrow to maintain a 
Tenant’s Assertion suit. 
 - 4 - 
 On December 3, 2018, less than one week after this interaction, CH Realty served 
Bolling with a notice entitled “Notice to Cure or Vacate.” The notice alleged that Bolling had 
violated his lease by “repeatedly” interacting with “management and other staff members” in a 
“loud, demeaning, disrespectful, rude and offensive” manner, thereby “disrupting the conduct of 
their business.” The notice stated that if Bolling did not remedy the alleged lease violations 
within 21 days, his lease would terminate in 30 days. At that point, it said, Bolling would be 
required to “vacate the premises and surrender them to the landlord.” If Bolling did not vacate, 
CH Realty would “proceed with legal action.”5 
 On December 5, 2018, Bolling wrote a letter to CH Realty’s counsel, stating that he 
“categorically den[ied] the allegation[s]” in the notice. Later, at trial, Bolling unequivocally 
stated regarding those allegations, “I did none of this.” 
 Despite Bolling’s requests, CH Realty continued to place the late payment notices on 
Bolling’s door, multiple times per month, throughout the pendency of Bolling’s Tenant’s 
Assertion suit. During this period, Bolling recalled, Prasasouk, using her contacts as the building 
manager, discussed Bolling’s personal information with other tenants in the building without his 
consent, including information regarding “the state of [his] tenancy.”6 
 In January 2019, while Bolling’s tenant’s assertion suit was still pending, CH Realty 
declined Bolling’s request to renew his year-long lease. CH Realty’s legal counsel sent an email 

5 Prior to terminating a lease due to a tenant’s “material noncompliance by [a] tenant 
materially affecting health and safety,” a landlord must provide the tenant with a notice that (a) 
“specif[ies] the acts and omissions constituting the breach” and (b) “stat[es] that the rental 
agreement will terminate upon a date not less than 30 days after receipt of the notice if the breach 
is not remedied in 21 days and that the rental agreement shall terminate as provided in the 
notice.” Code § 55.1-1245. 

6 Code § 55.1-1209 states that “[n]o landlord or managing agent shall release information 
about a tenant or prospective tenant in the possession of the landlord or managing agent to a third 
party,” subject to certain defined exceptions. 
 - 5 - 
informing Bolling that it “would be willing” to allow him to move out of his unit after the 
expiration of his lease rather than requiring him to pay an increased month-to-month rate. 
Bolling’s counsel responded by email that Bolling was “very puzzled” by the message because 
Bolling had sent repeated, timely requests to renew his lease, to which he received no reply. In 
response, CH Realty’s counsel urged that Bolling “plan to move on.” 
The General District Court’ s Judgment and Its Aftermath 
 On February 7, 2019, the general district court rendered judgment in favor of Bolling on 
his Tenant’s Assertion claim. The court granted Bolling $1,567.75 in partial abatement of his 
rent, plus over $1,500 in attorney fees and court costs. The court also made a finding that CH 
Realty’s continued placement of late payment notices on Bolling’s door was in retaliation for 
Bolling’s filing the Tenant’s Assertion.7 
 Immediately after the court rendered judgment, CH Realty’s counsel advised Bolling, in 
person, that CH Realty wanted Bolling to vacate the unit. CH Realty also continued to decline 
Bolling’s requests to renew his original one-year lease, so Bolling’s lease converted to a month-
to-month tenancy. 
 Between March and May 2019, CH Realty prevented Bolling from paying rent through 
its online portal. He was instead required to pay his rent by obtaining a certified check from a 
bank. Additionally, during this general period, Bolling also began noticing that his name would 
be “scratched off the list” of tenants in line to obtain pest control services. On some occasions, 
this caused pest control not to service his unit. 

7 As a court not of record, the general district court’s findings are not generally available 
for appellate court review. Here, however, the evidence before the court in this case included a 
letter written by CH Realty’s counsel, in which he noted that the general district court rendered 
the above-mentioned finding. 
 - 6 - 
 In one instance, police officers responded to Bolling’s apartment and told Bolling that CH 
Realty had reported a smell of marijuana coming from his apartment. Per Bolling’s testimony, 
this report was false. In another instance, in November 2019, Bolling’s landlord8 advised a 
fellow tenant whose car was vandalized that the vandal had likely been looking for Bolling’s car. 
As Bolling testified, he found this allegation incredible due to the distance between the two 
vehicles and their dissimilar appearances. 
Van Dorn’ s Period as Landlord 
 The record indicates that Van Dorn became the owner of the building in either November 
or December 2019. 
 Bolling testified that he and another tenant, Mona Atari, a white woman, had several 
negative encounters while Van Dorn managed the property.9 First, on December 4, 2019, Atari 
attempted to physically block Bolling from entering the elevator with her, claiming that the 
elevator was “not working.” Bolling, nevertheless, entered the elevator, which in fact operated 
as normal. Bolling sent an email that night to Van Dorn staff reporting the incident. He also sent 
a follow-up email in which he asked, “Will someone please inform her that I found this behavior 
to be reprehensible and unacceptable.” Over the ensuing days, Bolling sent multiple follow-up 
emails about the incident and requested that a copy of his letter be sent to Atari. According to 
Bolling, Van Dorn ignored Bolling’s repeated complaints and never took any action regarding the 
incident. 

8 The record is not entirely clear when ownership of the building changed hands. 
However, this singular incident is not essential to our decision in this case. 

9 Bolling testified that Atari asked Bolling to serve as a witness in a slip-and-fall case she 
was planning to bring against CH Realty, and Bolling refused because, as a witness, she wanted 
him to lie for her. Bolling noted that, from his point of view, many of her actions were in 
response to this initial engagement between them. 
 - 7 - 
On December 10, 2019, Van Dorn staff member, Brandon Cook, called 911 after Atari 
told Cook that Bolling approached her in the parking lot, the two exchanged words, and she felt 
“threatened.” Van Dorn called the police on Bolling. After investigating the event, police

DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL OF FLORIDA
 SECOND DISTRICT

 THE BANK OF NEW YORK MELLON f/k/a THE BANK OF NEW
 YORK AS TRUSTEE FOR THE BENEFIT OF THE CERTIFICATE
 HOLDERS OF THE CWABS INC. ASSET-BACKED
 CERTIFICATES, SERIES 2007-BC3,

 Appellant,

 v.

 MICHAEL FERNANDEZ and DIANNA FERNANDEZ,

 Appellees.

 No. 2D2025-1819

 November 4, 2026

Appeal from the Circuit Court for Hillsborough County; Jennifer X.
Gabbard, Judge.

Eric M. Levine and Adam G. Schwartz of Atlas | Solomon LLP, Stuart, for

Alan Borden of Debt Relief Legal Group, LLC, Tampa, for Appellees.

GUARD, Judge.
 The Bank of New York Mellon (Bank) appeals an adverse final
judgment denying its foreclosure of a mortgage based on a failure to
prove a default. Because the undisputed evidence at trial was that
Michael and Dianna Fernandez had not made a payment since June
2017 and no defense allowed them to stop paying their mortgage, we
reverse.
  I.
 In 2007, the Fernandezes executed a $160,000 note secured by a
mortgage on their home. In 2012, the Fernandezes filed Chapter 13
bankruptcy. During that bankruptcy, the Fernandezes entered a
modification agreement with the then servicer of their loan, modifying the
terms of their mortgage. Then, on August 21, 2015, Bank of America,
N.A. (Bank of America), who was the Bank's servicer at that time,
reversed four previous payments made in 2015. While a Bank of
America payment history shows those reversals, the payment history
contains no explanation of why those payments were reversed. At trial,
the Bank's witness was unable to testify regarding the reason for the
reversals other than to speculate about what would normally cause such
reversals. At trial, Dianna Fernandez testified that she made the
reversed payments and that funds for those payments were never
returned to her.
 The effect of the reversals was that it placed the Fernandezes' loan
in default by four payments. Despite that fact, from August 2015
through April 2017, the Fernandezes continued to make their monthly
payments, and Bank of America accepted those payments. In May 2017,
Bank of America returned the Fernandezes' May 2017 payment because
it was for less than the total amount owed as it did not include the four
reversed payments. Approximately two times in or around May 2017,
Dianna Fernandez went into a Bank of America branch and attempted to
make a single mortgage payment. Bank of America refused to take those
payments. That same year, Bank of America sued to foreclose on the
loan but voluntarily dismissed its case before trial.
 In January 2021, the Bank sought again to foreclose on the
Fernandezes' home. In its complaint, the Bank alleged that "[t]here has

 been a default under the note and mortgage, as modified, held by
Plaintiff in that the payment due January 1, 2017, and all subsequent
payments have not been made." The January 1, 2017, date in the
complaint was only accurate if the four reversed payments should have
been reversed. At trial, evidence and testimony showed that the last
payment the Fernandezes made was in May 2017. Though, Bank of
America returned that payment. Dianna Fernandez admitted that their
last accepted payment was made in April 2017. She also admitted that
they did not have sufficient funds to bring the mortgage current when
the action was filed. In their answer and affirmative defenses, the
Fernandezes asserted one defense relevant to this appeal. In their
second affirmative defense, the Fernandezes alleged:

 The trial court did not cite any authority, and it is unclear whether
it relied on the Fernandezes' second affirmative defense in reaching its
conclusion or something else. The Bank timely appealed.
 II.
 As explained below, we conclude that there was legally sufficient
evidence that the Fernandezes defaulted on the note and mortgage after
May 2017. We also hold that, under these circumstances, the Bank's
failure to accept the May 2017 payment did not excuse the Fernandezes
from their ongoing obligations under the note and mortgage. A dispute
over the proper accounting of payments with a bank or servicer does not,
without more, excuse a borrower's obligation to make timely payments.
On remand, the trial court should remove the principal amount of the
four reversed payments, interest before June 2017, and any fees claimed
against the Fernandezes before July 2017. Also, because the main issue
litigated below concerned the four reversed payments, the trial court may
reduce any attorney's fees awarded by the amounts spent litigating the
four reversed payments.
 A.
 This case reaches us after a bench trial. We have held that we
review the legal conclusions of a trial court after a bench trial de novo.
Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v. Dias, 331 So. 3d 755, 760 (Fla. 2d DCA 2021)
 4
 (quoting Jasser v. Saadeh, 91 So. 3d 883, 884 (Fla. 4th DCA 2012)). We
also have stated that we review the legal sufficiency of the evidence in a
civil, nonjury trial de novo. Mace v. M&T Bank, 292 So. 3d 1215, 1219
(Fla. 2d DCA 2020) (citing Norman v. Padgett, 125 So. 3d 977, 978 (Fla.
4th DCA 2013)). We have explained that legally sufficient evidence is
equal to competent substantial evidence. Id. We have further
commented that the competent substantial evidence standard is met
when there is properly admitted evidence that has "a 'definite probative
value.' " Id. (quoting Savage v. State, 120 So. 3d 619, 621 (Fla. 2d DCA
2013)).
 B.
 To be entitled to foreclose a mortgage, a lender must prove (1) an
agreement, (2) a default, (3) a proper acceleration, and (4) the amount
owed or due. Ernest v. Carter, 368 So. 2d 428, 429 (Fla. 2d DCA 1979).
The trial court found that the bank failed to prove the second element, a
default. Each failed monthly payment is a separate default. Bartram v.
U.S. Bank Nat'l. Ass'n, 211 So. 3d 1009, 1021-22 (Fla. 2016) (holding
each new default is a separate cause of action for statute of limitations
purposes); Singleton v. Greymar Assocs., 882 So. 2d 1004, 1006-07 (Fla.
2004) (concluding that a second foreclosure action founded on
subsequent, different default was not barred by dismissal of a prior
action); U.S. Bank Home Mortg. v. Boivin, 403 So. 3d 421, 427-28 (Fla. 2d
DCA 2025) (discussing the interplay between the separate, subsequent
default concept and a laches defense); Grdic v. HSBC Bank USA, N.A. as
Tr. for Registered Holders of Ace Secs. Corp., 267 So. 3d 473, 476 (Fla. 2d
DCA 2019) (examining when statute of limitations runs in a foreclosure
action when subsequent defaults occur). Putting aside for the moment
the four reversed payments, the Bank presented legally sufficient

 5
 evidence that the Fernandezes failed to make payment and were in
default from June 2017 onwards.
 In Lunn Woods v. Lowery, this court dealt with a foreclosure appeal
not dissimilar to this appeal. See 577 So. 2d 705, 706 (Fla. 2d DCA
1991). In that case, a plaintiff sought to foreclose a security interest
under an agreement for deed. Id. In its complaint, the plaintiff sought to
foreclose based on both a failure to make payments and to timely pay
real estate taxes. Id. At trial, the defendant proved that the plaintiff had
misapplied payments and no payments were missed. See id. But the
evidence showed that the defendant failed to timely pay the taxes. Id.
The trial court denied the foreclosure. Id. We reversed. Id. In reversing,
we stated that "despite the court having found an improper application of
payments, it was error to deny foreclosure on that basis since there was
uncontradicted evidence of [the defendant's] breach of the covenant to
pay real estate taxes and assessments." Id. at 707 (citing Heimer v.
Albion Realty & Mortg. Inc., 300 So. 2d 31 (Fla. 3d DCA 1974)).
 Here, the Bank alleged a continuing default from January 2017
forward. The dispute at trial centered over the four reversed payments
from 2015, ignoring the missed payments from June 2017 onwards.
While the trial court found—and the record supports—that the
Fernandezes paid and did not have returned the four 2015 payments,
that result does not change the failure to pay every month from June
2017 forward. Each of those missed payments was a separate default
that entitled the Bank to a foreclosure, and the trial court's conclusion to
the contrary is erroneous.
 C.
 That brings us to whether there was a basis, equitable or
otherwise, for the trial court to deny the Bank's right to foreclose. The

 6
 final judgment itself does not state any legal basis on which the trial
court relied. That is not surprising given neither party argued any such
basis with precision at trial. What we are left with in the final judgment
is a finding that "Defendants['] May 2017 payment was returned by the
Plaintiff, and subsequent attempts to pay directly at the servicer, Bank of
America, were not accepted after May 2017." Those facts alone do not
excuse the subsequent defaults by the Fernandezes. It was only after the
trial court entered final judgment that various defenses and equitable
principles were raised by the Bank in its motion for rehearing to the trial
court. The trial court denied the Bank's motion for rehearing without
any analysis.
 We have recognized that foreclosure can be refused by a trial court
where (1) the mortgagee waives or is estopped from accelerating because
of misconduct or unfulfilled conditions, (2) the mortgagor tenders
payment after default but before acceleration, or (3) the mortgagor's
failure to make timely payments was stopped by a misunderstanding or
excusable neglect coupled with some misconduct by the mortgagee which
contributed to the default. Lunn Woods, 577 So. 2d at 707 (citing
Campbell v. Werner, 232 So. 2d 252 (Fla. 3d DCA 1970)); see also David
v. Sun Fed. Sav. & Loan Ass'n, 461 So. 2d 93, 96 (Fla. 1984) (refusing to
prevent a foreclosure without one of those three "established principles of
equity" being proven). While not clearly under either the Fernandezes'
second affirmative defense or the trial court's findings, the second and
third equitable principles above are close enough to both to cause us to
analyze whether either was proven.
